A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
A.q: A 55-year-old woman has a new pigmented longitudinal band in the nail of one thumb that has widened over six months and is broader proximally than distally. Pigment extends onto the proximal nail fold. What is the concern, and what is the sign at the nail fold called?
opts: Onychomycosis
Onychomycosis produces thickening, crumbling, debris, and onycholysis rather than a discrete pigmented longitudinal band with periungual extension.
Subungual haematoma

Subungual haematoma is on the melanoma differential and does migrate distally as the nail grows, which is what distinguishes it. A band that is widening proximally over months is behaving in the opposite way.
Nail unit melanoma; Hutchinson sign

Correct. New or evolving longitudinal melanonychia in one digit with increasing width, irregular colour or spacing, and proximal widening or a triangular shape raises nail unit melanoma. Pigment on the periungual skin is Hutchinson sign, and the thumb and great toe are high-yield sites.
Benign longitudinal melanonychia
Benign longitudinal melanonychia appears on the differential, and single-digit involvement with proximal widening is the pattern that argues against it.
A.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 84

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
A.q: A 44-year-old man has a purulent collection in the axilla at the site of an old puncture wound, and a student asks how this differs from a furuncle. How does a cutaneous abscess differ in origin from a furuncle?
opts: Abscess is superficial; furuncle epidermal
Both are deep. An abscess involves the dermis and deeper tissues and a furuncle involves the follicle and adjacent subcutaneous tissue; epidermal infection describes impetigo.
Abscess is sterile; furuncle infected
An abscess is a collection of purulent material from bacterial infection. A sterile neutrophilic collection would raise pyoderma gangrenosum instead.
Abscess from inoculation; furuncle from a follicle

Correct. An abscess is a collection of purulent material within the dermis and deeper tissues, often due to traumatic inoculation of bacteria into the skin, compared with furuncles, which arise from infected hair follicles.
Abscess involves apocrine, furuncle eccrine glands
Apocrine gland inflammation describes hidradenitis suppurativa. Neither an abscess nor a furuncle is defined by eccrine involvement.
A.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 113

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
A.q: A 40-year-old man whose brother died of melanoma asks how to monitor his own skin between annual clinic visits. What should patients be taught about melanoma self-examination?
opts: Monthly, including scalp, palms, soles, nails

Correct. Patients should perform monthly self-examination using ABCDE and ugly-duckling principles, including the scalp, back, palms, soles, and nails, with prompt assessment of evolution, bleeding, or ulceration.
Annually, limited to sun-exposed skin
Restricting examination to sun-exposed sites would miss acral lentiginous and nail unit melanoma, which occur on palms, soles, and nail units and are not clearly ultraviolet driven.
Report only lesions over 6 mm
Diameter is one letter of the rule; evolution, asymmetry, border, and colour all warrant assessment regardless of size.
Focus on counting total naevi
Naevus count contributes to risk assessment, but the self-examination principles are about recognising the lesion that differs from its neighbours and that is changing.
A.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 56

A.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
A.q: A 25-year-old woman with several common warts on the hands asks whether treatment will get rid of the virus for good. What treatment principle applies to all cutaneous warts?
opts: Cryotherapy eradicates it and prevents recurrence

Cryotherapy is a treatment option but does not eradicate the virus, and it may cause pain, blistering, and pigment change. Promising eradication sets up the patient for a recurrence they were told could not happen.
Treat all warts at diagnosis
Observation is reasonable because many warts resolve spontaneously, and plantar warts specifically do not require therapy unless painful.
Biopsy every wart first
Biopsy is generally unnecessary and is reserved for atypical, bleeding, ulcerated, growing, or refractory lesions and for immunocompromised patients.
No therapy eradicates the virus; recurrence happens

Correct. No therapy eradicates human papillomavirus with certainty and recurrence can occur. Treatment is chosen according to location, symptoms, age, pregnancy status, immune status, and the risk of scarring or dyspigmentation, avoiding excessive freezing or destruction.
A.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 149

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
A.q: A 64-year-old man has newly diagnosed mycosis fungoides confined to patches and plaques on the trunk, and his family asks why he has not been offered chemotherapy. What is the treatment philosophy in mycosis fungoides?
opts: No treatment at any stage
The disease may remain confined to skin for years or decades, which makes indolence a real feature, but stage-directed skin-directed treatment is offered rather than nothing.
Immediate combination chemotherapy
This is precisely the approach the lecture warns against, since aggressive early therapy has not been shown to cure or prevent progression and carries a real risk of harm.
Indefinite high-dose corticosteroids
Indefinite systemic corticosteroids are not the described management and would carry substantial cumulative toxicity.
Stage-directed, skin-directed therapy

Correct. Management is complex. Early aggressive treatment has not been proven to cure disease or prevent progression, and overly aggressive therapy may cause complications and premature death, so treatment is stage-directed and skin-directed.
A.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 75

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
A.q: A 15-year-old boy presents with facial lesions. Examination shows open and closed comedones across the forehead and nose with no papules, pustules, or nodules. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
opts: A topical retinoid combined with an oral antibiotic

Adding an oral antibiotic is the regimen for moderate papulopustular and mixed acne, and requires inflammatory lesions to justify it. This patient has none, so the antibiotic has no inflammatory target and adds resistance risk.
An oral contraceptive pill
Oral contraceptives are considered for patients with hyperandrogenism or when acne is unresponsive to both topical retinoids and antibiotics. They are also not an option for a male patient.
A topical retinoid

Correct. For comedonal, non-inflammatory acne the guideline is a topical retinoid, which is comedolytic and anti-inflammatory and normalises the follicular hyperkeratinisation. If it is not tolerated, azelaic acid or salicylic acid may be substituted.
Topical benzoyl peroxide alone

Benzoyl peroxide is a first-line drug especially for mild acne and suppresses Cutibacterium acnes, but its role is antimicrobial and keratolytic rather than primarily comedolytic. The retinoid is the agent named for comedonal disease.
A.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 32

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
A.q: A 6-year-old girl had impetigo three weeks ago. She now presents with facial oedema, tea-coloured urine, and hypertension. Her mother asks whether the antibiotics failed. What is the most accurate explanation?
opts: Glomerulonephritis; antibiotics do not prevent it

Correct. Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis may follow impetigo, especially in 3 to 7 year olds, and is characterised by sudden oedema, haematuria, and hypertension. Antibiotics do not prevent it because activation of the immune response most often precedes antibiotic treatment.
Glomerulonephritis; earlier antibiotics would have
The diagnosis is right but the causal claim is wrong, and it wrongly assigns blame to the treatment. The immune activation precedes antibiotics, which is exactly why they do not prevent it.
Treatment failure needing a new antibiotic
The skin infection has resolved; this is a delayed immune-mediated renal complication rather than persistent bacterial infection. Changing antibiotics would not address it.
Rheumatic fever after the skin infection
Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is the complication named as following impetigo, and its features are renal rather than cardiac or articular.
A.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 97

A.io: 11 — Identify medical care strategies for pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions for adult and elderly populations
A.q: A 72-year-old woman has more than twenty rough scaly papules scattered across a bald, sun-damaged scalp, with no single lesion standing out from the rest. When is field-directed rather than lesion-directed therapy indicated for actinic keratoses?
opts: When a single lesion has clear borders
An isolated lesion with clear borders is precisely the situation in which liquid nitrogen cryotherapy is preferred.
When multiple lesions occupy a field of sun-damaged skin

Correct. Field-directed therapy is indicated when multiple lesions occupy a field of sun-damaged skin, reflecting that chronic ultraviolet injury produces dysplastic change across a field rather than in isolated spots. Lesion-directed cryotherapy is preferred for isolated or few lesions with clear borders.
When the lesion is thick, indurated, and bleeding
Those features raise concern for squamous cell carcinoma and call for biopsy rather than any destructive or topical field therapy.
Only in immunosuppressed patients
Immunosuppression is a referral indication alongside diagnostic uncertainty and high lesion burden, but it is not what defines the choice between lesion-directed and field-directed therapy.
A.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 14

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
A.q: A 58-year-old woman with obesity has multiple soft growths in both axillae and on the neck. How is an acrochordon best described morphologically, and where do they characteristically occur?
opts: A soft pedunculated papilloma in areas of friction

Correct. An acrochordon is a fibroepithelial pedunculated papilloma with a narrow stalk and broad tip, occurring in areas of friction — the neck, axilla, and groin. Incidence is increased in women and in obesity, and they vary from over 1 mm to as large as 10 mm.
A firm nodule with a keratin core on the sole
A central keratin core on a weight-bearing surface describes a clavus, which results from localised mechanical pressure.
A hard conical keratotic projection
A hard conical keratotic projection is a cutaneous horn, which arises from an underlying benign or malignant lesion.
A bright red friable papule that bleeds
A bright red friable pedunculated papule that bleeds readily after trauma describes pyogenic granuloma.
A.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 30

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
A.q: A 23-year-old woman has a firm, bulbous nodule at the site of an ear piercing done two years ago. It extends well beyond the original piercing site and has continued to enlarge, with occasional itching. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Foreign-body granuloma
A foreign-body granuloma is on the differential but forms around retained material and does not enlarge progressively over years beyond the wound.
Dermatofibroma
Dermatofibroma is a firm dermal nodule with a brown halo and a dimple sign, most commonly on the legs, and it is not related to a wound.
Keloid
Correct. A keloid is a fibroproliferative overgrowth of dense fibrous tissue that extends BEYOND the wound margins, develops slowly, continues to enlarge for months to years, and shows no regression.
Hypertrophic scar
A hypertrophic scar develops rapidly within four weeks, remains confined within the original wound margins, and flattens with time — the opposite of this course.
A.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 13

A.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
A.q: A 41-year-old janitorial supervisor reports several weeks of progressively dry, sore hands. She washes her hands frequently and handles detergents and cleaning solutions throughout her shift. Examination shows a glazed, well-demarcated erythematous eruption with scaling over the dorsal hands and distal forearms, ending abruptly at the wrists. She denies any new jewellery, gloves, cosmetics, or topical products, and patch testing performed previously was negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Allergic contact dermatitis

Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction to a specific allergen, and patch testing is the test that diagnoses it. Her patch testing was negative and she denies any new gloves, jewellery, or topical products, which removes the allergen this diagnosis requires.
Atopic dermatitis of the hands

Adult atopic dermatitis affects the hands, but it requires a personal or family history of atopy and produces poorly demarcated lichenified plaques. The sharply demarcated, glazed eruption ending at the wrists follows an exposure boundary rather than an atopic distribution.
Irritant contact dermatitis

Correct. Irritant contact dermatitis is the most common form of contact dermatitis and results from chemicals or friction that disrupt the skin barrier. It is frequently occupational, with healthcare and janitorial workers cited as the classic examples, and mild irritants such as soaps produce subacute symptoms progressing over weeks. Hands and forearms are the commonest sites.
Dyshidrotic eczema

Dyshidrotic eczema produces crops of intensely pruritic deep-seated vesicles on the palms, lateral fingers, and soles that desiccate and desquamate over weeks. There are no vesicles here, and the eruption is on the dorsal rather than palmar surface.
A.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 80

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
A.q: A 17-year-old girl has moderate papulopustular and mixed acne of the face and upper back that has not responded to eight weeks of a topical antimicrobial. What regimen is recommended?
opts: A topical retinoid and an oral antibiotic

Two-thirds correct, and the missing third matters: benzoyl peroxide is recommended alongside antibiotic therapy to reduce resistance. Omitting it is the commonest way a correct-looking regimen goes wrong.
A topical retinoid alone
A topical retinoid alone is the regimen for comedonal disease. Moderate inflammatory acne that has already failed topical therapy needs systemic treatment added.
An oral antibiotic alone, indefinitely

Oral antibiotics should be prescribed for the shortest time necessary, and monotherapy without benzoyl peroxide invites resistance in Cutibacterium acnes. It also leaves the follicular hyperkeratinisation untreated.
A retinoid, an oral antibiotic, benzoyl peroxide

Correct. Moderate papulopustular and mixed acne is treated with a topical retinoid and an oral antibiotic and topical benzoyl peroxide. Benzoyl peroxide is specifically added whenever an antibiotic is used, to reduce the risk of bacterial resistance.
A.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 33

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
A.q: A 58-year-old man with diabetes has an extremely painful lesion on the back of the neck with malaise, chills, and a fever of 38.5 degrees Celsius. Examination shows a deep indurated plaque with several separate openings draining pus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Hidradenitis suppurativa
Hidradenitis suppurativa affects apocrine-bearing skin of the axilla, groin, breasts, and perineum with recurrence more than twice in six months, not the posterior neck acutely.
Cellulitis
Cellulitis produces spreading erythema, warmth, and tenderness with indistinct borders and no discrete draining openings.
Carbuncle

Correct. A carbuncle is two or more confluent furuncles arising in several hair follicles with separate heads, and systemic symptoms of malaise, chills, and fever are more common with a carbuncle than a furuncle.
Cutaneous abscess
An abscess follows traumatic inoculation of bacteria rather than arising from hair follicles, and it presents as a single collection.
A.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 63

A.io: 6 — Discuss the implications for treatment
A.q: A 67-year-old woman has a probable but unconfirmed diagnosis, and a treatment with meaningful adverse effects is being considered. What factors govern the decision to treat when the diagnosis carries some uncertainty?
opts: The cost of treatment alone
Cost and affordability are recognised barriers to adherence rather than the framework for deciding whether treatment is indicated.
Withhold until the diagnosis is certain
Certainty is often unattainable, and the naturalistic approach treats before a definitive diagnosis in unstable patients specifically because waiting can be harmful.
Probability, success, tolerance, risk-benefit

Correct. The value of treatment versus no treatment is a linear function of the probability of disease, together with the likelihood of success and the ability to tolerate treatment, weighed as risk against benefit.
Probability of disease alone
Probability is one input, but the likelihood of success, tolerability, and the risk-benefit balance all bear on whether treating is worthwhile.
A.cite: 1. svClinical Reasoning and Problem Solving.pptx, Slide 27

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pigmented skin lesions
A.q: A 64-year-old man has multiple light to dark brown macules with well-defined but irregular borders over the shoulders and dorsal hands, tending to coalesce where he has had severe sunburns. They do not fade in winter. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Lentigo maligna
Lentigo maligna is asymmetric with irregular border and colour and darker areas within it, and dermoscopy is essential; it would stand out from its uniform neighbours.
Melasma
Melasma produces symmetric hyperpigmented patches on the face, particularly in women, rather than macules on the shoulders and hands.
Ephelides
Freckles are small light brown symmetric macules 3 to 5 mm that become more pronounced in spring and summer and FADE in winter, in fair-skinned individuals.
Solar lentigo

Correct. Solar lentigines arise from proliferation of basal melanocytes with increased melanin production, strongly associated with older age, sun damage, and tanning. They are well-defined with irregular borders and tend to coalesce at sites of severe sunburn.
A.cite: CMS I Pigmented Skin Lesions - Shahsv-2.pptx, Slide 14

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
A.q: A 21-year-old man presents with sudden pain and swelling over the sacrum in the gluteal cleft. Examination shows a warm, tender, erythematous fluctuant mass with purulent drainage. What is the appropriate management of this acute presentation?
opts: Oral antibiotics alone
An antibiotic will not evacuate a fluctuant collection, and fluctuance is specifically the palpation finding indicating fluid. Drainage is required.
Incision and drainage

Correct. An acute pilonidal abscess requires incision and drainage. The condition arises when a dimple over the coccyx draws in hair and debris leading to follicular plugging, and ingrown hairs prevent drainage and promote abscess formation.
Immediate wide surgical excision of the natal cleft
Definitive excision addresses chronic disease with sinus tracts. It is not the management of an acute abscess presentation.
Magnetic resonance imaging before any intervention
No diagnostic testing is usually needed. Imaging would delay the drainage that relieves the abscess.
A.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 43

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
A.q: A 48-year-old woman with papulopustular rosacea has Demodex-associated disease that has not responded to topical metronidazole. What topical agent is described as superior for this situation?
opts: Brimonidine gel
Brimonidine is a topical vasoconstrictor aimed at the erythema of rosacea rather than at the inflammatory papules and pustules or the mite burden.
Azelaic acid 15 to 20 percent

Azelaic acid is effective for both papulopustular and erythematotelangiectatic rosacea through anti-inflammatory and anti-keratinising effects, so it is a legitimate option. But it is not the agent singled out for Demodex-associated disease.
Ivermectin 1 percent cream

Correct. Ivermectin 1 percent cream is described as superior to metronidazole for Demodex-associated papulopustular rosacea, reflecting the contribution of Demodex folliculorum mite overgrowth to the pathogenesis.
Metronidazole 0.75 to 1 percent gel at a higher frequency

Metronidazole is the first-line topical for papulopustular disease, and it has already failed here. Increasing the frequency of an agent described as inferior for Demodex-associated disease does not address the reason it failed.
A.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 69

A.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
A.q: A 42-year-old man has recurrent poorly demarcated erythematous patches with greasy yellow scale over the scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, and behind both ears. The itching is worse when he sweats. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Seborrheic dermatitis
Correct. Seborrheic dermatitis produces poorly demarcated pruritic erythematous plaques with greasy or yellow scaling at sebum-rich sites, and pruritus is increased by perspiration.
Psoriasis
Scalp psoriasis produces well-demarcated plaques with dry silvery scale rather than greasy yellow scale, and it favours extensor surfaces elsewhere.
Tinea capitis
Tinea capitis is predominantly a disease of preadolescent children and produces scaly patches with hair loss and broken hairs rather than greasy facial scaling.
Atopic dermatitis
Adult atopic dermatitis affects the flexures, hands, neck, face, and eyelids with dry lichenified plaques, and it requires a personal or family history of atopy.
A.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 94

A.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
A.q: A 26-year-old woman has two round, sharply circumscribed, slightly erythematous scaly plaques on the forearm, each with an advancing scaly border and a clearer centre. Where should the specimen for potassium hydroxide microscopy be taken from?
opts: A plucked hair from within the plaque
A plucked hair is used for potassium hydroxide microscopy when dermatophyte folliculitis is suspected. This is a glabrous skin lesion with an advancing scaly edge.
Normal skin adjacent to the lesion
Uninvolved skin contains no organism. Perilesional sampling belongs to direct immunofluorescence in autoimmune blistering disease, not to fungal microscopy.
The centre of the lesion, where the change began
The centre has cleared, which means the organism has moved outward. Sampling there yields the lowest density of fungal elements and produces false negatives.
The active advancing border of the lesion

Correct. The potassium hydroxide specimen is taken from the active border, where the viable organism is concentrated. Culture is added for high clinical suspicion when the potassium hydroxide preparation is negative.
A.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 26

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
A.q: A 46-year-old man in the American Southeast has a painful lesion on the thigh with a central violaceous area surrounded by a rim of blanched skin and then a large area of erythema. What is this sign, and what organism is responsible?
opts: Crowe's sign, from a caterpillar reaction

Crowe's sign is intertriginous freckling in neurofibromatosis type 1, a genetic condition unrelated to envenomation. It describes small pigmented macules of the axillae and groin rather than a necrotic lesion at a bite site.
The red, white, and blue sign, from a black widow spider bite

The sign is correctly named but attributed to the wrong spider. The black widow has a red hourglass on the underside of the abdomen and produces crampy abdominal pain and muscle spasms rather than a necrotic lesion.
Hutchinson sign, from a hobo spider bite

Hutchinson sign is lesions on the tip of the nose in herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Hobo spider bites are painless with induration and paraesthesia and are the predominant cause of necrotic arachnidism in the Pacific Northwest.
The red, white, and blue sign, from a brown recluse spider bite

Correct. The hallmark of a brown recluse bite is the red, white, and blue sign — a central violaceous area surrounded by a rim of blanched skin surrounded by a large erythematous area. Loxosceles reclusa has a dark brown violin-shaped marking on the cephalothorax and is abundant in the American Midwest and Southeast.
A.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 60

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
A.q: A 22-year-old bartender develops streaky, bizarrely shaped erythema and blistering on the forearms two days after an outdoor shift squeezing limes. The affected areas later become hyperpigmented. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Ordinary sunburn

Sunburn occurs without a chemical contactant history and follows the pattern of exposure rather than the drip marks of a liquid. The differential lists it precisely on the grounds of that missing contactant.
Drug-induced phototoxicity

Drug-induced phototoxicity resembles an exaggerated sunburn across sun-exposed skin in a patient taking a systemic drug. No medication is reported, and the streaky distribution reflects topical contact.
Phytophotodermatitis

Correct. Phytophotodermatitis follows contact with furanocoumarins, also called psoralens, found in limes, celery, parsley, and related plants, followed by ultraviolet exposure. The streaky shapes trace where the juice ran, and postinflammatory hyperpigmentation follows.
Allergic contact dermatitis to citrus

Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed hypersensitivity requiring prior sensitisation, and it does not need ultraviolet light to appear. The interaction of the chemical with light is what defines this reaction.
A.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 100

A.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
A.q: A 9-month-old boy is brought in for a diaper rash of one week. Examination shows beefy erythema involving the inguinal folds, with peripheral scale and several small papules and pustules on the thighs a short distance beyond the main area of redness. He completed a course of amoxicillin two weeks ago. What finding most strongly indicates the infectious complication rather than simple irritant disease?
opts: The recent amoxicillin course

Antibiotic exposure genuinely raises the risk and belongs in the history, but it is a risk factor rather than a physical finding. Plenty of infants develop irritant dermatitis after antibiotics without any candidal component.
Scaling at the edge
Peripheral scale accompanies candidal disease, but scaling is also produced by irritant dermatitis, which causes erythema, scaling, papules, or erosions. On its own it does not identify the organism.
Fold involvement with satellites

Correct. Whether the skin folds are involved is the finding that distinguishes irritant from candidal disease. Irritant diaper dermatitis affects the convex surfaces and generally spares the inguinal folds because they are less exposed to urine and feces; candidal disease produces beefy erythema in the folds with satellite papules and pustules.
Erythema in the diaper area
Erythema is common to every form of diaper dermatitis and is the reason the child presented. A finding shared by the irritant and candidal forms alike cannot separate them.
A.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 107

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
A.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with widespread superficial skin peeling and a positive Nikolsky sign but entirely normal mucous membranes. What diagnosis does the preserved mucosa most suggest?
opts: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms
That syndrome presents with rash, fever, eosinophilia, and internal organ involvement rather than superficial epidermal peeling with a positive Nikolsky sign.
Toxic epidermal necrolysis
Toxic epidermal necrolysis produces severe mucosal erosions alongside detachment of more than 30 percent of the body surface area. Preserved mucosa does not fit.
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
Correct. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome spares the mucosa and is toxin-mediated, which is exactly how it is separated from Stevens-Johnson syndrome on the differential.
Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Mucosal erosions are a defining feature of Stevens-Johnson syndrome — the presentation includes erosions of the lips, mouth, and conjunctivae. Entirely normal mucosa argues against it.
A.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 82

A.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
A.q: A 44-year-old woman with a history of plaque psoriasis was given a two-week course of oral prednisone by an urgent care clinician for back pain. Four days after finishing it she develops fever lasting several days followed by the sudden appearance of widespread sheets of small pustules on erythematous skin. She appears unwell. What has most likely occurred?
opts: Acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis from the prednisone

A drug-induced pustular eruption is a reasonable thought, but the temporal relationship here is to steroid withdrawal rather than to steroid exposure, and the patient's established psoriasis supplies the substrate pustular psoriasis requires.
Pustular psoriasis precipitated by systemic steroid withdrawal

Correct. Pustular psoriasis of von Zumbusch type is a rare, severe form associated with other forms of psoriasis and may follow systemic steroid withdrawal. It is abrupt and life-threatening, begins with several days of fever, and is commonly mistaken for bacterial or viral infection.
Impetigo herpetiformis

Impetigo herpetiformis is the pustular psoriasis of pregnancy, occurring typically in the third trimester with erythematous patches whose margins are studded with subcorneal pustules. Nothing indicates this patient is pregnant.
A widespread bacterial skin infection

This is the mistake the lecture warns about explicitly: pustular psoriasis is commonly mistaken for bacterial or viral infection. The context of pre-existing psoriasis and recent systemic steroid withdrawal identifies the true cause.
A.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 160

A.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
A.q: A Wood's lamp examination is performed on a 6-year-old girl with suspected tinea capitis and shows no fluorescence. What is the correct interpretation?
opts: It confirms Microsporum infection
Microsporum is the species a Wood lamp can support, so a negative result argues against it rather than confirming it.
It excludes nothing

Correct. A Wood lamp may rapidly support Microsporum infection, but Trichophyton tonsurans — the most common species — usually does not fluoresce. Confirmation rests on potassium hydroxide microscopy and fungal culture.
It indicates a bacterial cause
Coral-red fluorescence under a Wood's lamp identifies erythrasma, a bacterial infection. Absence of fluorescence says nothing about a bacterial cause on the scalp.
It means oral therapy can be avoided
The route of therapy is determined by the site rather than by fluorescence. Scalp infection requires oral therapy because topical agents do not reach the hair shaft.
A.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 14

A.io: c — Identify medical care strategies for cutaneous viral and fungal infections for infant, child, adolescent, adult and elderly populations
A.q: A 7-year-old girl is being treated for tinea capitis and her school has asked whether she must stay at home. What advice about school attendance and household measures is correct?
opts: No household measures are needed
Transmission occurs from infected persons, pets, fallen hairs, clothing, combs, hats, and furniture, and fungal particles remain viable for months. Fomites matter.
Stay out of school until the scalp is clear
Requiring complete clearance would keep a child out for weeks or months of oral therapy unnecessarily, since exclusion is generally not needed once effective treatment has begun.
No exclusion once treated; do not share hair items

Correct. School exclusion is generally unnecessary once effective treatment has started. Patients should avoid sharing personal hair items and should clean clippers, combs, brushes, bedding, and hats, and household contacts may use a sporicidal shampoo.
All household contacts take oral antifungals
Household contacts may use a sporicidal shampoo rather than systemic therapy, which would expose asymptomatic people to a drug requiring hepatic consideration.
A.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 17

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
A.q: A 54-year-old man with non-purulent cellulitis of the leg is started on cephalexin. Forty-eight hours later he still has fever and the affected area has extended. What should be considered?
opts: Deep vein thrombosis alone
Deep vein thrombosis is on the differential and should be considered, but it would not explain fever with expanding erythema, and it does not carry the surgical urgency of the correct answer.
A normal first-day treatment response

Cellulitis may look and feel worse during the first day as destroyed pathogens release enzymes that increase local inflammation, which makes this genuinely true at 24 hours. But fever usually resolves within 24 hours of antibiotics, and persistence beyond 48 hours demands reassessment.
Allergy to cephalexin
A drug allergy would produce a new pruritic eruption or systemic hypersensitivity features rather than extension of the original infected area with continuing fever.
Necrotizing fasciitis

Correct. The differential specifically states that necrotizing fasciitis should be considered if there is no response to antibiotics within 48 hours. It may initially be diagnosed as cellulitis, with the patient sent home and returning worse.
A.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 108

A.io: 7 — Recall counseling strategies to help patients adhere to treatment plans
A.q: A 58-year-old man with limited health literacy is being offered several treatment options with different risks. Why must clinicians be able to communicate evidence on prognosis, treatment, testing, and prevention effectively?
opts: To ensure patients accept the chosen plan
The purpose is to enable understanding of risks and options rather than to secure compliance with a predetermined decision.
To help patients understand risks and options
Correct. Healthcare providers must be able to effectively communicate evidence on prognosis, treatments, diagnostic testing, and prevention to help patients understand their risks and options.
To shorten the consultation
Effective communication of evidence generally takes time, and time is listed among the limitations of evidence-based practice rather than a benefit.
To transfer the decision to the patient
Helping patients understand risks and options supports shared decision-making rather than abdicating clinical responsibility.
A.cite: 1. svClinical Reasoning and Problem Solving.pptx, Slide 28

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
A.q: A 41-year-old man with a rapidly expanding painful ulcer of the shin is being investigated for an underlying systemic cause. What systemic conditions are most closely associated with pyoderma gangrenosum?
opts: Inflammatory bowel disease and arthritis

Correct. Pyoderma gangrenosum is a neutrophilic dermatosis with dysregulated innate immune activation, and inflammatory bowel disease heads the list of key associated conditions alongside inflammatory arthritis and haematologic disease.
Celiac and autoimmune thyroid disease
Celiac disease and autoimmune thyroid disease are the high-priority associations of dermatitis herpetiformis, for which all patients should be screened for celiac disease.
Diabetes and gastrointestinal malignancy
That set belongs to acanthosis nigricans, where the skin change is a marker of insulin resistance and, in the malignant form, of gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma.
Sarcoidosis and streptococcal infection
Sarcoidosis, in the form of Löfgren syndrome, and group A streptococcal infection are the associations of erythema nodosum.
A.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 57

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
A.q: A 22-year-old man reports six weeks of intense itching that is worst at night. Examination shows excoriated papules with thin thread-like linear burrows in the finger webs, volar wrists, and axillae. His partner has begun to itch as well. The head and neck are spared. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atopic dermatitis
Atopic dermatitis requires a personal or family history of atopy, favours flexures, and does not produce burrows or spread to close contacts.
Bedbug bites
Bedbug bites are painless wheals and papules in linear groups of three on exposed skin, not burrows in the finger webs with nocturnal itch over weeks.
Dermatitis herpetiformis
Dermatitis herpetiformis produces grouped intensely pruritic vesicles on extensor surfaces and shows granular immunoglobulin A deposits rather than burrows.
Scabies

Correct. Scabies produces almost always severe itching with intense nocturnal pruritus appearing 4 to 6 weeks after infestation, favouring the interdigital webs, volar wrists, axillae, and genitals with the head and neck spared. The thread-like burrow is pathognomonic.
A.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 9

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
A.q: A 27-year-old man develops widespread wheals within 20 minutes of eating shellfish. What mechanism underlies this reaction, and what class of trigger does it represent?
opts: Immune complex deposition
Immune complex deposition with vessel damage describes urticarial vasculitis, whose lesions persist beyond 24 hours and leave bruising. This reaction is immediate and transient.
A delayed type IV reaction
A delayed cell-mediated reaction takes days rather than 20 minutes and produces dermatitis rather than transient wheals. That mechanism belongs to allergic contact dermatitis.
Immunoglobulin E mediated, an immunologic trigger

Correct. Urticaria results from mast cell degranulation releasing histamine, prostaglandins, and leukotrienes, producing transient dermal oedema. Immunologic immunoglobulin E mediated triggers include foods such as shellfish, nuts, and eggs, drugs including penicillin, and insect stings.
Immunoglobulin E mediated, a non-immunologic trigger

The mechanism is right but the classification contradicts it — an immunoglobulin E mediated reaction is by definition immunologic. Non-immunologic triggers act on mast cells directly without antibody involvement.
A.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 36

A.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
A.q: A 62-year-old woman has a chronic plaque on the ankle showing thickening and hardening of the skin with exaggerated surface markings, and adjacent skin showing accumulation of loose grey-white cornified fragments. What are these two secondary changes called?
opts: Scaling and lichenification, respectively
The two terms are correct but assigned to the wrong findings. Reversing them would describe the thickened plaque as a surface scale and understate the chronicity the lichenification records.
Lichenification and scaling, respectively
Correct. Lichenification is thickening and hardening of the skin, and scaling is accumulation of loose or adherent cornified fragments of the epidermis, typically grey or white.
Excoriation and crust, respectively
An excoriation is a scratch or abrasion where the top layer of skin wears off, and crust is dried serum. Neither describes epidermal thickening or cornified accumulation.
Erosion and ulceration, respectively
Erosion is partial loss of the epidermis and ulceration is full-thickness loss extending to the dermis or deeper. Both are losses of tissue, whereas the findings described are additive.
A.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 18

A.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
A.q: A 79-year-old man has severe xerosis of both lower legs and a barrier preparation is being chosen for him. What consideration should guide the choice of vehicle?
opts: Avoid occlusive vehicles in xerosis
Occlusion is what retains water in the stratum corneum, which is exactly what impaired hydration in xerosis requires. A thick ointment applied within minutes of bathing is the recommended approach.
Lotions are the most occlusive
This reverses the ranking. Lotions have the highest water content and the least occlusive effect, so choosing one for severe xerosis gives the least barrier protection of the three.
Ointments are more occlusive than creams

Correct. Emollients and barrier preparations are the foundation of treatment for many inflammatory conditions, and ointments are generally more occlusive than creams or lotions. Common uses include xerosis, eczema, irritant dermatitis, and diaper dermatitis.
Creams and ointments are equally occlusive
Vehicle choice has a real effect on occlusion and therefore on barrier repair. Treating it as cosmetic discards a genuine therapeutic lever.
A.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 40

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
A.q: An 8-year-old boy develops multiple erythematous papules arranged in linear streaks after handling a caterpillar. What is the term for the aggregate of medical effects caused by caterpillars, moths, and butterflies?
opts: Cercarial dermatitis
Cercarial dermatitis follows exposure to cercaria-infested water and is managed symptomatically with antihistamines and oatmeal baths.
Erucism

Erucism is the specific caterpillar dermatitis rather than the umbrella term, and management extends beyond corticosteroids to antihistamines, topical menthol or camphor preparations, analgesia, and hair removal.
Arachnidism
Necrotic arachnidism refers to spider bites. Antivenom is used in selected black widow envenomations.
Lepidopterism

Correct. Lepidopterism is the aggregate of medical effects caused by caterpillars, moths, and butterflies. Gypsy moth caterpillar contact causes erucism, a pruritic dermatitis with erythematous papules in linear streaks. Management is symptomatic, and the hairs are removed by stripping.
A.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 48

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
A.q: A 30-year-old woman has intensely itchy finger-web lesions and a scraping is taken from a burrow. What is the definitive method of diagnosing scabies, and what dermoscopic finding supports it?
opts: A burrow ink test alone
The burrow ink test, in which blue or black ink is applied to a suspected lesion, is a useful supportive tool. But microscopic identification is what makes the diagnosis definitive.
Potassium hydroxide showing spaghetti and meatballs
Short hyphae with clusters of yeast described as spaghetti and meatballs is the potassium hydroxide finding in pityriasis versicolor, a fungal condition.
Microscopy of the mite, ova, or feces

Correct. Definitive diagnosis is by microscopic identification of the organism, ova, or feces, obtained by skin scraping. The classic dermoscopic finding is the delta-wing jet sign, representing the dense scabies head, body, eggs, and burrow.
Microscopy plus a positive Nikolsky sign
Nikolsky sign is epidermal separation on rubbing, positive in pemphigus. It has no role in diagnosing an infestation.
A.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 14

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
A.q: A 67-year-old woman has a slow-growing 1 cm papule on the nose with a pearly translucent quality and visible telangiectasias that become more apparent when the skin is stretched. There is central erosion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Keratoacanthoma
Keratoacanthoma grows rapidly over 6 to 8 weeks as a dome-shaped nodule with a central keratin plug rather than enlarging slowly over years.
Basal cell carcinoma

Correct. Nodular basal cell carcinoma is a papule or nodule with central erosion growing slowly over years, with a pearly or translucent quality and visible telangiectasias accentuated by stretching the skin. It is the most common form of cancer.
Squamous cell carcinoma
Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma presents as a small red conical hard nodule that may ulcerate, or a non-healing ulcer or warty nodule, rather than a pearly translucent papule.
Sebaceous hyperplasia
Sebaceous hyperplasia produces soft whitish-yellow papules with a central dell, and dermoscopy distinguishes it from basal cell carcinoma.
A.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 35

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
A.q: A 9-year-old presents with a fever above 39.5 degrees Celsius for three days, headache, and now a rash that began on the ankles and wrists and is spreading centrally. What is the treatment, and does his age change it?
opts: Withhold until serology returns
The indirect immunofluorescence assay is the gold standard test, but waiting for it costs the time in which treatment determines survival.
Amoxicillin; doxycycline is contraindicated

The usual paediatric caution about tetracyclines does not override treatment here — doxycycline dosing for children is specified, and delayed or inadequate treatment leads to severe and life-threatening complications.
Supportive care only

The disease is life threatening if not treated, with severe cardiac, gastrointestinal, hepatic, neurological, ophthalmological, renal, and pulmonary manifestations following delayed or inadequate treatment.
Doxycycline, used in children for this infection

Correct. Rocky Mountain spotted fever is treated with doxycycline in adults at 100 mg every 12 hours for 5 to 10 days, the same in pregnant women, and in children at 2.2 mg per kilogram every 12 hours. The illness is life threatening if untreated.
A.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 86

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
A.q: A 22-year-old woman is treated for scabies and asks what she should do with her sheets and clothing. What environmental measure is specified for bedding and clothing?
opts: No environmental measures needed
Scabies may also be acquired from the bedding or underclothing of an infested person, which is why the environmental step exists.
Bag for 24 hours
A day is not long enough. The 14-day isolation period reflects how long mites can survive off the host.
Discard all bedding and clothing
Laundering at high heat or bagging for 14 days is sufficient, so discarding possessions imposes cost without added benefit.
Wash, or bag for 14 days
Correct. Bedding and clothing should be washed or set aside for 14 days in a plastic bag in a warm area, and high heat at 60 degrees Celsius is needed to kill mites.
A.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 18

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pigmented skin lesions
A.q: A 7-year-old has a solitary, asymptomatic, pink, hairless, firm dome-shaped papule on the cheek that grew over several weeks and has since been stable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Molluscum contagiosum
Molluscum lesions are pearly dome-shaped papules with characteristic central umbilication, and they are usually multiple.
Spitz nevus

Correct. A Spitz nevus is usually benign with a phase of growth, fast or slow, followed by a stable period. It is solitary, asymptomatic, pink or red, hairless, firm, and dome-shaped, several millimetres to centimetres, usually on the face, neck, or extremities, and it sometimes resembles melanoma.
Pigmented spindle cell nevus
The Reed nevus is a sharply circumscribed darkly pigmented papule on the extremities of adults in their thirties, not a pink dome-shaped lesion in a child.
Common acquired melanocytic nevus
Common acquired naevi are skin-coloured, brown, or pink with homogeneous colour and are usually under 6 mm, and they develop slowly rather than growing over weeks.
A.cite: CMS I Pigmented Skin Lesions - Shahsv-2.pptx, Slide 42

A.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
A.q: A 24-year-old man has tinea corporis, and the clinician wants an antifungal that works by destroying the fungal cell membrane rather than by blocking ergosterol synthesis. Which agent belongs to that class, and how is the class recognised by name?
opts: Terbinafine, an allylamine, recognisable by the ending -fine

Correct. The allylamine class works by destroying the cell membranes of fungi, preventing growth and ultimately killing them, and its members end in -fine: terbinafine and naftifine. Imidazoles instead block synthesis of ergosterol, a vital component of the fungal cell membrane.
Ketoconazole, an imidazole, recognisable by the ending -fine
Ketoconazole is an imidazole, and imidazoles block ergosterol synthesis rather than destroying the membrane directly. The naming clue also belongs to the allylamines.
Griseofulvin, an allylamine favoured for Trichophyton infection
Griseofulvin is often favoured for Microsporum infection in tinea capitis, whereas terbinafine is generally favoured for Trichophyton. Griseofulvin is not an allylamine.
Nystatin, a polyene that treats both Candida and dermatophytes
Topical nystatin treats Candida only, which is precisely why topical azoles are preferred when a dermatophyte may also be present.
A.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 5

A.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
A.q: A 5-year-old boy has multiple small flesh-coloured papules scattered over the trunk, and the clinician examines each one closely. What is the characteristic morphological feature of a molluscum contagiosum lesion?
opts: A stuck-on look with comedone-like openings
A stuck-on appearance with comedone-like openings on dermoscopy describes seborrheic keratosis.
A rough grey surface with thrombosed capillaries
A rough greyish surface with visible red or black dots representing thrombosed dilated capillaries describes verruca vulgaris. Trimming the surface makes those capillaries more prominent.
Central umbilication of a pearly dome-shaped papule
Correct. Lesions are discrete, smooth-surfaced, firm, flesh-coloured, dome-shaped pearly papules averaging 3 to 5 mm, and central umbilication is characteristic.
Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base
Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base are the hallmark of herpes simplex virus and herpes zoster.
A.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 134

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
A.q: A 34-year-old woman with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and polycystic ovary syndrome has velvety hyperpigmented plaques of the neck and axillae. What is the primary management?
opts: Weight loss and glycaemic control

Correct. Primary management is treating the underlying cause through weight loss and glycaemic control, discontinuing any offending drug. Metformin reduces insulin resistance and may improve the skin findings.
Laser therapy or dermabrasion
Dermabrasion and laser are cosmetic measures listed alongside the topicals. Choosing a procedure over metabolic management treats the marker rather than the disease it marks.
Topical retinoids

Topical retinoids, salicylic acid, and ammonium lactate are used for cosmetic improvement. They address the appearance while leaving the insulin resistance that produced it untreated, which is why they are secondary.
Topical corticosteroids
Acanthosis nigricans is a proliferative response to hyperinsulinaemia rather than an inflammatory dermatosis, so there is no inflammation for a corticosteroid to suppress.
A.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 25

A.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
A.q: A 26-year-old woman presents with painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base. The clinician performs a bedside Tzanck smear, which shows cytologic changes consistent with a herpesvirus. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Confirm with viral polymerase chain reaction

Correct. A Tzanck smear provides rapid evaluation of vesicular lesions for herpesvirus cytologic changes, but polymerase chain reaction is preferred for confirmation. Viral polymerase chain reaction detects the genetic material of the virus and identifies which herpesvirus is responsible.
Accept the Tzanck smear as definitive

A Tzanck smear shows herpesvirus cytologic changes but cannot distinguish herpes simplex virus from varicella zoster virus. Treating it as definitive attributes more specificity to the test than it has.
Bacterial culture and sensitivity

Bacterial culture and sensitivity identifies bacteria and determines appropriate antibiotic therapy. The cytology has already pointed to a virus, so a bacterial culture answers a question that is no longer being asked.
Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin

Direct immunofluorescence detects abnormal immune deposits such as antibodies or complement in skin tissue and is used for autoimmune blistering disease. It is not the confirmatory test for a viral vesicular eruption.
A.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 32

A.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
A.q: A 71-year-old woman has a sacral wound showing full-thickness loss of skin extending into the dermis, and a second area on the heel showing partial loss involving only the epidermis. What are these two findings called?
opts: Fissure and excoriation, respectively
A fissure is a break in the skin and an excoriation is a scratch or abrasion where the top layer wears off. Neither term is defined by the depth relationship the question describes.
Ulceration and erosion, respectively
Correct. Ulceration is full-thickness loss of the skin extending to the dermis or deeper, whereas erosion is partial loss of the skin of only the epidermis. Depth is the entire distinction.
Erosion and ulceration, respectively
The two terms are correct but assigned to the wrong findings. Reversing them would mean documenting a full-thickness wound as superficial, which changes both the prognosis and the management.
Scar and scale, respectively
A scar is abnormal formation of connective tissue and scale is accumulation of loose or adherent cornified epidermal fragments. Neither describes tissue loss by depth.
A.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 17

A.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
A.q: A 29-year-old dental hygienist develops a painful, swollen index finger with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, preceded by burning and tingling. A colleague suggests incision and drainage. What is the correct management?
opts: A topical antifungal and a dry hand
That approach belongs to chronic paronychia, where Candida albicans is the most common pathogen and the cause is prolonged wet work.
Incise and drain, then give antivirals
This is the specific error the lecture warns against. The lesion is not an abscess, and incising it delays healing while creating a portal for secondary infection.
Do not incise; cover it and give antivirals

Correct. Incision and drainage does not treat herpes simplex virus and can delay healing. Lesions should be covered, hand hygiene used, contact with mucosa and broken skin avoided until healed, and early oral acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir may shorten the episode.
Observe without treatment or precautions
The episode does resolve, but covering the lesions and avoiding contact with mucosa and broken skin are needed to prevent transmission, and early antivirals may shorten it.
A.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 128

A.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
A.q: A 22-year-old woman is prescribed topical tretinoin for acne. What counselling is most important before she starts?
opts: Start at full frequency immediately
Starting at full frequency maximises the irritation and dryness that cause patients to abandon retinoid therapy altogether. Gradual introduction is specifically advised.
Combine with a potent corticosteroid

Combining a retinoid with a potent facial corticosteroid introduces the exposure that drives perioral dermatitis and facial atrophy. Irritation is managed by gradual introduction and emollients instead.
Start gradually; expect irritation

Correct. The important clinical considerations for topical retinoids are irritation, dryness, and photosensitivity; therapy should begin gradually, and pregnancy precautions apply. Common agents include adapalene, tretinoin, tazarotene, and trifarotene.
No pregnancy precautions are needed
Pregnancy precautions apply to topical retinoids despite the route of administration. Dismissing them on the grounds that the drug is topical is the most consequential error available here.
A.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 44

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
A.q: A 30-year-old man has a raised, firm scar that developed within four weeks of a surgical incision. It remains within the original incision line and has flattened slightly over the past year. What management options apply?
opts: Excision alone, which never recurs
It is worth noting that excision of a keloid carries a 50 to 100 percent recurrence rate; even for hypertrophic scars, excision is one option among several rather than a guaranteed cure.
No treatment is ever appropriate
Hypertrophic scars remain stable and regress with time, which is genuinely reassuring, but treatment options exist for symptoms and appearance and need not be withheld.
Intralesional steroid, sheeting, or laser

Correct. Hypertrophic scar management includes intralesional injection of corticosteroid or 5-fluorouracil, compression therapy and silicone sheeting, surgical excision, and pulsed dye laser, which reduces scar erythema by reducing neovascularisation.
Cryotherapy is always contraindicated
Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen appears among keloid treatments, where it flattens lesions but can cause hypopigmentation. It is not universally contraindicated.
A.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 23

A.io: b — Identify medical strategies for common benign skin lesions in infants, adolescents, adults and the elderly
A.q: A 4-year-old boy has a flat pink-purple patch on one side of the face that has been present since birth and has grown in proportion with him. Which statement best describes a nevus flammeus?
opts: Present at birth; involutes by school age
Involution is the hemangioma pattern. The absence of regression is what makes nevus flammeus a lifelong lesion with psychosocial consequences.
Present at birth; darkens and never involutes

Correct. Nevus flammeus is a congenital vascular lesion of dilated superficial dermal capillaries through the entire depth of the dermis, without endothelial proliferation. It is present at birth, grows in size with the child, does not involute, and becomes darker and thicker.
Appears at six months; proliferates then involutes
That pattern describes an infantile hemangioma, which has a rapid proliferative phase followed by slower involution. Nevus flammeus is present from birth and never involutes.
An acquired adult capillary proliferation
Acquired capillary proliferation in adults describes cherry angioma. Nevus flammeus is congenital and involves dilatation without proliferation.
A.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 78

A.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
A.q: A 30-year-old woman in her third trimester develops erythematous patches whose margins are studded with small pustules, accompanied by fever, chills, malaise, diarrhea, nausea, and joint pains. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pemphigoid gestationis

Pemphigoid gestationis is a pregnancy-associated blistering disease that typically begins periumbilically with urticarial lesions progressing to tense bullae. Its lesions are bullae rather than margins studded with subcorneal pustules.
Impetigo

Despite the similar name, impetigo is a superficial bacterial infection producing honey-coloured crusts, most often around the nose and mouth in children. It does not produce systemic symptoms of this kind or a pustule-studded advancing margin in a pregnant woman.
Impetigo herpetiformis

Correct. Impetigo herpetiformis is the psoriasis of pregnancy, occurring typically in the third trimester with erythematous patches whose margins are studded with subcorneal pustules. Onset is accompanied by fever, chills, malaise, diarrhea, nausea, and arthralgia.
Generalised candidiasis

Cutaneous candidiasis favours warm, moist, occluded sites and produces beefy erythema with satellite pustules. It does not produce a systemically unwell pregnant patient with pustules studding the margins of erythematous patches.
A.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 161

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
A.q: A 31-year-old man has folliculitis that has recurred repeatedly despite topical treatment, and cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus each time. What additional measure addresses the likely reservoir?
opts: Mupirocin to the nares for the carrier state

Correct. Recurrent or recalcitrant folliculitis raises the Staphylococcus aureus carrier state, and mupirocin ointment is used for it. Nasal swabs of the patient and family members are taken to evaluate carriage.
An antibacterial soap alone
Antibacterial soaps such as Dial or Lever 2000 are part of general treatment along with good hygiene and loose clean clothing. They do not eradicate nasal carriage.
A potassium hydroxide mount of a hair

A potassium hydroxide wet mount using a plucked hair is done to rule out dermatophyte folliculitis, which is a reasonable step in resistant cases. But the cultures have already identified the organism.
Oral ciprofloxacin
Ciprofloxacin is used for widespread or resistant Pseudomonas folliculitis after water exposure. It is not the agent for staphylococcal carriage.
A.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 46

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
A.q: A 17-year-old girl has a bright red, friable, pedunculated papule on the finger pad that appeared rapidly after she injured the finger and bleeds easily when bumped. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Cherry angioma
Cherry angiomas are smooth firm papules under 5 mm that increase with age on the trunk, not rapidly growing friable lesions after trauma.
Amelanotic melanoma
Amelanotic melanoma is on the differential and is why histology is often sent, but the classic history of rapid growth after trauma in a young patient fits the benign lesion.
Pyogenic granuloma

Correct. Pyogenic granuloma is an acquired benign vascular tumour arising as a response to injury or hormonal factors, common in children, young adults, and pregnancy, most often on the head, neck, and fingers, and it bleeds readily.
Dermatofibroma
Dermatofibroma is a firm nodule with a brown halo and positive dimple sign, most commonly on the legs, and it does not bleed spontaneously.

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
A.q: A 30-year-old woman with erythema multiforme triggered by recurrent herpes simplex virus has had four episodes in twelve months. What management addresses the recurrences?
opts: Continuous topical corticosteroids
Topical corticosteroids are used for localised lesions during an episode. Applying them prophylactically to clear skin exposes her to atrophy without preventing anything.
Suppressive oral acyclovir or valacyclovir

Correct. Oral acyclovir or valacyclovir is used when the eruption is triggered by herpes simplex virus, and a prior episode is itself a risk factor for recurrence. Suppressing the trigger is what prevents the next episode.
Continuous oral antihistamines
Oral antihistamines are used for pruritus during an acute episode. They relieve a symptom without touching the viral trigger, so the eruptions would continue at the same rate.
Avoid anti-inflammatories and sulfonamides

Those drugs are genuine triggers in other patients and the history should be reviewed, but this woman's trigger is already identified as herpes simplex virus. Avoiding an unrelated exposure would not help.

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
A.q: A 46-year-old runner has a hyperkeratotic lesion on the sole, and a student asks how to tell a callus from a wart at the bedside. How do the skin lines behave in a callus compared with a verruca vulgaris, and why does this matter?
opts: Lines run through a callus but are broken by a wart
Correct. Skin lines run through both corns and calluses, whereas verruca vulgaris interrupts the skin lines. This is a bedside sign that requires no equipment.
Lines run through both
Skin lines run through corns and calluses only. A wart interrupts them, which is what makes the comparison informative.
Lines are broken by a callus, run through a wart
The two are reversed. A clinician applying this rule would treat a wart as a pressure lesion and a callus as viral, and would pursue the wrong management for both.
Lines are broken by both
The sign is useful precisely because the two behave differently. Discarding it removes a simple discriminator.

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
A.q: A 21-year-old woman returns from a tropical beach holiday with an intensely itchy, raised, serpentine track on the foot that has advanced a few centimetres over the past two days. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Cutaneous larva migrans

Correct. Cutaneous larva migrans results from animal hookworm larvae in which the human is a dead-end host, producing an erythematous, raised, vesicular, linear or serpentine cutaneous trail that progresses 2 to 3 cm per day with intense pruritus.
Scabies
Scabies burrows are 1 to 10 mm and static, in the finger webs and flexures, rather than a track advancing centimetres per day.
Tungiasis
Tungiasis produces discrete erythematous papules enlarging over weeks into firm translucent nodules on the feet after barefoot soil contact.
Contact dermatitis
Allergic contact dermatitis from a plant produces linear streaks of vesicles that are static rather than advancing daily.

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
A.q: A 16-year-old girl is evaluated for a lesion on the finger pad that appeared rapidly after she injured the finger and bleeds easily when bumped. Examination shows a bright red, friable, pedunculated papule. What is the diagnosis, and what is notable about its name?
opts: Pyogenic granuloma, a granulomatous infection
This accepts the name at face value, which is the misconception the lecture corrects. The lesion is neither infectious nor granulomatous.
Amelanotic melanoma
Malignant melanoma is on the differential and is the reason histology may be sent, but the classic history of rapid growth after trauma with easy bleeding in a young patient fits the benign lesion.
Pyogenic granuloma; the name is a misnomer

Correct. Pyogenic granuloma is an acquired vascular lesion that is misnamed, being neither infectious nor granulomatous. It is a benign vascular tumour common in children, young adults, and pregnancy, arising as a response to injury or hormonal factors, most often on the head, neck, and fingers.
Cherry angioma
Cherry angiomas are smooth firm deep red papules under 5 mm that occur with increasing age on the trunk. They do not appear rapidly after trauma on a finger in an adolescent.

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
A.q: A 49-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has severe leg pain after a minor injury. Over hours the skin has changed from red-purple to blue-grey, bullae with thick purple fluid have appeared, and the area that was exquisitely tender is now numb. He is febrile and tachycardic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Necrotizing fasciitis

Correct. Necrotizing fasciitis progresses rapidly with skin colour changing from red-purple to blue-grey, bullae containing thick pink or purple fluid, and loss of tenderness as superficial nerves are destroyed — an ominous sign.
Cellulitis
Cellulitis produces the four cardinal signs of inflammation and remains tender; failure to respond within 48 hours or loss of tenderness should raise necrotizing fasciitis instead.
Erysipelas
Erysipelas produces a raised plaque with a clear line of demarcation and high fever, but not blue-grey discoloration, haemorrhagic bullae, or anaesthesia.
Pyoderma gangrenosum
Pyoderma gangrenosum produces a rapidly expanding painful ulcer with undermined violaceous borders and is culture negative, and it worsens with debridement rather than requiring it.
