A.io: b — Identify medical care strategies for pigmented skin lesions in adult and elderly populations
A.q: A 32-year-old fair-skinned woman has numerous moles under 6 mm with homogeneous surface and colour. One lesion is very dark brown to black. What is the significance of that lesion?
opts: It is a Spitz nevus; always benign
Spitz naevi are solitary, pink or red, hairless, firm, and dome-shaped, usually benign but sometimes resembling melanoma. They are not dark brown or black.
It is a blue nevus; no evaluation
Blue naevi are blue, blue-grey, or blue-black and occur at characteristic sites including the dorsal hands and feet, scalp, and sacral region, and larger lesions are biopsied.
It is suspicious and warrants evaluation

Correct. Common acquired melanocytic naevi are usually less than 6 mm with homogeneous surface and colour, round to oval with sharp demarcation. A very dark brown or black lesion on a light-skinned individual is specifically flagged as suspicious.
It is expected with many moles; no action

Increased numbers of moles do raise melanoma risk, which makes this superficially reassuring reasoning. But a single lesion diverging in colour from its neighbours is the specific finding singled out as suspicious.

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
A.q: A 35-year-old woman with dermatitis herpetiformis achieves rapid relief on dapsone and asks whether that is the whole treatment. What is the most important additional element of management?
opts: Indefinite dapsone monotherapy

This is directly contrary to the mechanism: removing gluten removes the antigenic drive. Committing the patient to indefinite dapsone with its haematological toxicity while leaving the cause in place is the wrong trade.
A gluten-free diet for six weeks
The dietary restriction is lifelong rather than a time-limited trial. Reintroducing gluten restores the antigen and with it the eruption and the celiac disease risk.
A strict lifelong gluten-free diet

Correct. Dapsone provides rapid symptom relief but the long-term management is a strict gluten-free diet, because the disease is driven by immunoglobulin A antibodies against epidermal transglutaminase in patients consuming dietary gluten. All patients should also be screened for celiac disease.
High-potency topical steroids alone
Topical high-potency steroids are used for localised flares, not as the long-term strategy. They do nothing about the systemic gluten-driven process or the associated celiac disease.

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
A.q: A 78-year-old fair-skinned farmer has a small red, conical, hard nodule on the pinna that has ulcerated and grown over two months. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Actinic keratosis
Actinic keratoses are small sandpapery papules 0.2 to 0.6 cm. Rapid growth, ulceration, and a hard nodule are the red flags that mark progression beyond that stage.
Keratoacanthoma
Keratoacanthoma is on the differential and can regress, which is exactly why biopsy is the only reliable way to distinguish it from squamous cell carcinoma.
Basal cell carcinoma

Basal cell carcinoma is the most common form of cancer and is driven by intense intermittent exposure, but its nodular form is a pearly translucent papule with telangiectasias rather than a hard conical ulcerating nodule.
Squamous cell carcinoma

Correct. Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common form of skin cancer, usually following prolonged cumulative sun exposure, and may arise from an actinic keratosis. The classic presentation is a small red conical hard nodule that may ulcerate, or a non-healing ulcer, warty nodule, or irregular pink plaque with haemorrhagic crust.
A.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 22

A.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
A.q: A 47-year-old woman presents with an intensely itchy eruption on both wrists and ankles that has been present for two months. Examination shows small, flat-topped, shiny violaceous papules, some coalescing into plaques, over the volar wrists and ankles. Fine white lines are visible across the surface of the plaques. She also has lacy white streaks on the buccal mucosa. What are the surface lines called?
opts: Collarette of scale
A collarette of scale is the trailing rim of scale seen in the herald patch of pityriasis rosea after central clearing. It is a peripheral rim rather than fine lines crossing the lesion surface.
Wickham striae

Correct. Fine white lines visible on the surface of lichen planus plaques are known as Wickham striae. Oral lichen planus can occur with or without cutaneous disease and often presents with erosive lesions or Wickham striae, as it does here.
Koebner phenomenon

Koebner phenomenon is the development of lesions at sites of trauma, and it does occur in lichen planus. But it describes where new lesions appear, not the white lines on the surface of existing ones.
Civatte bodies
Civatte bodies are apoptotic keratinocytes seen in the lower epidermis on histopathology of lichen planus. They are a microscopic finding, not something visible at the bedside.
A.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 176

A.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
A.q: A 21-year-old man treated for pityriasis versicolor returns two months later frustrated that the pale patches persist despite his completing the full course. What is the most accurate explanation?
opts: It is treatment failure needing oral therapy
Systemic therapy is reserved for extensive, recurrent, or topical-refractory disease. Treating persistent pigment change as failure exposes the patient to unnecessary systemic antifungal therapy.
Vitiligo is developing at the sites
Vitiligo is on the differential and produces complete depigmentation without scale. Pityriasis versicolor produces partial pigment change that recovers over months.
It is now contagious to the household
Pityriasis versicolor is not considered contagious, since it results from overgrowth of an organism that normally inhabits the skin.
Pigment recovery lags months behind clearance
Correct. Hypopigmentation reflects altered melanocyte function and reduced tanning, and recovery can lag months after yeast clearance. The persistence of pallor does not indicate treatment failure.

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
A.q: A 73-year-old man who worked outdoors for forty years has multiple pink papules 0.3 to 0.5 cm on the bald scalp and dorsal hands. Several are more apparent to the examining hand than to the eye. None is indurated, ulcerated, or bleeding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Seborrheic keratosis
Seborrheic keratoses are stuck-on velvety or warty papules rather than rough sandpapery lesions felt more than seen.
Squamous cell carcinoma
The most important distinction is early squamous cell carcinoma, flagged when a lesion is thick, indurated, ulcerated, enlarging, painful, or bleeding — all specifically absent here.
Actinic keratosis

Correct. Actinic keratoses are small 0.2 to 0.6 cm flesh-coloured, pink, or slightly hyperpigmented papules with a characteristic sandpaper texture on palpation, so a lesion may be more apparent by touch than by sight, on chronically sun-exposed skin.
Verruca vulgaris
Common warts have a rough greyish surface with thrombosed capillaries and interrupt the skin lines, typically on the hands of younger patients.
A.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 12

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pigmented skin lesions
A.q: A 19-year-old woman has a blue-grey papule under 1 cm on the dorsum of the hand. What are blue naevi composed of?
opts: Deeply pigmented dermal melanocytes

Correct. Blue naevi are composed of deeply pigmented spindle or epithelioid melanocytes in the dermis. Diagnosis is clinical for small lesions and by biopsy for larger ones, with observation and biopsy or excision if changes are noted.
Dilated dermal capillaries
Dilated dermal vessels produce vascular lesions that blanch. Blue naevi are pigmented and do not blanch.
Lipid-laden macrophages
Lipid-laden macrophages form xanthelasma, which warrants hyperlipidaemia screening.
Melanocytes within the epidermis
The melanocytes lie in the dermis, which is what gives the lesion its blue colour, and larger lesions require biopsy rather than clinical diagnosis alone.
A.cite: CMS I Pigmented Skin Lesions - Shahsv-2.pptx, Slide 40

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
A.q: A 30-year-old woman with moderate hidradenitis suppurativa of both axillae has not responded to topical therapy. What is the rationale for adding spironolactone?
opts: It shrinks sinuses when injected into the lesion
Intralesional triamcinolone acetonide is what decreases the size of draining sinuses. Spironolactone is taken orally and acts systemically.
An immunosuppressant blocking tumour necrosis factor
Tumour necrosis factor blockade describes infliximab, which is used for severe disease. Spironolactone works through androgen suppression instead.
An antibiotic suppressing the organism

Topical clindamycin and erythromycin and systemic antibiotics are used, but hidradenitis suppurativa is an inflammatory apocrine disease rather than a primary infection, and spironolactone has no antibacterial action.
An aldosterone antagonist that lowers androgens

Correct. Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist that inhibits ovarian and adrenal production of androgens. Combination birth control pills are used similarly, reducing luteinising hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone secretion.

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
A.q: A 61-year-old man has several soft yellowish papules with a central dell on the forehead and is worried they are skin cancer. What is the pathophysiology of sebaceous hyperplasia, and what is its malignant potential?
opts: Eccrine duct proliferation; low malignant risk
Eccrine duct proliferation describes syringoma. Neither lesion carries a described malignant potential, but the gland of origin here is sebaceous.
Reduced sebocyte turnover; no malignant potential

Correct. With age the turnover of sebocytes, the sebum-producing epithelial cells, slows down; the cells then crowd inside the gland and the gland enlarges. The “hyperplasia” is sebocytes accumulating because they are not being replaced, not dividing faster — slower turnover and a bigger gland are not a contradiction. No known potential for malignant transformation, though patients commonly present fearing skin cancer.
Fibrous overgrowth with local invasion
Overgrowth of dense fibrous tissue describes a keloid, which enlarges but does not invade.
Ultraviolet dysplasia that may become carcinoma
Ultraviolet-induced keratinocytic dysplasia describes actinic keratosis, a premalignant lesion. Sebaceous hyperplasia is benign.
A.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 109

B.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 74-year-old man presents with a two-month history of intense itching followed by blistering. Examination shows numerous 1 to 3 cm tense, firm bullae on the trunk, flexural surfaces of the arms, and the axillary and inguinal folds. Rubbing the skin adjacent to a blister does not cause the epidermis to slough. There is a single small erosion in the mouth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Dermatitis herpetiformis

Dermatitis herpetiformis produces intensely pruritic grouped vesicles and papules on extensor surfaces such as elbows, knees, and buttocks. It does not produce large tense bullae in flexural and intertriginous distribution in an elderly man.
Bullous pemphigoid

Correct. Bullous pemphigoid damages the epithelial basement membrane, producing subepithelial blistering, and classically presents after age 60 with tense 1 to 3 cm bullae on the trunk, extremity flexures, and axillary and inguinal folds. A pruritic prodrome may precede the bullae by weeks to months, and Nikolsky's sign is negative.
Pemphigus vulgaris

Pemphigus produces flaccid bullae that rupture easily, leaving painful bleeding erosions, and Nikolsky's sign is positive. This patient's bullae are tense and firm and the skin does not slough on rubbing, which is the distinction the comparison table draws.
Bullous impetigo

Bullous impetigo occurs chiefly in children and produces flaccid, superficial bullae that rupture to leave a collarette of scale and honey-coloured crust. It is a superficial bacterial infection rather than a subepithelial autoimmune blistering disease.

B.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
B.q: A 63-year-old man presents with a lesion on the temple that he is unable to describe, and the clinician has not yet formed an impression. What is the recommended first step when evaluating any premalignant or malignant cutaneous lesion?
opts: Characterise the lesion before naming it

Correct. The foundational approach is to describe before naming: characterise each lesion systematically by primary lesion type, colour, surface texture, border definition, size, distribution, palpability, ulceration, and bleeding before assigning a diagnosis.
Name the likely diagnosis, then seek support
Naming first and confirming afterwards is the reasoning pattern that produces anchoring, which is why the sequence is deliberately reversed.
Refer every pigmented lesion
Referral criteria exist for specific findings, and describing the lesion is what determines whether they are met.
Photograph and review next visit
Serial photography has a role in surveillance but does not substitute for systematic characterisation at the first encounter.
B.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 4

B.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 68-year-old woman presents with chronic bilateral lower-leg swelling, pruritus, and skin discoloration. Examination demonstrates poorly demarcated erythematous plaques, pitting edema, and brown hyperpigmentation around both medial ankles. Pedal pulses are diminished. What is the most appropriate next step before prescribing compression therapy?
opts: Order patch testing

Patch testing diagnoses allergic contact dermatitis, which is worth considering in chronically treated legs but is not the priority. It does not establish arterial status, and compression would still be unsafe if arterial disease were present.
Obtain a bacterial wound culture

A culture is indicated when infection is suspected, and no ulcer, purulence, warmth, or fever is described. It also would not answer the question the diminished pulses raise, which is whether compression is safe.
Perform a skin biopsy

Biopsy is reserved for atypical or diagnostically uncertain disease and would delay care in a presentation that is clinically characteristic. It also leaves the arterial question that governs compression safety unanswered.
Perform an ankle-brachial index

Correct. Compression is the cornerstone of management only once adequate arterial circulation has been established. An ankle-brachial index or toe pressure should be obtained when peripheral arterial disease is suspected — as the diminished pulses here suggest — before initiating substantial compression.

B.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
B.q: A 63-year-old woman with obesity has a burning rash under both breasts. Examination shows well-demarcated beefy erythematous patches in the folds with peripheral scale and several small papules and pustules on adjacent skin just beyond the main area of redness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Erythrasma
Erythrasma produces an asymptomatic brownish intertriginous patch that fluoresces coral-red, without satellite lesions or beefy erythema.
Contact dermatitis
Contact dermatitis requires an exposure and traces the shape of the contactant rather than following the moist folds with satellite lesions.
Tinea corporis
Tinea corporis produces annular plaques with an advancing scaly border and central clearing rather than confluent fold erythema with satellites.
Cutaneous candidiasis
Correct. Candidal intertrigo produces well-demarcated erythematous patches in warm moist folds with satellite papules and pustules beyond the main area, and pruritus with burning pain is typical.
B.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 71

B.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
B.q: A 72-year-old man presents with vesicles in the right ophthalmic division distribution, including lesions on the tip of his nose. What does that finding signify?
opts: Zoster sine herpete
Dissemination is defined by lesions beyond the affected and adjacent dermatomes. Antiviral therapy is required regardless, and isolation alone would leave the eye untreated.
Hutchinson sign, which increases ocular risk

Correct. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus involves the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. Hutchinson sign — lesions on the tip or side of the nose — increases ocular risk, but its absence does not exclude eye involvement, and systemic antiviral therapy should be started immediately.
Hutchinson sign, whose absence would exclude eye disease

The sign's presence raises risk but its absence specifically does not exclude eye involvement. Relying on a negative sign to skip ophthalmological assessment is the error this caveat exists to prevent.
Disseminated zoster

Ramsay Hunt syndrome is herpes zoster oticus — peripheral facial palsy with painful vesicles of the ear canal, auricle, or oropharynx, sometimes with hearing loss, tinnitus, or vertigo. The nose is not its territory.
B.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 103

B.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
B.q: A 69-year-old man who has worked outdoors for forty years is examined. Several pink papules 0.3 to 0.5 cm are visible on the scalp, and running a hand across the skin reveals further lesions that could not be seen at all. What is the characteristic tactile finding?
opts: Boggy and fluctuant
Bogginess suggests an inflammatory or infective process such as a kerion in tinea barbae rather than a dysplastic keratinocytic lesion.
Sandpaper texture

Correct. Actinic keratoses are small 0.2 to 0.6 cm flesh-coloured, pink, or slightly hyperpigmented papules with a characteristic sandpaper texture on palpation, and a lesion may be more apparent by touch than by sight. The skin must therefore be palpated, not only inspected.
Velvety texture
A velvety texture describes acanthosis nigricans and seborrheic keratosis. Inspection alone would miss the lesions this condition is known for.
Pearly with telangiectasias
Pearly translucency with telangiectasias accentuated by stretching the skin is the hallmark of nodular basal cell carcinoma.
B.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 12

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
B.q: A 62-year-old man has several soft whitish-yellow papules 3 to 5 mm on the forehead, each with a central dell. He is worried they are skin cancer. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sebaceous hyperplasia

Correct. Sebaceous hyperplasia is a common benign condition of enlarged sebaceous glands from changing sebocyte turnover with age, presenting as single or multiple whitish-yellow or skin-coloured soft papules 2 to 9 mm with a central dell.
Basal cell carcinoma
Basal cell carcinoma is the principal differential and dermoscopy distinguishes them; it is a pearly translucent papule with telangiectasias and often central erosion.
Syringoma
Syringomas are firm skin-coloured 1 to 2 mm papules of the lower eyelids appearing at puberty, more common in females.
Xanthelasma
Xanthelasma consists of soft yellow cholesterol plaques at the medial eyelids rather than discrete papules with a central dell.
B.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 110

B.io: a — Interpret a potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation and recognize fungal elements
B.q: A 62-year-old man with thickened, discoloured toenails is having a specimen taken to confirm onychomycosis before oral therapy is started. From where should the specimen be taken?
opts: The most proximal accessible diseased nail bed or subungual debris

Correct. Sampling should be from the most proximal accessible diseased nail bed and subungual debris, where viable organism is concentrated, using potassium hydroxide microscopy, periodic acid-Schiff stain of clippings, fungal culture, or polymerase chain reaction.
The surrounding proximal nail fold
The proximal nail fold is the site of paronychia rather than of nail plate infection, and sampling it would not demonstrate the organism within the nail.
The distal free edge of the nail plate
The distal edge contains the oldest, most degraded material with the lowest yield of viable organism. Distal lateral disease causes debris and crumbling there, but it is not the best sampling site.
A plucked hair from the affected limb
A plucked hair is used for potassium hydroxide microscopy in dermatophyte folliculitis and tinea capitis.
B.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 51

B.io: b — Identify medical strategies for common benign skin lesions in infants, adolescents, adults and the elderly
B.q: A 3-week-old infant, born prematurely, has a bright red papule on the scalp that was a faint blanched area with fine telangiectasias at birth and has grown noticeably in the past fortnight. What growth pattern should the parents be told to expect?
opts: No change during childhood
The lesion is defined by its biphasic growth pattern, which is what distinguishes it from a capillary malformation.
Rapid growth, then slow involution

Correct. Infantile hemangiomas have a unique growth pattern of rapid proliferation followed by slower involution, with rapid growth during the neonatal period and most growth in the first 4 to 6 months. The earliest sign is blanching of the involved skin followed by fine telangiectasias and then a red macule.
Rapid growth with malignant risk
Hemangiomas of infancy are the most common tumours of infancy and most are medically insignificant. Malignant transformation is not a feature.
Steady growth with no involution
Growth in proportion to the child without involution describes nevus flammeus, which is present at birth, remains for life, and becomes darker and thicker.
B.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 66

B.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
B.q: A 45-year-old man has red, itchy, circular patches on the forearm, and the clinician is distinguishing tinea corporis from nummular eczema. What is the distinguishing feature?
opts: Only tinea corporis is pruritic
Nummular eczema is intensely pruritic and tinea corporis may be asymptomatic or pruritic. Itch does not separate them.
Tinea corporis clears centrally; eczema does not

Correct. Both present as red or pink itchy circular patches. Tinea corporis is a fungal infection with an annular appearance, whereas nummular eczema is non-infectious and coin-shaped without central clearing.
Only tinea corporis is well demarcated
Both are well demarcated — nummular eczema is described as well-demarcated and tinea corporis as sharply circumscribed.
Nummular eczema clears centrally; tinea does not
The two are reversed. A clinician using this rule would treat a dermatophyte infection with a corticosteroid and produce tinea incognito.
B.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 27

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
B.q: A 36-year-old pregnant woman and her 7-year-old son both develop erythema migrans after a camping trip. What is first-line oral antibiotic therapy for Lyme disease, and what alternative applies to children and pregnant women with early disease?
opts: Intravenous ceftriaxone for all stages
Intravenous ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, or penicillin G is used for certain manifestations including acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans and arthritis, rather than for all patients.
Doxycycline, or amoxicillin in pregnancy

Correct. Antibiotics are indicated in all stages. Doxycycline is first line, with amoxicillin as an alternative first-line agent for early disease including erythema migrans, particularly in children and pregnant women.
Amoxicillin, with doxycycline for failure
The hierarchy is reversed. Doxycycline is the first-line agent generally, with amoxicillin as the alternative in specific populations.
No antibiotics for stage 1
Antibiotics are indicated in all stages, and treating early disease is what prevents dissemination.
B.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 79

B.io: 4 — Discuss clinical principles and decision-making
B.q: A student uses the VINDICATE mnemonic to build a differential for a 72-year-old man brought to the emergency department with confusion. What do the letters stand for?
opts: Vascular, inflammatory, neurological, drug-related, idiopathic, cardiac, allergic, toxic, environmental
Several of these categories are plausible in isolation but they are not the letters of this mnemonic, and a misremembered framework produces a differential with systematic gaps.
A checklist for appraising evidence
Evaluating the quality and validity of evidence is a step in evidence-based practice, separate from this mnemonic.
A physical examination sequence
VINDICATE is a differential diagnosis framework organised by disease category rather than an examination sequence.
Vascular, infectious, neoplastic, degenerative, iatrogenic, congenital, autoimmune, trauma, endocrine

Correct. VINDICATE is a category-based framework: vascular, infectious, neoplastic, degenerative, iatrogenic, congenital, autoimmune, trauma, and endocrine or metabolic. Applied to confusion it yields stroke, meningitis, brain tumour, Alzheimer disease, and so on.
B.cite: 1. svClinical Reasoning and Problem Solving.pptx, Slide 16

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
B.q: A 26-year-old Black man reports tender bumps on his neck and jawline that appear after shaving. Examination shows erythematous papules, several with a visible central hair shaft curving back into the skin. What is the underlying process?
opts: A foreign body reaction to re-entrant hair

Correct. Pseudofolliculitis barbae is a foreign body reaction to hair in any shaved area. The cut hair curves into the follicular wall and penetrates the skin to form a tender red papule or pustule, and it occurs commonly in Black men because of tightly curled facial hair together with keratin gene variations.
Apocrine gland occlusion
Apocrine gland involvement describes hidradenitis suppurativa, which affects the axilla, groin, breasts, and perineum with recurrent nodules and sinus tracts rather than the shaved beard area.
An allergic reaction to shaving products
Allergic contact dermatitis would produce a well-demarcated eruption over the whole area of product contact rather than discrete papules each containing a re-entrant hair shaft.
Follicular hyperkeratinisation with excess sebum

Follicular hyperkeratinisation, increased sebum, and proliferation of Cutibacterium acnes are three of the four factors in acne vulgaris, whose hallmark lesion is the comedone. There is no comedone in pseudofolliculitis barbae.

B.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 76-year-old woman has had six weeks of severe itching followed by numerous tense, firm 2 cm blisters on the trunk, axillae, and inner thighs. Rubbing adjacent normal skin does not cause it to slough. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Dermatitis herpetiformis
Dermatitis herpetiformis produces small grouped vesicles and papules on extensor surfaces, not large tense bullae in a flexural distribution.
Bullous pemphigoid

Correct. Bullous pemphigoid produces tense 1 to 3 cm bullae on the trunk, flexures, and intertriginous folds after age 60, often preceded by a pruritic prodrome of weeks to months, with a negative Nikolsky sign.
Erythema multiforme
Erythema multiforme produces fixed targetoid lesions with three concentric zones, typically acral, often following herpes simplex virus infection.
Pemphigus vulgaris
Pemphigus produces flaccid bullae that rupture easily leaving painful bleeding erosions, usually beginning in the mouth, with a positive Nikolsky sign.

B.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
B.q: A 62-year-old man with diabetes has three thickened, discoloured toenails with crumbling of the distal nail plate, subungual debris, and separation of the plate from the bed. He also has scaling between the toes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Chronic paronychia
Chronic paronychia inflames the proximal nail fold with thickened discoloured plates, and it follows prolonged wet work rather than distal crumbling with toe web scaling.
Nail psoriasis
Nail psoriasis produces pitting, oil-drop change, and onycholysis, usually with psoriatic plaques elsewhere, and it lacks subungual dermatophyte debris.
Nail unit melanoma
Nail unit melanoma produces a new or evolving pigmented longitudinal band in ONE digit with proximal widening, not thickening and crumbling of three nails.
Onychomycosis

Correct. Distal lateral onychomycosis produces debris, onycholysis, thickening, discoloration, and crumbling, and dermatophytes — especially Trichophyton rubrum — cause most cases. Coexisting tinea pedis is a recognised risk factor.
B.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 47

B.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 26-year-old man has three smooth, round bald patches on the scalp that appeared over a month. The underlying scalp is smooth without scale, redness, or scarring, and short hairs narrow at the root are visible at the margins. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Lichen planopilaris
Scarring alopecias destroy the follicle and leave loss of follicular openings with scarring, which this examination specifically excludes.
Trichotillomania
Hair-pulling produces irregular patches with hairs of varying length rather than smooth round patches with tapered exclamation point hairs.
Alopecia areata
Correct. Alopecia areata produces sudden round 1 to 4 cm patches of non-scarring hair loss with a smooth scalp, and exclamation point hairs at the margins are pathognomonic.
Androgenetic alopecia
Androgenetic alopecia produces gradual patterned thinning — frontotemporal recession and vertex loss in men — rather than discrete round patches appearing over weeks.

B.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
B.q: A 25-year-old woman has a painful eruption on the vermilion border preceded by a day of tingling and burning. Examination shows grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, some broken down into shallow painful ulcers. She has had similar episodes before. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Aphthous ulceration
Aphthous ulcers occur on non-keratinised intraoral mucosa rather than the vermilion border, and they are not preceded by grouped vesicles.
Herpes zoster
Herpes zoster follows a dermatome and stops at the midline, and a first episode does not recur at the same site repeatedly.
Herpes simplex virus

Correct. Herpes simplex produces grouped vesicles on an erythematous base that break down into shallow painful ulcers, preceded by tenderness, paraesthesia, or burning, and it is characterised by latency with lifelong recurrence at the same site.
Impetigo
Impetigo produces honey-coloured adherent crusts over erosions and is not preceded by a burning prodrome or recurrent at a fixed site.
B.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 119

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
B.q: A 59-year-old woman has a classic presentation of erysipelas with a sharply demarcated raised plaque of the shin and a fever of 39 degrees Celsius. What laboratory and imaging approach is appropriate?
opts: Blood and tissue cultures in every patient

Cultures have extremely low yield in erysipelas and are not cost effective. Delaying treatment for them is particularly unhelpful given that prompt treatment matters because of potentially rapid progression.
Magnetic resonance imaging for depth
Imaging is of low yield and not indicated in a classic presentation. Depth is inferred clinically from the raised, sharply demarcated plaque.
Clinical; cultures and imaging add little

Correct. Erysipelas is a clinical diagnosis in a classic presentation. Leukocytosis and raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are common, but blood and tissue cultures are not cost effective because of extremely low organism yield, and imaging studies are of low yield and not indicated.
No laboratory testing is ever useful
Leukocytosis and raised inflammatory markers are common and can support the clinical impression; it is cultures and imaging specifically that add little.

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
B.q: A 19-year-old returns from a tropical beach holiday with an intensely itchy, raised, serpentine track on the foot that has advanced a few centimetres over the past two days. What is the treatment?
opts: Oral albendazole or ivermectin

Correct. Cutaneous larva migrans results from larvae of animal nematodes, mostly dog and cat hookworms, in which the human is a dead-end host. The classic lesion is an erythematous, raised, vesicular, linear or serpentine trail progressing 2 to 3 cm per day. Treatment is albendazole 400 mg daily for 3 days or ivermectin.
Topical therapy alone
Topical therapy is described as less effective. Oral treatment is what clears the infestation.
Excision of an embedded flea
Tungiasis produces discrete enlarging nodules on the feet rather than a migrating serpentine track.
Surgical excision or cryotherapy
The diagnosis is right but surgical excision and cryotherapy are specifically not recommended, because the advancing larva is ahead of the visible track.
B.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 54

B.io: 4 — Discuss clinical principles and decision-making
B.q: A student proposes a rare diagnosis to explain a very typical presentation in a 30-year-old woman. What does the principle 'place your bets on uncommon manifestations of common conditions rather than common manifestations of uncommon conditions' mean in practice?
opts: An atypical presentation of a common disease is likelier

Correct. Common things occur commonly — when you hear hoof beats think of horses, not zebras. An unusual presentation of a common condition is more probable than a textbook presentation of something rare.
Assume the most serious diagnosis first
Ruling out the worst-case scenario belongs to the naturalistic approach in unstable patients rather than being the general principle of probability.
All diagnoses are equally likely until tested
Being aware of the base rate of disease for diagnoses on the differential is explicitly recommended, so they are not treated as equally likely.
Rare diagnoses should never be considered
The principle orders probabilities rather than forbidding rare diagnoses, and clinicians are also advised to actively seek alternative diagnoses.
B.cite: 1. svClinical Reasoning and Problem Solving.pptx, Slide 25

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 27-year-old woman develops a rash on the backs of her hands two days ago that has spread to the forearms and knees. Examination shows lesions with three concentric zones — a dusky centre, a pale ring, and an erythematous rim — fixed in place for four days. She had a cold sore two weeks ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Erythema multiforme

Correct. Erythema multiforme produces characteristic fixed target lesions with three concentric zones in an acral distribution. Over 50 percent of cases are triggered by herpes simplex virus, which the recent cold sore supplies.
Fixed drug eruption
A fixed drug eruption recurs at the same site with each exposure to a culprit drug and is usually a solitary dusky patch rather than widespread acral targets.
Pityriasis rosea
Pityriasis rosea follows a herald patch with a truncal eruption along the rib lines and does not produce concentric target lesions on the hands.
Urticaria
Urticarial wheals are migratory, blanch fully, and individual lesions last under 24 hours. Lesions fixed in place for four days exclude it.

B.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 29-year-old woman and her 31-year-old husband both have plaque psoriasis and ask about the likelihood their future children will be affected. What is the most accurate counselling?
opts: About 41 percent of their children
Correct. The figures given are 8 percent when one parent has psoriasis and 41 percent when both do, reflecting a genetic predisposition in which PSORS1 is the major susceptibility locus.
About 50 percent; autosomal dominant

Psoriasis occurs in people with a genetic predisposition involving multiple loci rather than following simple Mendelian inheritance. Quoting a dominant transmission figure misrepresents how the risk is actually conferred.
No increased risk; it is not heritable
This contradicts the stated risk figures and the identified susceptibility loci. Denying a genuine familial risk would leave the couple unprepared for a real possibility.
About 8 percent of their children
Eight percent is the figure for a single affected parent. Applying it to two affected parents understates the risk by roughly fivefold and would misdirect the counselling.

B.io: b — Identify medical strategies for common benign skin lesions in infants, adolescents, adults and the elderly
B.q: A 6-week-old infant has a bright red papule on the shoulder, and the clinician classifies the lesion by the depth of vessel involvement. What are the three types of infantile hemangioma, and which is the most common?
opts: Superficial, mixed, and deep; superficial commonest

Correct. The superficial type is the most common, with dilated vessels in the dermis surrounded by proliferating endothelial cells, presenting as a bright red papule, plaque, or nodule and previously called a strawberry hemangioma. The deep type is the least common.
Congenital, infantile, acquired
Infantile hemangiomas are congenital vascular lesions as a group; the subtypes are defined by the depth of vessel involvement.
Superficial, mixed, and deep; deep commonest
The deep type involves dilated vessels in the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue presenting as a pale, skin-coloured, red, or blue nodule, plaque, or tumour, and it is described as the least common.
Capillary, cavernous, arteriovenous
That older terminology is not the classification used here, which divides lesions by depth into superficial, mixed, and deep.
B.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 67

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
B.q: A 33-year-old man returns from a hotel stay with several itchy welts on exposed skin. Examination shows wheals and papules with a haemorrhagic punctum, arranged in rows of three. He did not feel the bites occur. What organism is responsible?
opts: Tunga penetrans
Tungiasis follows penetration of the adult female flea into human skin, producing enlarging papules and translucent nodules over the feet, and requires a travel history.
Cimex lectularius

Correct. Bedbugs are nocturnal feeders that hide in cracks and crevices of headboards, picture frames, and behind loose wallpaper. Bites are painless, multiple, and grouped in a linear fashion, and a row of three bites is known as breakfast, lunch, and dinner.
Sarcoptes scabiei

The delta-wing jet is a dermoscopic sign of the scabies mite within its burrow, not a bite pattern. Scabies produces intense nocturnal itching in the finger webs and flexures rather than painless welts on exposed skin.
Schistosome cercariae
Cercarial dermatitis follows exposure to cercaria-infested water, with prickling within 30 minutes and severe pruritus 10 to 12 hours later.
B.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 33

B.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 6-year-old boy is brought in with fever and a rash. Examination shows non-blanching deposits of blood in the skin, several measuring 6 mm across. What is the most appropriate interpretation of this finding?
opts: A wheal from dermal fluid
A wheal is a firm edematous plaque from fluid infiltration and it blanches. These lesions are non-blanching deposits of blood, which is the opposite finding.
Purpura, an emergency until proven otherwise

Correct. Purpura is a deposit of blood 4 mm or greater, and the lecture flags it explicitly as a medical emergency until proven otherwise. Combined with fever in a child this demands immediate evaluation.
Purpura, benign and observable
This applies the correct term to the wrong conclusion. Purpura carries the emergency designation, and treating it as benign in a febrile child is the error most likely to cause harm.
Petechiae, an emergency until proven otherwise

The urgency is right but the term is wrong: petechiae are deposits of blood 1 to 2 mm, and these lesions are 6 mm. Precision matters here because the size defines which term is being used to communicate the finding.

B.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 22-year-old woman develops an intensely itchy eruption three days after gardening. Examination shows erythematous papules, vesicles, and a few bullae in linear streaks across both forearms, with lesions at differing stages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Irritant contact dermatitis
Irritant dermatitis produces a glazed, sharply demarcated eruption over the whole area of contact rather than linear streaks of vesicles.
Herpes zoster
Herpes zoster produces grouped vesicles confined to one or two adjacent dermatomes that stop abruptly at the midline, not linear streaks crossing the forearms.
Allergic contact dermatitis

Correct. Urushiol sap from Toxicodendron species produces intensely pruritic vesicular lesions in linear distributions where the plant grazed the skin. Lesions erupt within 4 to 96 hours and may appear in multiple stages.
Cutaneous larva migrans
Cutaneous larva migrans produces a single serpentine track advancing 2 to 3 cm per day after soil contact, not multiple static linear streaks.

B.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: An 82-year-old woman living alone reports generalised itching and rough, flaking skin each winter, worse on the lower legs. She takes long hot showers daily using a scented bar soap. Examination shows dry skin with fine scale and a few superficial fissures on the shins, without erythematous plaques or vesicles. What is the most appropriate advice?
opts: A high-potency corticosteroid twice daily

There are no inflammatory plaques to treat — the examination records dry skin with scale and fissures only. A potent steroid on aged skin risks atrophy while doing nothing for the barrier deficit that is causing the itch.
A scented body wash daily

Fragrance-free products are recommended, and a gentle cleanser should be used only where needed. Extending a scented cleanser over the whole body daily increases both the detergent and the fragrance exposure.
Short lukewarm showers; emollient within minutes

Correct. Xerosis reflects impaired stratum corneum hydration promoted by aging, low humidity, hot water, and detergents. Management is short lukewarm showers, a gentle fragrance-free cleanser used only where needed, and a thick ointment or cream applied within minutes of bathing.
A keratolytic onto the fissures

Humectants such as urea or lactic acid do improve hydration and have a role, but keratolytics may sting fissured skin. Directing them onto the fissures is the one place they are most likely to be poorly tolerated.

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
B.q: A 28-year-old man has a healing surgical wound and asks why the scar keeps getting stronger over months. What accounts for the improving tensile strength of a maturing scar?
opts: Progressive cross-linking of collagen fibres
Correct. The four phases are hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling. As the scar matures its tensile strength improves because of progressive cross-linking of collagen fibres.
New elastin deposition
Hemostasis is the first phase and contracture is not one of the four, and it is collagen cross-linking rather than elastin that confers strength.
Vascular ingrowth
Involution describes the natural history of an infantile hemangioma rather than a phase of wound healing, and vascular ingrowth does not confer tensile strength.
Strength is fixed at the time of closure
The phases are right, which makes this the closest wrong answer, but tensile strength continues to improve as cross-linking progresses rather than being fixed at closure.
B.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 11

B.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
B.q: A 66-year-old woman has a slow-growing 1 cm papule on the nose with a pearly translucent quality and visible telangiectasias that become more apparent when the skin is stretched. There is central erosion. What subtype is this?
opts: Nodular basal cell carcinoma

Correct. Nodular basal cell carcinoma is a papule or nodule with central erosion, growing slowly over years to 1 to 2 cm or larger, with a pearly or translucent quality and visible telangiectasias accentuated by stretching the skin. Basal cell carcinoma is the most common form of cancer, driven by ultraviolet light in fair-skinned people with intense intermittent exposure.
Nodular squamous cell carcinoma
Squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common skin cancer, and its nodule is red, conical, and hard rather than pearly and translucent.
Keratoacanthoma
Keratoacanthoma grows rapidly over 6 to 8 weeks and is dome-shaped with a central keratin plug, rather than enlarging slowly over years with a pearly rim.
Amelanotic melanoma
Amelanotic melanoma is a differential consideration, but the pearly translucency with stretch-accentuated telangiectasias is the characteristic basal cell finding.
B.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 35

B.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 52-year-old woman of Mediterranean descent presents with painful mouth erosions that began three months ago, followed by skin lesions. Examination shows flaccid bullae and widespread crusted erosions on the scalp, chest, axillae, and groin that bleed easily and are painful. Lateral pressure on normal-appearing skin causes the superficial layers to slip away. What does the biopsy most likely demonstrate?
opts: Acantholysis with intraepithelial blisters

Correct. Pemphigus is characterised by loss of keratinocyte-to-keratinocyte adhesion, termed acantholysis, producing intraepithelial blisters. The oral onset, flaccid easily ruptured bullae, and positive Nikolsky's sign all identify pemphigus, and biopsy demonstrating acantholysis is the diagnostic finding.
Granular immunoglobulin A at papillary tips

Granular immunoglobulin A at the papillary tips is the direct immunofluorescence finding of dermatitis herpetiformis, which presents with grouped pruritic vesicles on extensor surfaces rather than painful oral erosions and flaccid bullae.
Band-like lymphocytes in the dermis
A band-like lymphocytic infiltrate is the histological signature of lichen planus, which presents with pruritic purple polygonal papules rather than a blistering disorder with mucosal onset.
Neutrophils in a row at the junction

That light-microscopy description belongs to bullous pemphigoid. It is a real finding but attached to the wrong disease for a patient with oral-onset flaccid bullae and epidermal slippage on pressure.

B.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
B.q: A 32-year-old woman with recurrent genital herpes simplex virus type 2 infection is in a relationship with an uninfected partner. Which treatment approach also reduces transmission risk?
opts: Daily suppressive valacyclovir
Correct. Recurrent genital herpes may be managed with patient-initiated episodic therapy or daily suppressive therapy, and suppressive valacyclovir lowers herpes simplex virus type 2 transmission.
Prophylaxis for the uninfected partner
Suppression is given to the infected partner, in whom it reduces shedding. Treating an uninfected person has no target.
Patient-initiated episodic therapy

Episodic therapy is a legitimate option for managing recurrences and shortens individual episodes. But it treats outbreaks after they begin and does not carry the transmission-reduction benefit of daily suppression.
No antiviral therapy
Transmission can occur during asymptomatic shedding, which is precisely why suppressive therapy reduces risk beyond avoiding contact during outbreaks.
B.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 124

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
B.q: A 29-year-old Black man with pseudofolliculitis barbae cannot stop shaving because his employer requires a clean-shaven face. What advice about shaving technique is most appropriate?
opts: Use a multi-blade lift-and-cut razor
This is precisely the system to avoid. The closer the cut sits below the surface, the more readily the hair re-enters the skin, which is the mechanism of the disease.
Shave daily against the grain
Shaving against the grain cuts the hair below the surface and worsens the problem. Stopping shaving where possible is the first recommendation.
Avoid lift-and-cut razors; use a single blade

Correct. Patients should avoid lift-and-cut razor systems and look for mild razor angles with single or at most double blades, because those systems cut the hair below the skin surface where it can re-enter the follicular wall.
Keep shaving; rely on a topical steroid
Mild corticosteroids reduce inflammation and are part of treatment, but relying on them while continuing the provoking technique treats the consequence and leaves the cause.

B.io: c — Identify medical care strategies for cutaneous viral and fungal infections for infant, child, adolescent, adult and elderly populations
B.q: A 6-year-old has fifteen discrete, smooth, firm, flesh-coloured dome-shaped papules averaging 4 mm on the trunk and arms, each with a central dimple. His parents ask about treatment. What is a reasonable approach?
opts: Observation; procedures may scar or pigment

Correct. Molluscum contagiosum is a benign poxvirus infection, and observation is appropriate for many patients because procedures may blister, pigment, or scar. Approved options such as berdazimer gel and cantharidin exist when treatment is chosen.
Oral acyclovir
Acyclovir treats herpesvirus infections. Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a poxvirus and does not respond to it.
Salicylic acid 40 percent to each lesion
Salicylic acid 40 percent is a treatment for plantar warts. It is not among the options given for molluscum.
Curettage of every lesion at the first visit
Destructive procedures carry risks of blistering, pigment change, and scarring, which is the specific reason observation is offered first in a child with asymptomatic lesions.
B.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 136

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
B.q: A 36-year-old man has had hidradenitis suppurativa of both axillae for eight years despite antibiotics and repeated drainage, and asks whether anything can cure it. What offers the best chance of permanent cure?
opts: Intralesional triamcinolone acetonide injections
Intralesional triamcinolone decreases the size of draining sinuses, which is a useful symptomatic measure rather than a definitive one.
Incision and drainage of each cyst as it develops
Incision and drainage relieves individual large fluctuant cysts. Because the disease recurs in the same apocrine regions, repeated drainage never becomes a cure.
Topical clindamycin used indefinitely
Mild topical steroid creams combined with topical antibiotics are favoured for mild disease, but they do not eliminate the affected apocrine-bearing tissue.
Wide excision of the affected areas
Correct. Chances of permanent cure are best with wide excision of the affected areas. Large fluctuant cysts are incised and drained, but that manages an episode rather than curing the disease.

B.io: b — Identify medical care strategies for pigmented skin lesions in adult and elderly populations
B.q: A 38-year-old man with a family history of melanoma has more than 100 naevi, several at least 5 mm with irregular, indistinct borders. How is a dysplastic naevus diagnosed, and what is the management?
opts: Biopsy, excising where melanoma is a concern

Correct. Diagnosis of a dysplastic melanocytic nevus is by biopsy. Management includes observation, biopsy of all changing or developing lesions, excision where there is concern for melanoma, and sun protection. Family history is a risk factor, and dysplastic nevus syndrome may produce over 100 naevi by adolescence.
Clinical diagnosis; no biopsy needed

Clinical suspicion prompts the biopsy that establishes the diagnosis. Relying on inspection alone in a patient with dysplastic nevus syndrome and a family history of melanoma forfeits the histology that distinguishes dysplasia from melanoma.
No follow-up once documented
Changing or developing lesions must be biopsied, which requires ongoing surveillance rather than a single documentation visit.
Biopsy, then excise all naevi prophylactically
The diagnostic method is right but excising more than a hundred lesions is neither practical nor indicated. Excision is directed at lesions where melanoma is a concern.
B.cite: CMS I Pigmented Skin Lesions - Shahsv-2.pptx, Slide 44

B.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 70-year-old woman has itchy, discoloured skin over both lower legs. Examination shows poorly demarcated erythematous and brown-pigmented patches in the gaiter region of both legs, with pitting oedema and varicosities. She is afebrile and both legs are affected equally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Stasis dermatitis

Correct. Stasis dermatitis follows chronic venous hypertension and produces pruritic erythematous, violaceous, or hyperpigmented patches in the gaiter region of one or both legs, with oedema and brown haemosiderin staining.
Nummular eczema
Nummular eczema produces discrete coin-shaped plaques rather than confluent hyperpigmented change with oedema and varicosities.
Contact dermatitis
Contact dermatitis produces a sharply demarcated eruption in the shape of the contactant, and chronically treated legs would need an identified allergen.
Cellulitis
Distinguishing stasis dermatitis from cellulitis is the primary clinical priority. Cellulitis is almost never bilateral and produces warmth, tenderness, and often fever, none of which is present.

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
B.q: A 16-year-old football player develops acne confined to the shoulders and upper back under his pads. What predisposing factor does this represent?
opts: Genetic predisposition
Genetics is a key factor with a three-fold risk if a first-degree relative is affected, but inherited susceptibility does not create a distribution that matches sports equipment.
Acne mechanica from pressure on the follicle
Correct. Acne mechanica results from pressure on the skin — shoulder pads, orthopaedic casts, and helmets are the named examples — occluding the pilosebaceous follicle.
Endocrine acne from insulin resistance

Insulin resistance is proposed to stimulate androgen production and is listed among endocrine factors, but it would produce acne in the hormonally responsive sebaceous areas rather than confined to a pressure site.
Drug-induced acne from an anabolic steroid
Anabolic steroid use is a recognised cause and belongs in the history of any athlete, but the strictly pressure-mapped distribution under the pads points to a mechanical cause.

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
B.q: A 27-year-old pregnant woman has several lesions on the upper trunk consisting of a central arteriole with radiating capillaries. What is the mechanism, and what should be asked in the history?
opts: Dilated dermal capillaries present from birth
Congenital dilated dermal capillaries describe nevus flammeus, which is present at birth and persists for life.
Dilated existing vessels; ask about oestrogen and alcohol

Correct. Nevus araneus involves no vascular proliferation and is due to dilation of pre-existing vessels. Oestrogen excess states may be the cause, and lesions resolve after delivery or cessation of hormonal contraception. History should cover pregnancies, hormone use, alcohol, and high-risk medications for liver damage.
Capillary proliferation with age; no history needed
Capillary proliferation with increasing age describes cherry angioma. The spider angioma is a dilation of existing vessels, and its associations are exactly what make the history important.
Blood extravasated into the dermis
Deposits of blood in the skin are petechiae and purpura, which are non-blanching. Spider angiomas blanch and refill from the centre.
B.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 89

B.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: An 8-year-old boy has three smooth, non-scarring patches of hair loss on the scalp with exclamation point hairs at the margins and fine pitting of several fingernails. A potassium hydroxide preparation of plucked hairs is negative. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
opts: Oral prednisone
A systemic corticosteroid escalates well beyond what limited patchy disease requires and carries growth and adrenal considerations in a child. Topical therapy is the stated first line at this age.
Topical corticosteroids
Correct. Topical steroids are first line in children 10 years old and younger. The child is 8, which places him in that group and avoids the discomfort of intralesional injection in a young child.
Oral terbinafine

Terbinafine treats tinea capitis, the principal alternative cause of patchy childhood hair loss, and the negative potassium hydroxide preparation together with a smooth non-scaling scalp argues against it. Exclamation point hairs and nail pitting point elsewhere.
Intralesional corticosteroids
Intralesional steroids are first line in adolescents and adults. They are the right drug class delivered by the wrong route for this age group, which is why this is the most tempting wrong answer.

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 51-year-old woman with known rosacea reports a gritty foreign-body sensation, blurred vision, and photophobia. What is the most appropriate action?
opts: Reassure the patient that ocular symptoms are unrelated to rosacea
Ocular rosacea is a recognised subtype with potential corneal complications. Dismissing the connection is the error most likely to result in vision loss.
Urgent ophthalmology referral
Correct. Ocular rosacea with keratitis, visual symptoms, or corneal involvement warrants urgent ophthalmology referral. Visual symptoms and photophobia raise exactly those concerns.
Begin topical metronidazole and reassess in six weeks
Topical metronidazole is first-line for papulopustular skin disease. It does not treat ocular involvement, and six weeks of observation with visual symptoms risks permanent corneal damage.
Routine ophthalmology referral within three months
The referral destination is right but the urgency is wrong, and the delay is the harm. Corneal involvement can threaten sight, which is why the referral is specified as urgent.

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
B.q: A 54-year-old woman with obesity has multiple soft, skin-coloured pedunculated papules 2 to 6 mm on the neck and in both axillae. They are asymptomatic apart from occasional catching on clothing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Verruca vulgaris
Common warts are rough greyish papules with thrombosed capillaries, typically on the hands.
Acrochordon

Correct. Acrochordons are fibroepithelial pedunculated papillomas with a narrow stalk and broad tip, occurring in areas of friction such as the neck, axilla, and groin, with increased incidence in women and in obesity.
Neurofibroma
Cutaneous neurofibromas are soft nerve sheath tumours that may be sessile or pedunculated but occur with other features of neurofibromatosis such as cafe au lait macules.
Seborrheic keratosis
Seborrheic keratoses are beige to brown stuck-on papules and plaques with a velvety or warty surface rather than soft pedunculated growths.
B.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 30

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 26-year-old woman has painful red lumps on both shins for ten days. Examination shows bilateral tender erythematous nodules 2 to 4 cm on the anterior tibial surfaces. None has ulcerated, and several are fading to a bruise-like colour. She had a sore throat a month ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pyoderma gangrenosum
Pyoderma gangrenosum produces rapidly expanding painful ulceration with undermined violaceous borders. That these nodules do not ulcerate is the key distinguishing feature.
Insect bite reactions
Arthropod bites produce pruritic papules and wheals rather than deep tender nodules evolving over weeks in a symmetric pretibial distribution.
Erythema nodosum

Correct. Erythema nodosum is a septal panniculitis producing bilateral tender non-ulcerating nodules 1 to 5 cm on the anterior shins, evolving over 3 to 6 weeks through bruise-like colours. Group A streptococcus is the commonest infectious trigger.
Nodular vasculitis
Nodular vasculitis characteristically ulcerates and favours the posterior calves rather than the anterior shins.

B.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
B.q: A 38-year-old farmer has tender, boggy, pustular plaques in the beard area. Hairs in the affected area are easily removed. What therapy is required?
opts: Oral cephalexin
The finding points the other way. Easy hair removal distinguishes tinea barbae from bacterial folliculitis, which is the comparison the differential draws.
A change of shaving technique
Pseudofolliculitis barbae is a foreign body reaction to hair that has curved back into the skin, producing papules with a visible re-entrant hair shaft rather than boggy pustular plaques.
Oral antifungal therapy

Correct. Hair is easily removed in tinea barbae unlike in bacterial folliculitis, and a bacterial culture can be done to rule the latter out. Topical antifungals do not penetrate the hair follicle, so oral therapy with griseofulvin or terbinafine is required.
A topical antifungal cream alone
The diagnosis is right but the treatment is not. Topical antifungals can be applied but do not penetrate the hair follicle, so oral therapy is required.
B.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 22

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
B.q: A 58-year-old man with diabetes has an asymptomatic brownish patch in the crural region and scaling between the fourth and fifth toes. Under a Wood's lamp the affected skin fluoresces coral-red. What is first-line treatment for localised disease?
opts: Topical erythromycin

Correct. Erythrasma is a chronic superficial infection of intertriginous skin caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum invading the upper third of the stratum corneum. Coral-red fluorescence under a Wood's lamp is diagnostic, and first-line treatment for localised disease is topical erythromycin or clindamycin.
Topical miconazole
Cutaneous candidiasis is on the differential, and an antifungal cream such as miconazole is added if yeast is also present. But candidiasis does not produce coral-red fluorescence.
Topical terbinafine

Tinea cruris and tinea pedis are on the differential and occupy the same sites, which is what makes this tempting. But dermatophytes do not fluoresce coral-red, and that finding is what settles the diagnosis.
Topical mupirocin
Staphylococcus aureus causes folliculitis, furuncles, and impetigo. It does not produce a chronic asymptomatic intertriginous patch with coral-red fluorescence.

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 40-year-old woman has had urticarial lesions for two months. Individual lesions persist for more than 24 hours and resolve leaving brownish discoloration. She reports arthralgia. What should be suspected?
opts: Urticarial vasculitis

Correct. Urticarial vasculitis is distinguished by lesions persisting beyond 24 hours that leave bruising, with low complement levels and a biopsy showing leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Ordinary wheals blanch fully and last under 24 hours.
Ordinary chronic urticaria

Chronic urticaria is common in women aged 20 to 40, which makes this tempting, but its individual lesions last less than 24 hours and leave no residual mark. The persistence and bruising are the findings that force a different diagnosis.
Hereditary angioedema

Hereditary angioedema is considered when angioedema occurs without wheals, and C4 with C1-esterase inhibitor level and function are the right tests for it. This patient has wheals, which points away from it.
Anaphylaxis
Anaphylaxis is an acute systemic emergency rather than a two-month eruption. Nothing in this presentation suggests airway, respiratory, or circulatory involvement.

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 28-year-old woman has an annular eruption of the forearms and the clinician is distinguishing erythema multiforme from urticaria. What feature most reliably separates them?
opts: Only erythema multiforme itches
Urticaria is characteristically pruritic, and erythema multiforme is managed in part with oral antihistamines for pruritus. Itch is present in both and separates neither.
Wheals stay fixed for several days

This reverses the behaviour of the two eruptions. A clinician applying it would mark a migratory urticarial eruption as erythema multiforme and pursue an unnecessary search for a herpetic or mycoplasmal trigger.
Only erythema multiforme blanches
Urticarial wheals blanch fully, which is one of their listed features. Blanching is therefore a property of the alternative diagnosis rather than of erythema multiforme.
Wheals migrate and last under 24 hours

Correct. The differential states that urticarial wheals are pruritic, migratory, and blanch fully, with no fixed target lesions and individual lesions lasting less than 24 hours. Fixity over days is what identifies erythema multiforme.

B.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 46-year-old woman reports gradual hair thinning over several years. Examination shows diffuse thinning across the central and parietal scalp with preservation of the frontal hairline. There are no bald patches, no scaling, no scarring, and no exclamation point hairs. Several of her male relatives began balding in their twenties. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Alopecia areata
Alopecia areata produces sudden, round, smooth 1 to 4 cm patches with exclamation point hairs, all of which are recorded as absent. It is patchy and abrupt rather than diffuse and gradual.
Lichen planopilaris

Scarring alopecias destroy the follicle and leave loss of follicular openings with scarring. The examination specifically records no scarring, and the distribution follows a recognised androgenetic pattern instead.
Male-pattern hair loss

Male-pattern hair loss begins with recession of the frontal hairline in a triangular frontotemporal pattern followed by vertex loss. This patient's frontal hairline is specifically preserved, which is the finding that separates the two patterns.
Female-pattern hair loss

Correct. Female-pattern hair loss produces diffuse thinning of the central and parietal scalp without significant change to the frontal hairline. There is an increased frequency of balding among first-degree male relatives, which the family history here supplies.

B.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 38-year-old man presents with thick scaly plaques on both elbows and knees that have been present for years. Examination shows well-demarcated salmon-pink plaques with adherent silvery scale over the extensor elbows and knees, the sacrum, and the scalp. A linear plaque has developed along a surgical scar on his forearm. When scale is lifted from one plaque, pinpoint bleeding appears. What is this bleeding phenomenon called?
opts: Auspitz sign
Correct. Auspitz sign is the appearance of bleeding when scale is removed from a psoriatic plaque, produced by the dilated capillaries lying immediately beneath a thinned suprapapillary epidermis.
Wickham striae
Wickham striae are the fine white lines visible on the surface of lichen planus plaques. They are a surface pattern seen without any manipulation, not a response to removing scale.
Nikolsky sign

Nikolsky sign is the slipping away of the top layers of skin from the lower layers when rubbed, and it is positive in pemphigus and negative in bullous pemphigoid. It involves epidermal separation rather than pinpoint bleeding from a descaled plaque.
Koebner phenomenon

Koebner phenomenon is also present in this patient — it is the development of lesions at sites of trauma, which is what the linear plaque along the surgical scar represents. But it describes the scar lesion, not the bleeding on scale removal.

B.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
B.q: A 69-year-old man has a dermatomal vesicular eruption and a student asks where zoster most often appears. Which dermatomes are most frequently involved?
opts: Thoracic about 55 percent, cranial about 20 percent
Correct. Thoracic dermatomes are most frequently involved at about 55 percent, cranial at about 20 percent, with lumbar and sacral distributions following.
Lumbar in the majority
Lumbar involvement occurs but is less frequent than thoracic and cranial disease.
Cranial about 55 percent, thoracic about 20 percent
The two are reversed. Thoracic involvement is by far the commonest, and inverting the figures would skew expectations toward cranial disease.
No dermatome predominates
There is a clear and clinically useful predominance, which is why the percentages are taught.
