B.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 100

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
B.q: A 9-year-old boy has head lice that persisted after a first pediculicide application. Why is a multimodal approach recommended, and what does the World Health Organization recommend regarding pediculicide assessment?
opts: Head lice are self-limiting
Head lice do not clear spontaneously in a useful timeframe and are readily transmitted among children aged 3 to 12, in whom the infestation is common.
Resistance is rising; read the result at 24 hours

Correct. A multimodal approach is warranted because of increasing resistance, and the World Health Organization recommends that pediculicidal testing be read 24 hours after application. If treatment is not followed appropriately, patients tend to seek alternative care such as essential oils.
Resistance is falling; read it immediately
Resistance is increasing rather than decreasing, and immediate assessment would not allow time for the pediculicide to act.
Essential oils are first line
Patients turn to essential oils and similar remedies when conventional treatment is not followed appropriately, which is presented as a consequence of poor adherence rather than a recommendation.
B.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 30

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
B.q: A 14-year-old boy with neurofibromatosis type 1 has a large, diffuse soft tissue mass running along a nerve in the thigh. What is a plexiform neurofibroma, and what is the concern with it?
opts: A discrete nerve sheath tumour at the surface
That describes a cutaneous neurofibroma, which is a well-circumscribed solid tumour arising from peripheral nerves, sessile or pedunculated. Plexiform lesions are the larger, more extensive form.
A pigmented macule growing with the child

Growth in proportion to the child describes café au lait macules, which are flat pigmented lesions rather than tumours. A plexiform neurofibroma is a soft tissue mass in the covering of a nerve and is not a pigmentary change at all.
A large tumour in nerve covering that may invade

Correct. Plexiform neurofibromas are tumours in the tissue covering nerves, occurring anywhere except the brain and spinal cord. They are large and extensive and may be locally invasive, so clinical evaluation is needed.
A tumour confined to brain and spinal cord

Plexiform neurofibromas occur anywhere except the brain and spinal cord, so this names the one location from which they are excluded. Confining them intracranially would also remove the local invasiveness that makes clinical evaluation necessary.
B.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 101

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
B.q: A 30-year-old man has confirmed tungiasis of both feet after a trip abroad. What management is appropriate?
opts: Excision or cryotherapy, with tetanus cover
Correct. Management includes surgical excision or cryotherapy and topical agents, tetanus prophylaxis, and systemic antibiotics. Prevention centres on avoiding walking barefoot in endemic areas.
Professional extermination of the home
Extermination is required for bedbugs, which live in the domestic environment. The flea in tungiasis is embedded in the patient's skin.
Antihistamines and oatmeal baths alone
Symptomatic treatment with antihistamines and oatmeal baths is the approach to cercarial dermatitis, which is self-limited. Tungiasis requires removal of the embedded flea.
Oral albendazole for 3 days
Albendazole 400 mg daily for 3 days is the treatment for cutaneous larva migrans, a different soil-acquired parasitic condition.
B.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 40

B.io: b — Identify medical strategies for common benign skin lesions in infants, adolescents, adults and the elderly
B.q: A 4-month-old has a large facial hemangioma that is beginning to obstruct the visual axis of one eye. What is first-line treatment?
opts: Serial observation alone

Serial observation is appropriate when no treatment is needed, but blocked vision is a listed functional indication for treatment, and untreated visual obstruction at this age threatens permanent amblyopia.
Immediate surgical excision in all cases
Surgical excision is one option among several rather than the first-line approach for a functional complication.
Pulsed dye laser as the primary treatment
Pulsed dye laser targets superficial vessels to a depth of about 1.2 mm. It has a role but is not first line for a lesion causing functional compromise.
An oral beta-blocker such as propranolol

Correct. Beta-blockers are first-line treatment, for example oral propranolol or timolol. Indications for treatment include cosmetic concern, functional involvement such as blocked vision, deep ulceration, and infection.
B.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 73

B.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 24-year-old woman presents with an itchy rash on her forearm. She had a laceration dressed with an adhesive bandage four days ago. Examination shows a sharply demarcated rectangular erythematous plaque with tiny vesicles corresponding exactly to the adhesive portions of the dressing, and a rectangle of normal skin in the centre where the cotton pad had lain. The laceration itself is clean and healing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Herpes simplex virus reactivation

Herpes simplex produces grouped vesicles on an erythematous base that progress to pustules and painful erosions at a fixed site. It does not lay itself out in a rectangle matching a dressing, and the lesion here is pruritic rather than painful.
Allergic contact dermatitis to the adhesive

Correct. Patients allergic to the adhesive in an adhesive bandage present with a bandage-shaped rash that spares the middle area where the cotton lay. The eruption reproduces the shape of the contactant, which is the signature of allergic contact dermatitis.
Wound infection of the underlying laceration

A wound infection would centre on the laceration itself with surrounding warmth, tenderness, and purulence. The laceration here is clean and healing, and the reaction is confined to skin the adhesive touched while sparing the wound.
Cellulitis of the forearm

Cellulitis produces poorly demarcated erythema with warmth, tenderness, and often fever, spreading outward without regard to what was taped to the skin. Sharp adhesive-shaped borders with central sparing exclude it.

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 62-year-old woman has several uniformly tan-brown macules on the dorsal hands and face that have appeared gradually over years. One lesion is larger, asymmetric, and has irregular borders with darker areas within it. What should be done about that lesion?
opts: Treat it as a seborrheic keratosis and leave it alone

Seborrheic keratoses have a stuck-on appearance with comedone-like openings on dermoscopy. Neither feature is described, and attributing an asymmetric irregular lesion to a benign growth without examination is the error the differential is designed to prevent.
Evaluate it with dermoscopy for lentigo maligna

Correct. Lentigo maligna, which is melanoma in situ, is asymmetric with irregular border and colour and darker areas, and dermoscopy is described as essential. A solar lentigo that has diverged from its uniform neighbours requires that evaluation.
Treat it as a café-au-lait macule and observe
Café-au-lait macules are uniform tan patches, usually present from early life. A newly irregular lesion in an older adult with chronic sun exposure does not fit.
Reassure her that it is a solar lentigo like the others

Solar lentigines are uniformly pigmented, so the asymmetry, irregular border, and internal colour variation are precisely the features that separate this lesion from the others. Reassurance here would delay a melanoma in situ diagnosis.

B.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
B.q: A 61-year-old man has had erythematous scaly patches and plaques on the trunk for four years, several larger than 5 cm, that have been treated as psoriasis and eczema without lasting response. Pruritus is prominent. What features discriminate this from the inflammatory conditions it resembles?
opts: Pruritus
Pruritus is common in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma but is shared with psoriasis, eczema, and tinea, so it separates none of them.
A positive potassium hydroxide preparation
A positive potassium hydroxide preparation would indicate tinea corporis, which is one of the alternatives being excluded rather than a feature of lymphoma.
Chronicity, treatment resistance, odd sites

Correct. Mycosis fungoides may resemble psoriasis, eczema, or tinea, and the discriminators are chronicity, treatment resistance, and large or oddly distributed lesions. Early morphology is localised or generalised erythematous patches or scaly plaques, usually on the trunk, frequently greater than 5 cm.
Truncal involvement
Truncal involvement is typical of the early disease but is also seen in the inflammatory conditions on the differential.
B.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 74

B.io: b — Identify medical care strategies for pigmented skin lesions in adult and elderly populations
B.q: A 63-year-old man has multiple light to dark brown macules with well-defined but irregular borders that tend to coalesce over his shoulders, where he has had severe sunburns. What is the underlying process and its epidemiological association?
opts: Basal melanocyte proliferation with more melanin

Correct. Solar lentigines arise from proliferation of basal melanocytes with increased melanin production and are strongly associated with older age, present in about 90 percent by age 50, along with sun damage, tanning, a history of ephelides, and birth control use.
T cell destruction of melanocytes
T cell mediated destruction of melanocytes causes vitiligo, which produces depigmented rather than hyperpigmented lesions.
Dermal capillary proliferation
Capillary proliferation produces cherry angiomas, which are red and blanchable rather than brown macules.
Somatic mutation present from birth
Somatic mutations underlie congenital melanocytic naevi, which are evident at birth or shortly after rather than acquired with cumulative sun exposure.
B.cite: CMS I Pigmented Skin Lesions - Shahsv-2.pptx, Slide 13

B.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
B.q: A 74-year-old man still has burning, stabbing pain four months after a thoracic zoster eruption cleared. What is first-line treatment?
opts: Long-term opioids
The definition is right but routine long-term opioid therapy is specifically to be avoided, and it carries dependence and falls risk in the elderly patients most affected.
Acetaminophen alone

Almost all patients have pain during the acute eruptive phase, and acetaminophen or a non-steroidal agent is used for mild acute pain. That is not postherpetic neuralgia, which is defined by persistence.
Antivirals
Seven days is far too short a threshold, and antivirals are acute-phase therapy rather than treatment for established neuropathic pain.
Gabapentin or a tricyclic antidepressant

Correct. Pain persisting 90 days or more after rash onset is the commonly used definition. First-line treatment is gabapentin or pregabalin, an appropriate tricyclic antidepressant, or topical lidocaine, with a capsaicin patch as a further option.
B.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 109

B.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 29-year-old woman has burning and small bumps around her mouth. Examination shows grouped monomorphic erythematous papules and papulopustules on the chin and nasolabial folds, with a narrow band of normal skin next to the lip margin. There are no comedones. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Impetigo
Impetigo produces honey-coloured adherent crusts over shallow erosions, usually in children, rather than monomorphic papules with perioral sparing.
Perioral dermatitis

Correct. Perioral dermatitis produces grouped monomorphic papules, papulovesicles, or papulopustules around the mouth, nose, or eyes, with a narrow zone beside the vermilion border characteristically spared.
Acne rosacea
Rosacea produces central facial erythema with flushing and telangiectasias, and it does not spare a band beside the vermilion border.
Seborrheic dermatitis
Seborrheic dermatitis produces more prominent greasy scale involving the scalp, eyebrows, glabella, and nasolabial folds rather than monomorphic papulopustules.

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 45-year-old fair-skinned woman reports facial flushing that worsens with sun exposure, hot drinks, and alcohol. Examination shows persistent central facial erythema with telangiectasias across the cheeks and nose, and she describes her skin as stinging easily. There are no papules, no pustules, and no comedones. What subtype does she have?
opts: Phymatous rosacea
Phymatous rosacea produces tissue hypertrophy, classically rhinophyma of the nose, and is the subtype for which female sex is not a risk factor. No hypertrophic change is described.
Papulopustular rosacea

The papulopustular subtype adds transient central facial papules and pustules on a background of erythema. The examination here records neither, which is the single finding separating the two subtypes.
Erythematotelangiectatic rosacea

Correct. The erythematotelangiectatic subtype produces persistent central facial erythema, flushing, and telangiectasias with sensitive stinging skin, and specifically no papules or pustules. It is the most common subtype.
Acne vulgaris
Acne vulgaris is distinguished by open and closed comedones in younger patients with a perioral and chin distribution, and it lacks persistent flushing. The absence of comedones is what excludes it.

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
B.q: A 45-year-old man has a small area of cellulitis of the forearm with minimal pain, no systemic signs, and no comorbidity. In which patient with cellulitis is no diagnostic workup required?
opts: Any patient already on antibiotics
Current antibiotic use does not remove the need for assessment, and failure to respond within 48 hours should raise necrotizing fasciitis.
Limited area, no systemic signs

Correct. Cellulitis is usually a clinical diagnosis, and no workup is needed when there is a limited area of involvement, minimal pain, no systemic signs, and no risk factor for serious illness such as extremes of age or immunocompromise.
Any patient who is afebrile
Fever may be absent depending on severity, so a normal temperature alone does not establish that the patient is low risk. Extent, pain, and comorbidity all contribute.
Any cellulitis of the lower leg
The lower leg is the most common site, so this describes the majority of cases rather than a low-risk subset. Site does not determine whether investigation is needed.

B.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 6-month-old girl is brought to the clinic by her father for a rash that has been present for three weeks. He reports she is difficult to settle at night and rubs her face against the bedsheet rather than scratching it. Her father has allergic rhinitis and her older brother has asthma. On examination there are weeping inflammatory patches and crusted plaques over both cheeks and the extensor surfaces of the forearms. The antecubital and popliteal fossae are clear. There is no fever, no purulent drainage, and no history of new detergents, soaps, or foods. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atopic dermatitis, infantile pattern

Correct. In infants atopic dermatitis produces weeping inflammatory patches and crusted plaques on the cheeks, scalp, and extensor surfaces, and rubbing commonly replaces scratching at this age. The family history of allergic rhinitis and asthma completes the atopic triad, and roughly 80 percent of patients have a personal or family history of atopy.
Seborrheic dermatitis

Seborrheic dermatitis affects sebum-rich sites and produces greasy, flaking, yellow scale over poorly demarcated erythematous plaques. The scalp is the characteristic site, and weeping, crusted extensor plaques with nocturnal pruritus are not its presentation.
Allergic contact dermatitis

Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction that produces a well-demarcated rash in the shape of the contactant at the site of exposure. The father denies new detergents, soaps, or foods, and a symmetric cheek-and-extensor distribution does not match any contact pattern.
Atopic dermatitis, childhood pattern

The condition is right but the pattern is wrong for the age. The childhood pattern is dry, ill-defined red plaques and scaly patches on flexural skin, particularly the antecubital and popliteal fossae — which this infant's examination specifically records as clear.

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 29-year-old woman presents with painful red lumps on both shins that appeared ten days ago. Examination shows bilateral tender erythematous nodules 1 to 5 cm on the anterior tibial surfaces. None has ulcerated, and several are fading to a bruise-like colour. She had a sore throat three weeks ago. What is the key distinguishing feature of this condition?
opts: The nodules do not ulcerate

Correct. That the nodules do not ulcerate is named as the key distinguishing feature. Erythema nodosum is a septal panniculitis without vasculitis, evolving over 3 to 6 weeks from bright red through the bruise-like colours the stem describes.
The nodules followed a streptococcal infection

Group A Streptococcus is the most common infectious trigger, and a throat culture with an antistreptolysin O titre is used to look for it. A trigger supports the diagnosis without being a feature of the lesions themselves.
The nodules are located on the anterior shins

The anterior tibial surface is the characteristic location and it supports the diagnosis, but the nodules may also appear on the thighs, forearms, and trunk. Site is typical rather than distinguishing.
The nodules are bilateral
Bilateral involvement is characteristic and helps separate it from a unilateral infectious process, but many panniculitides and vasculitides are also bilateral.

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 73-year-old man has multiple actinic keratoses scattered across a bald scalp, and the clinician explains that treating only the individual visible lesions may be insufficient. What concept does this reflect?
opts: Photoallergy
Photoallergy is an immunologic drug-induced mechanism confirmed by photopatch testing. It is unrelated to the distribution of premalignant keratinocytic lesions.
Koebner phenomenon
Koebner phenomenon occurs in psoriasis and lichen planus, where new lesions develop where the skin has been injured. It is not what makes actinic keratoses multifocal.
Field cancerisation
Correct. Actinic keratoses represent a field cancerisation process, meaning the ultraviolet-induced mutations extend through the surrounding skin rather than being confined to the visible lesions.
Pathergy
Pathergy is the worsening of pyoderma gangrenosum with trauma or debridement. It has no bearing on ultraviolet-induced keratinocytic dysplasia.

B.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
B.q: A 7-year-old boy is seen for a recurrent, intensely pruritic rash. Examination shows poorly demarcated erythematous plaques with excoriations and lichenification of the antecubital and popliteal fossae. His mother reports a history of asthma. There is no fever, drainage, crusting, or tenderness. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: Systemic prednisone

Systemic corticosteroids are reserved for severe disease and carry rebound and growth concerns in children. Escalating to a systemic agent before a site-appropriate topical has been tried is treating above the severity the examination shows.
Emollients alone, without a steroid

Emollients are the foundation of barrier repair but do not control established inflammation. This child already has excoriated, lichenified plaques, so withholding an anti-inflammatory leaves the active disease untreated.
Topical steroid plus emollient

Correct. Treatment combines barrier repair with inflammation control: low to medium potency topical corticosteroid for the body, applied sparingly, with an emollient applied after rinsing. Neither element alone is adequate, which is what makes this the complete answer.
Oral cephalexin

An oral antibiotic treats secondary bacterial infection, and the stem records no fever, drainage, crusting, or tenderness to suggest one. Treating an uninfected flare with an antibiotic exposes the child to a drug with no target.

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
C.q: A 37-year-old woman has a firm nodule on the lower leg and reports that it occasionally hurts when knocked. What is notable about the symptom profile of a dermatofibroma?
opts: Invariably painful
Most are asymptomatic. Requiring pain for the diagnosis would exclude the majority of lesions.
Always pruritic, never painful
Slight pruritus can occur, but pain is the symptom for which this lesion is specifically noted.
Symptomatic only if over 3 cm
The lesion is characteristically 0.5 to 1 cm, so a size threshold of that kind would apply to almost none of them.
The commonest painful skin tumour

Correct. Dermatofibroma is usually asymptomatic, sometimes with a history of insect bite, and when symptomatic may cause slight pruritus or pain — it is described as the most common painful skin tumour.
C.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 45

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 68-year-old man who has lost 9 kg without trying is found to have new velvety hyperpigmented thickening of the axillae, neck, and, unusually, the palms and oral mucosa, which developed rapidly over three months. He is not obese and his fasting glucose is normal. What is the most appropriate concern?
opts: Postinflammatory hyperpigmentation
Postinflammatory hyperpigmentation requires a history of prior inflammation at the affected site and produces flat pigment change rather than velvety thickening.
Paraneoplastic acanthosis nigricans

Correct. Malignant acanthosis nigricans is paraneoplastic, especially with gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma. Rapid onset, unusual sites including the palms and mucosa, and the absence of obesity or insulin resistance in an older patient with weight loss all point away from the common benign form.
Confluent and reticulated papillomatosis
Confluent and reticulated papillomatosis has a reticulate pattern and responds to minocycline. It does not involve the oral mucosa or carry a paraneoplastic association.
Insulin-resistant acanthosis nigricans

This is the most common form, driven by hyperinsulinaemia stimulating keratinocyte and fibroblast proliferation, and it is the right answer in most patients. Here the normal glucose, absent obesity, rapid onset, and mucosal involvement all argue against it.
C.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 22

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
C.q: A 44-year-old runner has a painful lesion on the plantar surface of the forefoot. Pressing straight down on it reproduces the pain, whereas squeezing it from the sides does not. The skin lines run through the lesion, and paring it reveals a central cone of hard keratin. What is the diagnosis?
opts: Verruca vulgaris

A wart interrupts the skin lines rather than allowing them to run through, may hurt with side pressure rather than downward pressure, and shows a blackened centre from thrombosed capillaries. All three features point away from it here.
Callus

A callus follows a broad area of pressure, producing diffuse thickening that is larger than a corn, irregular in shape, and lacks a central core. It is usually painless, whereas this lesion has both a core and downward tenderness.
Epidermoid cyst
An epidermoid cyst is a moveable round protruding mass with a central punctum that may drain foul-smelling keratin. It is not a hyperkeratotic pressure lesion of a weight-bearing surface.
Clavus (corn)
Correct. A clavus results from pressure on a localised area, creating a cone-shaped central core of hard keratin. Pain occurs on direct downward pressure, and the skin lines run through the lesion.
C.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 7

C.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
C.q: A 24-year-old wrestler has two itchy round plaques on the forearm. Examination shows sharply circumscribed slightly erythematous scaly rings with an advancing scaly border and a clearer centre. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pityriasis rosea
Pityriasis rosea follows a herald patch with a truncal eruption along the rib lines rather than isolated annular plaques on a forearm.
Tinea corporis

Correct. Tinea corporis produces one or more circular, sharply circumscribed, slightly erythematous dry scaly plaques with an annular appearance and central clearing, acquired from contact with infected humans or animals.
Nummular eczema
Nummular eczema is the classic mimic — both are red, itchy, and circular — but its plaques are uniform throughout WITHOUT central clearing.
Granuloma annulare
Granuloma annulare produces an annular ring of flesh-coloured papules WITHOUT scale, and it is characteristically asymptomatic.
C.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 24

C.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 23-year-old man reports a single 4 cm oval salmon-coloured scaly plaque on his back ten days ago, followed by a shower of smaller similar lesions across the trunk whose long axes run along the rib lines. He feels well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Secondary syphilis
Secondary syphilis mimics pityriasis rosea closely and classically involves the palms and soles, which are not described, and it lacks the solitary herald patch.
Pityriasis rosea

Correct. A herald patch precedes the exanthem in 50 to 90 percent of cases: a 2 to 5 cm oval salmon-coloured plaque that clears centrally, followed 1 to 2 weeks later by smaller lesions in the Christmas tree pattern.
Tinea corporis
A solitary annular scaly plaque resembles the herald patch closely, which is why this is the classic trap. But tinea does not produce a widespread secondary eruption aligned along the rib lines.
Guttate psoriasis
Guttate psoriasis produces raindrop-shaped papules 2 to 3 weeks after a streptococcal or upper respiratory infection, without a preceding herald patch.
C.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 169

C.io: b — Discuss unique considerations of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus skin infections, including risk factors, presentation, and treatment
C.q: A 7-year-old boy and his mother, who teaches at his school, both present with honey-crusted perioral lesions. In which patient with impetigo should a culture be obtained rather than relying on clinical appearance alone?
opts: Any patient with honey-coloured crusting
Honey-coloured adherent crust is the classic appearance of non-bullous impetigo and is what allows a clinical diagnosis. It is a reason not to culture rather than a reason to.
A healthcare worker or teacher

Correct. Cultures are obtained if the patient is at high risk for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection, with healthcare workers and teachers given as the examples, or if acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a concern.
Any patient on topical mupirocin
Mupirocin is adequate for most cases of limited non-bullous impetigo and as effective as oral therapy. Its use does not itself indicate culture.
Any child under five
Impetigo is common in infants and children and is most often diagnosed by clinical appearance. Age alone does not create the resistance risk that prompts culture.
C.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 93

C.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
C.q: A 7-year-old boy has scaly patches on the scalp with areas of hair loss and visible black dots where hairs have fractured. A potassium hydroxide preparation confirms fungal elements. His mother asks whether a medicated cream will be enough. What is the correct response?
opts: An antifungal shampoo alone
Selenium sulfide or ketoconazole shampoo reduces viable spore shedding and is a useful adjunct during early systemic treatment, but it explicitly does not replace oral therapy.
No treatment; it resolves after puberty

Changes in sebum fatty acid content after puberty are believed to inhibit dermatophyte growth, but waiting years in an infected 7-year-old leaves an active, transmissible infection with a risk of scarring alopecia.
Oral therapy; topicals miss the hair shaft
Correct. Tinea capitis requires oral therapy; topical agents alone do not penetrate the infected hair shaft. Antifungal shampoo reduces viable spore shedding but does not replace oral treatment.
A topical cream to the lesion and beyond
That instruction belongs to localised tinea corporis. The scalp differs because the organism resides within the hair shaft, where topical agents cannot reach.
C.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 15

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
C.q: A 31-year-old woman with obesity who smokes has recurrent painful nodules and draining lesions in both axillae and the groin, with five episodes in six months. Examination shows inflamed nodules and several sinus tracts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Acne vulgaris
Acne is called the resemblance for which hidradenitis is nicknamed acne inversa, but acne affects hormonally responsive sebaceous areas of the face, chest, and back and its hallmark is the comedone.
Hidradenitis suppurativa

Correct. Hidradenitis suppurativa is inflammation of apocrine glands affecting the axilla, groin, breasts, or perineum, and its three diagnostic elements are typical lesions, characteristic distribution, and recurrence more than twice in six months.
Furunculosis
A furuncle is a deep-seated infection of a single hair follicle presenting as a firm tender nodule with one opening, and it does not form sinus tracts over months.
Carbuncle
A carbuncle is two or more confluent furuncles with separate heads arising acutely, usually with fever and malaise, rather than a chronic recurrent process.
C.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 70

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
C.q: A 27-year-old woman has an itchy papular eruption two days after swimming in a freshwater lake. What is the management of cercarial dermatitis?
opts: Doxycycline for 5 to 10 days

Doxycycline treats rickettsial infection and is first line for Lyme disease. Cercarial dermatitis is caused by a flatworm larva rather than a bacterium, and there is no organism left to treat by the time the rash appears.
Antihistamines and oatmeal baths
Correct. Management is symptomatic: antihistamines, oatmeal baths, antipruritic lotions, aspirin for pain control, proper washing and hygiene, and topical or oral glucocorticoids.
Extermination of the water source
Extermination is the environmental step for bedbugs. Avoidance of infested water is the relevant preventive measure here.
Oral albendazole for 3 days

Albendazole treats cutaneous larva migrans. In cercarial dermatitis the human is not a viable host and the organism dies in the skin, so the problem is the inflammatory reaction rather than an ongoing infestation.
C.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 91

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
C.q: A 24-year-old traveller returns from a rural area having walked barefoot on sandy soil. He has several erythematous papules on the feet that have enlarged over weeks into firm, somewhat translucent yellow nodules 4 to 10 mm across, some painful. What is the diagnosis and how is it confirmed?
opts: Tungiasis, confirmed by dermoscopy visualising ovoid eggs

Correct. Tungiasis is infestation by penetration of the adult female flea into human skin to lay eggs. Solitary or multiple erythematous papules enlarge over weeks to 4 to 10 mm, sometimes forming a firm translucent nodule, and dermoscopy is used to visualise the ovoid eggs.
Cercarial dermatitis, confirmed by history of freshwater exposure
Cercarial dermatitis follows swimming in cercaria-infested water and produces urticaria-like lesions and papules rather than persistent translucent nodules.
Scabies, confirmed by skin scraping
Scabies favours the finger webs, wrists, axillae, and genitals with burrows and intense nocturnal itch rather than nodules on the feet after soil exposure.
Cutaneous larva migrans, confirmed by the serpentine trail

Cutaneous larva migrans also follows contact with contaminated soil, which makes it a genuine consideration. But it produces an erythematous, raised, serpentine trail advancing 2 to 3 cm per day rather than discrete enlarging nodules.
C.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 40

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
C.q: A 44-year-old man from Connecticut presents with a swollen, painful knee two years after an untreated tick bite. What is the classic manifestation of stage 3 late persistent Lyme disease?
opts: Monoarticular arthritis of a large joint

Correct. Stage 3 occurs months to years later, affecting skin, central nervous system, and musculoskeletal systems, with monoarticular or oligoarticular arthritis of the knee or weight-bearing joints as the classic manifestation.
Symmetric small-joint polyarthritis
The arthritis of late Lyme disease is monoarticular or oligoarticular and favours large weight-bearing joints rather than a symmetric small-joint pattern.
Cranial nerve palsies and meningitis
Cranial nerve palsies, meningitis, and radiculopathies belong to stage 2 early disseminated infection, occurring days to weeks after the bite.
A rash starting on ankles and wrists
A rash starting on the ankles and wrists is characteristic of Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
C.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 75

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 57-year-old man has confirmed toxic epidermal necrolysis with epidermal detachment of 45 percent of his body surface area. What is the mandatory disposition?
opts: A burn unit or intensive care unit

Correct. Burn unit or intensive care admission is mandatory for all cases of toxic epidermal necrolysis, together with immediate discontinuation of all suspect drugs, fluid resuscitation estimated as for major burns, and non-adhesive biological dressings.
A surgical ward for debridement
Wound care uses non-adhesive biological dressings such as biobrane or porcine xenograft. Aggressive surgical debridement is not the described approach.
Emergency department observation
The eruption progresses over days, so waiting for stabilisation in an emergency department delays the resuscitative and wound care that determine survival.
A general medical ward

A general ward cannot provide the fluid resuscitation, wound care, and temperature and infection control this condition demands. With mortality up to 30 to 35 percent, the level of care is not discretionary.
C.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 90

C.io: 4 — Discuss clinical principles and decision-making
C.q: A clinician seeing a 38-year-old woman with chest pain lists the diagnoses her initial cues suggest, then gathers further data to decide which are consistent with what has been observed. What does the hypothetico-deductive method involve?
opts: Propose hypotheses, then test them against the data

Correct. The hypothetico-deductive method proposes hypotheses and tests whether they are acceptable or not by deciding whether the data are consistent with what has been observed. It runs from initial history, examination, and screening cues through hypothesis generation to hypothesis evaluation.
Treat symptoms before a diagnosis is reached
Treating before a definitive diagnosis describes the naturalistic or event-driven approach, used mostly in emergency medicine.
Recognise patterns automatically
Fast, automatic pattern recognition is the intuitive system used in straightforward or common situations, contrasted with the more deliberate, controlled process.
Rank diagnoses purely by frequency
Base rates matter and common things occur commonly, but the method is defined by generating and testing hypotheses against the data.
C.cite: 1. svClinical Reasoning and Problem Solving.pptx, Slide 19

C.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 23-year-old woman presents with the sudden appearance of two smooth, round bald patches on her scalp, each about 3 cm across, that developed over three weeks. The underlying scalp is smooth without scaling, erythema, or scarring. Short hairs that are narrow at the root and normal in calibre at the tip are visible at the margins. She has a history of eczema and her mother has hypothyroidism. What finding is pathognomonic for the diagnosis?
opts: A history of atopy

Risk is genuinely increased with family history, atopy, and autoimmune disease, so these details support the diagnosis. Risk factors raise the pretest probability but are never pathognomonic for anything.
Round patches of loss

The areas of hair loss are often round and the scalp is often very smooth, which is typical, but roundness is also seen in tinea capitis and in traction and trichotillomania patterns. Typical is not the same as pathognomonic.
Exclamation point hairs

Correct. Exclamation point hairs are pathognomonic for alopecia areata. Their growth ability is changing in real time, which produces a hair that is thinner at the root but normal in calibre at the top — exactly the description given here.
Sudden onset over three weeks
Sudden onset of 1 to 4 cm patches is characteristic, but abrupt hair loss also occurs in telogen effluvium and in traumatic alopecias. Tempo narrows the differential without identifying the disease.
C.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 138

C.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
C.q: A 61-year-old woman with obesity has a well-demarcated erythematous patch in the inframammary fold with several small papules and pustules on adjacent skin just beyond the main area of redness. What topical choice covers both possibilities?
opts: Topical erythromycin
Coral-red fluorescence identifies erythrasma caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum, which is treated with topical erythromycin or clindamycin.
Topical terbinafine
Central clearing is the annular pattern of tinea rather than a candidal feature, and terbinafine is an allylamine aimed at dermatophytes.
Topical nystatin
The finding is right but the drug choice is wrong in the way that matters. Nystatin treats Candida only, so if a dermatophyte is also present it will be left untreated.
A topical azole

Correct. Satellite papules and pustules accompany the well-demarcated erythematous patches of candidal intertrigo. Topical nystatin treats Candida only, whereas topical azoles treat both Candida and dermatophytes.
C.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 72

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
C.q: A 41-year-old man in Connecticut has an expanding erythematous oval lesion 9 cm across with central clearing and a darker punctate centre at the site of a recent tick bite. He has mild fatigue. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Cellulitis
Cellulitis produces confluent warm tender erythema with indistinct borders rather than an expanding ring with central clearing.
Tinea corporis
Tinea corporis produces an annular plaque with an advancing SCALY border, and it does not expand to 9 cm within days of a tick bite.
Lyme disease

Correct. Stage 1 early localised Lyme disease is characterised by erythema migrans: a large expanding erythematous round or oval lesion over 5 cm with central clearing and often a darker punctate centre at the bite site, also called a bull's-eye.
Rocky Mountain spotted fever
Rocky Mountain spotted fever produces fever, headache, and a rash beginning on the ankles and wrists that spreads centrally, not a single expanding annular lesion.
C.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 72

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 26-year-old woman develops an itchy eruption of 2 to 4 mm erythematous papules across the upper chest and forearms a few hours after her first sunny weekend of spring. Her face, exposed year-round, is unaffected. She takes no medication. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Systemic lupus erythematosus
Photosensitive lupus produces persistent plaques with an abnormal antinuclear antibody panel, which is the test performed to exclude it.
Sunburn
Sunburn produces confluent erythema, warmth, and tenderness across all exposed skin rather than discrete pruritic papules sparing the face.
Polymorphous light eruption

Correct. Polymorphous light eruption is the commonest idiopathic photodermatosis, appearing 30 minutes to hours after ultraviolet exposure in the first sunny days of spring, with papules on the décolletage and forearms and sparing of habitually exposed skin.
Phytophotodermatitis
Phytophotodermatitis follows contact with furanocoumarins in plants and produces streaky erythema and blistering that traces where the juice ran.
C.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 105

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
C.q: A 44-year-old man in Tennessee has a painful lesion on the thigh two days after cleaning out a closet. Examination shows a central violaceous area surrounded by a rim of blanched skin, and beyond that a large area of erythema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Black widow spider bite
Black widow envenomation produces localised erythema, piloerection, and sweating within 30 minutes followed by crampy abdominal pain and muscle spasms rather than a necrotic-looking target lesion.
Cellulitis
Cellulitis produces confluent spreading erythema with warmth and tenderness, without a blanched rim around a violaceous centre.
Hobo spider bite
Hobo spider bites are painless with induration and paraesthesia within 30 minutes, and the spider is the predominant cause of necrotic arachnidism in the Pacific Northwest rather than the Southeast.
Brown recluse spider bite

Correct. The hallmark of a brown recluse bite is the red, white, and blue sign — a central violaceous area surrounded by a rim of blanched skin surrounded by a large erythematous area. Loxosceles reclusa is abundant in the American Midwest and Southeast and shelters in undisturbed places.
C.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 60

C.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 19-year-old man develops an intensely pruritic vesicular eruption in linear streaks two days after clearing brush. What immunological mechanism underlies allergic contact dermatitis, and what is its most common cause in the United States?
opts: Delayed type IV reaction, most often to nickel
The mechanism is right and nickel is genuinely the most common metal allergen, but urushiol sap is the most common cause overall.
Direct barrier disruption, no immune role
Direct barrier disruption without immunological sensitisation describes irritant contact dermatitis, which is the other major type of contact dermatitis and the more common of the two.
Immediate type I reaction to urushiol

The allergen is right but the mechanism is wrong. Immediate immunoglobulin E mediated reactions are what skin-prick testing evaluates, whereas allergic contact dermatitis is delayed and cell-mediated — which is why patch testing, not prick testing, diagnoses it.
Delayed type IV reaction, most often to urushiol

Correct. Allergic contact dermatitis is an immunologic cell-mediated, delayed, type IV hypersensitivity reaction. Urushiol sap of Toxicodendron species, found in poison ivy, poison sumac, and poison oak, is the most common cause, and roughly 50 to 75 percent of people in the United States are allergic to these plants.
C.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 85

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 55-year-old man is admitted with widespread painful erythema progressing to flaccid bullae and confluent epidermal detachment of about 40 percent of the body surface area, with a positive Nikolsky sign and severe mucosal erosions. What distinguishes this from Stevens-Johnson syndrome?
opts: A prodrome

A prodrome of fever and malaise occurs in both. In toxic epidermal necrolysis it includes high fever, stinging eyes, and painful swallowing 1 to 3 days before the skin findings, but its presence does not separate the two.
Mucosal involvement
Mucosal erosions occur in both conditions — they are among the defining features of Stevens-Johnson syndrome itself. Using mucosal involvement to separate them would misclassify most patients.
A positive Nikolsky sign
Nikolsky sign is a feature of epidermal detachment and appears across the spectrum. It is also used to distinguish these conditions from erythema multiforme rather than from one another.
Detachment over 30 percent

Correct. The two conditions sit on one spectrum and are separated by the percentage of body surface area involved: Stevens-Johnson syndrome has less than 10 percent detachment, and toxic epidermal necrolysis has more than 30 percent, with mortality up to 30 to 35 percent.
C.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 88

C.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
C.q: A 27-year-old man has scaly annular plaques of the groin and scaling between the toes, and a student asks how these infections are named. How are dermatophyte infections classified, and what does the naming convey?
opts: By species: Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton
There are three genera of dermatophytes and species identification guides drug choice in tinea capitis. But the tinea naming system itself refers to body site rather than organism.
By depth of dermal invasion
Dermatophytes infect only dead keratin in the stratum corneum, hair, and nails, so they do not invade the dermis at all.
By the patient's age
Age matters epidemiologically — tinea capitis is predominantly preadolescent and tinea pedis is the most common dermatophyte infection in adults — but it is not what the tinea names denote.
By body location: capitis, corporis, cruris, pedis
Correct. Dermatophyte infections are classified by body location: tinea capitis for scalp, barbae for beard, corporis for body, manuum for hand, cruris for the inguinal creases, and pedis for feet.
C.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 7

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
C.q: A 38-year-old man in Oregon has a painless bite on the forearm that has become indurated with a large surrounding erythematous area. In which region of the United States is the hobo spider the predominant cause of necrotic arachnidism?
opts: The Gulf Coast
The Gulf Coast is not the region associated with this spider. Hobo spiders predominate in the Pacific Northwest, where they are frequently mistaken for brown recluses.
The Northeast
Erythema migrans is the stage 1 lesion of Lyme disease, a tick-borne spirochaetal infection.
The Midwest and Southeast

The Midwest and Southeast is brown recluse territory, and the red, white, and blue sign is its hallmark. Hobo spiders are often mistaken for brown recluses, which is exactly the confusion this distinction addresses.
The Pacific Northwest

Correct. The hobo spider, also called the aggressive house spider, is the predominant cause of necrotic arachnidism in the Pacific Northwest. The bite is painless, with induration and paraesthesia of the bite site within 30 minutes, a large erythematous area, and vesicle formation during the first 36 hours.
C.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 64

C.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 34-year-old man presents with an itchy, scaling annular plaque on the trunk. The clinician wishes to confirm the presence of fungal elements at the bedside before starting treatment. What is the most appropriate test?
opts: Tzanck smear

A Tzanck smear provides rapid evaluation of vesicular lesions for herpesvirus cytologic changes, with polymerase chain reaction preferred for confirmation. The lesion here is a scaling annular plaque rather than a vesicular eruption.
Nail clipping with periodic acid-Schiff stain
Nail clipping with periodic acid-Schiff stain evaluates suspected onychomycosis. It is the correct test for fungal nail disease specifically, and this lesion is on the trunk.
Potassium hydroxide wet preparation

Correct. A potassium hydroxide wet preparation detects fungal elements in skin, hair, or nail samples, and it is the appropriate bedside confirmation before treating a suspected dermatophyte infection.
Mineral oil preparation

A mineral oil preparation is a rapid bedside test, but it is used to confirm scabies by identifying the Sarcoptes scabiei mite, its eggs, or its fecal pellets. It is the right kind of test aimed at the wrong organism.
C.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 28

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
C.q: A 31-year-old woman develops an itchy pustular eruption two days after using a hotel hot tub. Examination shows follicular papules and pustules over the trunk, buttocks, and proximal limbs, sparing the face, neck, palms, and soles. She is afebrile. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Shower after hot tub use to prevent it

Showering after contact with contaminated water specifically does not prevent infection. Prevention depends on continuous water filtration, frequent monitoring of chlorine levels, and frequent water changes.
Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
That regimen targets methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, whereas the organism here is a gram-negative rod acquired from contaminated water. The antibiotic would not cover it.
Reassurance; most resolve in 2 to 10 days

Correct. Pseudomonas folliculitis is usually self-limiting and most cases resolve without specific treatment, clearing in 2 to 10 days. A wet dressing of 5 percent acetic acid may be applied for 20 minutes 2 to 4 times daily for symptom relief.
Oral ciprofloxacin for all patients
Ciprofloxacin is reserved for widespread or resistant cases. Prescribing it routinely for a self-limiting eruption exposes the patient to a fluoroquinolone with no benefit over observation.
C.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 52

C.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 38-year-old man has a blotchy eruption on the trunk whose edges cannot be traced, and the clinician documents it as poorly demarcated. What does this term convey?
opts: Smaller than 1 cm
Size is documented separately from demarcation. A 1 cm threshold separates macules from patches and papules from nodules, but it has no bearing on how sharply a lesion is bounded.
Irregular, blotchy, poorly defined borders
Correct. A poorly demarcated lesion has an irregular or blotchy appearance without well-defined borders, in contrast to a well-demarcated lesion, which has clearly defined borders.
Elevated above the surrounding skin
Elevation belongs to primary morphology, distinguishing papules, nodules, and plaques from flat lesions. Demarcation is an independent descriptor.
Clear borders but irregular internal colour
Clearly defined borders make a lesion well demarcated regardless of its internal colour variation. Demarcation describes the edge, not the interior.
C.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 20

C.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
C.q: A 71-year-old man reports three days of burning pain in a band across the left flank, followed by an eruption. Examination shows grouped vesicles on an erythematous base confined to a single band that stops abruptly at the midline. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Bullous impetigo
Bullous impetigo produces fragile superficial bullae on intact skin, mainly in children, without a prodrome of dermatomal pain.
Allergic contact dermatitis
Allergic contact dermatitis from urushiol produces linear vesicular streaks where the plant grazed the skin, crossing anatomical boundaries freely.
Herpes simplex virus
Herpes simplex produces grouped vesicles at a fixed site, often recurrent, but it does not follow a dermatome or stop at the midline.
Herpes zoster

Correct. Herpes zoster is reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus, preceded by dermatomal dysesthesia or pain, with grouped herpetiform vesicles on an erythematous base confined to one or two adjacent sensory nerves that stop abruptly at the midline.
C.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 98

C.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
C.q: A 23-year-old woman has plantar warts that are not painful and do not interfere with walking. What is the appropriate management?
opts: Cryotherapy every 2 to 3 weeks regardless of symptoms
Cryotherapy every 2 to 3 weeks is an option when treatment is indicated, but it may cause pain, blistering, and pigment change — all of which are unjustified for an asymptomatic lesion.
Oral antiviral therapy to eradicate human papillomavirus
No therapy eradicates human papillomavirus with certainty, and oral antivirals are not among the treatments for cutaneous warts.
Daily salicylic acid 40 percent indefinitely to prevent recurrence
Salicylic acid 40 percent is a treatment for symptomatic plantar warts rather than indefinite prophylaxis, and treatment choice should account for location, symptoms, and risk of scarring.
No therapy is required unless they are painful
Correct. Plantar warts do not require therapy unless they are painful. They can cluster together to form a mosaic wart, and treatment when needed is salicylic acid 40 percent or cryotherapy.
C.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 145

C.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 9-year-old girl develops an abrupt eruption of numerous small raindrop-shaped scaly papules and plaques over the trunk and proximal limbs. Her mother reports she was treated for a sore throat about two and a half weeks ago. She is otherwise well. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Systemic corticosteroids tapered over four weeks

Systemic steroids are specifically hazardous in psoriasis: pustular psoriasis may follow systemic steroid withdrawal, and that form is abrupt and life-threatening. Prescribing them here risks converting a self-limited eruption into a dangerous one.
Reassurance, with topical steroids if needed

Correct. Guttate psoriasis presents as raindrop-shaped erythematous papules and plaques, typically in children 2 to 3 weeks following a streptococcal infection or upper respiratory infection. No treatment is needed, though phototherapy and topical steroids may be used.
Topical mupirocin to the affected areas

Mupirocin is a topical antibacterial. The streptococcal infection that triggered this eruption was in the throat and has already been treated; the skin lesions are an immune-mediated psoriatic response rather than a cutaneous bacterial infection.
Oral methotrexate

Methotrexate belongs to moderate-to-severe disease or to plaque psoriasis that has failed topical therapy. Committing a child with a self-limited post-streptococcal eruption to an antimetabolite is treating far above the disease.
C.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 164

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pigmented skin lesions
C.q: A 26-year-old woman with vitiligo affecting more than 5 percent of her body surface area is being counselled on treatment. What is first-line, and why is one phototherapy option preferred over another?
opts: Surgical grafting for all patients
Management is multifactorial and depends on the extent of disease, with topical therapy and phototherapy preceding surgical approaches.
Psoralen with ultraviolet A preferred
This inverts the safety comparison. Psoralen with ultraviolet A is the option associated with increased skin cancer risk, which is why narrow band ultraviolet B is preferred.
Topical therapy alone at any extent
Topical therapy is used when there is limited surface involvement below 5 percent. Relying on it for extensive disease under-treats the patient.
Phototherapy; narrow band ultraviolet B

Correct. Phototherapy is first line in patients with more than 5 percent body surface area involvement, and narrow band ultraviolet B is preferred over psoralen with ultraviolet A, which carries adverse effects including increased skin cancer risk. Combination of topical therapy with phototherapy is ideal.
C.cite: CMS I Pigmented Skin Lesions - Shahsv-2.pptx, Slide 25

C.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
C.q: A 70-year-old man has a painful vesicular eruption in a band across one side of the chest. What is the single most characteristic distributional feature of herpes zoster?
opts: It crosses the midline symmetrically
This is the direct inversion of the defining feature. A bilateral symmetric eruption should prompt a different diagnosis entirely.
It is generalised over trunk and face
That distribution describes primary varicella rather than reactivation, and varicella shows multiple stages simultaneously.
It stops abruptly at the midline

Correct. Blisters are confined to the cutaneous distribution of one or two adjacent sensory nerves and abruptly stop at the midline. Thoracic dermatomes are most frequently involved at about 55 percent, followed by cranial at about 20 percent.
It is confined to skin folds
Flexural and intertriginous distribution suggests candidal intertrigo, erythrasma, or inverse psoriasis rather than a dermatomal viral reactivation.
C.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 100

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
C.q: A 48-year-old man has soft yellow plaques on the medial aspects of both upper eyelids. What do they contain?
opts: Keratin within an epithelial cyst
The composition is right but stopping at cosmesis discards the reason the lesion matters. The association with lipid disorders and increased cardiac risk is exactly what makes screening worthwhile.
Eccrine duct neoplasms
Keratin within enclosed epithelium describes an epidermoid cyst, which is a firm moveable nodule with a central punctum rather than a soft yellow eyelid plaque.
Lipid-laden macrophages

Correct. Xanthelasma consists of soft yellow cholesterol plaques formed by collections of lipid-laden macrophages. They are associated with lipid disorders, so screening for hyperlipidaemia is indicated, and they may signify increased cardiac risk.
Dilated capillaries
Syringomas are eccrine duct neoplasms of the lower eyelids appearing at puberty, and they are firm skin-coloured papules rather than soft yellow plaques.
C.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 104

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
C.q: A 6-year-old boy has several lesions around the nose and mouth that began as small blisters and now show golden-yellow adherent crusts over shallow erosions. There is palpable submandibular lymphadenopathy. He is afebrile. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Ecthyma
Ecthyma deepens into dermal ulceration with a thicker grey-yellow crust and is predisposed to by tissue damage or immunocompromise.
Perioral dermatitis
Perioral dermatitis produces grouped monomorphic papules and papulopustules with sparing beside the vermilion border, and it affects young women rather than children.
Impetigo

Correct. Non-bullous impetigo is the commoner form: a macule evolves into a vesicle or pustule that ruptures, leaving honey-coloured adherent crust over an erosion, typically perioral in children, with regional lymphadenopathy common.
Herpes simplex virus
Herpes simplex produces grouped vesicles on an erythematous base progressing to pustules and painful erosions, rather than honey-coloured crusts.
C.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 87

C.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 31-year-old man with progressive frontotemporal recession and early vertex thinning asks about treatment. He and his partner are not planning a pregnancy and he has no contraindications. Which statement about the two principal medical therapies is correct?
opts: Minoxidil works best at the frontal hairline
The region is wrong. Minoxidil prevents further loss and may lead to regrowth but is primarily effective in the crown region of the scalp, which is the opposite of what this states.
Finasteride's sexual effects are permanent

About 2 percent of men taking finasteride report decreased libido and erectile function, but these effects are reversible when the drug is stopped. Telling a patient they are permanent would wrongly deter effective treatment.
Finasteride is topical and minoxidil oral
The routes are reversed. Minoxidil is the topically applied agent and finasteride is the oral one, so a patient given this advice would apply and swallow the wrong drugs.
Finasteride is oral and works best with minoxidil

Correct. Finasteride prevents further hair loss and may provide some regrowth, and works best in combination with minoxidil. Dihydrotestosterone is the androgen chiefly responsible for the follicular miniaturisation, which is what the enzyme inhibition addresses.
C.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 148

C.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
C.q: A 39-year-old man with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome has red-purple plaques on the trunk and on the hard palate. What causes Kaposi sarcoma, and what does it arise from?
opts: Human immunodeficiency virus, in endothelium
Human immunodeficiency virus creates the immunodeficiency that permits epidemic disease, but human herpesvirus 8 is the causative agent, which is why the classic and endemic forms occur without it.
Ultraviolet damage to dermal fibroblasts
Ultraviolet damage drives keratinocyte carcinomas and melanoma rather than this vascular tumour.
Human papillomavirus, in keratinocytes
Human papillomavirus infects keratinocytes and produces warts. Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular endothelial neoplasm.
Human herpesvirus 8, in vessel-lining cells

Correct. Kaposi sarcoma develops in the cells lining blood and lymph vessels and is associated with human herpesvirus 8. It produces red or purple macules, plaques, or nodules on skin or mucous membranes and can involve internal organs.
C.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 63

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 47-year-old fair-skinned woman reports facial flushing worsened by sun, hot drinks, and alcohol. Examination shows persistent central facial erythema with telangiectasias across the cheeks and nose. There are no comedones. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Acne vulgaris
Acne vulgaris is distinguished by open and closed comedones in younger patients and lacks persistent flushing. The absence of comedones excludes it.
Acne rosacea

Correct. The erythematotelangiectatic subtype produces persistent central facial erythema, flushing, and telangiectasias with sensitive stinging skin, triggered by sun exposure, heat, alcohol, and spicy food.
Systemic lupus erythematosus
A malar rash spares the nasolabial folds and is accompanied by systemic features, and it does not flush with hot drinks and alcohol.
Seborrheic dermatitis
Seborrheic dermatitis produces greasy scale in the nasolabial folds and scalp rather than persistent erythema with telangiectasias.
C.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 66

C.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
C.q: A 74-year-old man has a keratotic lesion on the ear that has enlarged over six weeks and now bleeds when he shaves. Which findings in a keratotic lesion are red flags for squamous cell carcinoma?
opts: Rapid growth, pain, bleeding, and ulceration
Correct. Red flags for squamous cell carcinoma include rapid growth, pain, bleeding, and ulceration, and the same features in an actinic keratosis prompt biopsy to exclude early carcinoma.
A pearly translucent surface with telangiectasias
Pearly translucency with telangiectasias is the hallmark of nodular basal cell carcinoma.
A stuck-on appearance with comedone-like openings
That describes seborrheic keratosis, a benign lesion, though an inflamed seborrheic keratosis does appear on the squamous cell carcinoma differential.
Sandpaper texture and small size
A sandpapery 0.2 to 0.6 cm papule is the description of an uncomplicated actinic keratosis, which is the lesion these red flags distinguish from.
C.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 22

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
C.q: A 24-year-old woman is given silicone gel sheeting for a keloid on the chest and asks how it works and how long she must wear it. What is the theoretical basis for using it?
opts: It delivers corticosteroid transdermally
Silicone sheeting is not a drug delivery system. Corticosteroid for keloids is given by intralesional injection.
It cools the scar, reducing blood flow
The proposed mechanism is an increase rather than a decrease in temperature, and the duration is far longer than two weeks.
It warms the scar, raising collagenase activity
Correct. The theory is that occlusive dressings such as silicone gel sheets increase the temperature of the scar and thereby collagenase activity. They are worn 12 to 24 hours a day for up to a year.
It induces tissue hypoxia
Tissue hypoxia with fibroblast degeneration and collagen degradation is the proposed mechanism of compression therapy, which is a different modality using spandex pressure devices.
C.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 16

C.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
C.q: A 34-year-old man has an itchy, sharply demarcated plaque on the proximal medial thigh extending from the crural fold. The scrotum is not involved. He also has scaling between his toes. What does the scrotal sparing indicate?
opts: It supports tinea cruris

Correct. In tinea cruris the scrotum is typically spared, and scrotal involvement suggests candidal intertrigo, which commonly involves the scrotum. His coexisting tinea pedis fits, since the two often occur together.
It indicates inverse psoriasis

Inverse psoriasis affects flexural sites but is not distinguished by scrotal sparing, and psoriasis is characterised by well-demarcated plaques with silver scale rather than an advancing fungal border.
It has no diagnostic significance
The distribution is precisely what separates the two commonest groin diagnoses, so discarding it removes the most useful bedside discriminator.
It indicates erythrasma
Erythrasma involves the inner thighs, crural region, and scrotum and fluoresces coral-red under a Wood's lamp. Scrotal involvement is typical of erythrasma rather than excluded by it.
C.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 33

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 55-year-old woman asks about treatment for photoaging. What topical agent is approved for this indication, and what should she be told to expect?
opts: Tretinoin, with initial irritation over 6 to 12 months

Correct. Tretinoin 0.025 to 0.1 percent is the only approved topical agent for photoaging. It stimulates collagen synthesis, inhibits matrix metalloproteinase activity, and reduces fine lines and dyspigmentation; therapy is started low and titrated, with initial retinoid dermatitis expected.
Hydroquinone
Pigment-directed agents address dyspigmentation but do not reverse the dermal structural damage. Tretinoin is the agent named for the photoaging indication.
Tretinoin, with results in two weeks and no irritation

The agent is right but the expectations are wrong in both directions. Promising rapid results without warning about retinoid dermatitis is the counselling failure that makes patients stop before the minimum 6 to 12 months of use required.
Topical corticosteroids nightly
Prolonged topical corticosteroid use causes atrophy, striae, and telangiectasia, which would compound rather than treat photoaged skin.
C.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 119

C.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
C.q: A 20-year-old man presents in late summer with numerous well-defined hypopigmented macules 4 to 5 mm over the upper back and shoulders, some coalescing. They did not tan with the rest of his skin. Scraping the surface reveals fine scale. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pityriasis versicolor

Correct. Pityriasis versicolor is caused by overgrowth of lipid-dependent Malassezia and produces velvety tan, pink, or white scaling macules 4 to 5 mm on the neck, upper arms, trunk, and groin. Hypopigmentation reflects altered melanocyte function and reduced tanning.
Pityriasis alba
Pityriasis alba produces ill-defined hypopigmented patches with fine scale, usually on the face of atopic children rather than the upper trunk of a young adult.
Vitiligo
Vitiligo produces COMPLETE depigmentation with distinct margins and no scale, and the patches fluoresce under a Wood's lamp.
Postinflammatory hypopigmentation
Postinflammatory change requires preceding inflammation at the site and does not produce fine scale on scraping.
C.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 78

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
