C.q: Four women in their twenties present on the same clinic list with acne of differing severity and history. For which patient is a combined oral contraceptive most appropriate as acne therapy?
opts: A woman planning pregnancy soon
A patient planning pregnancy is not an appropriate candidate for contraceptive-based therapy, and the treatment goal and the reproductive goal are in direct conflict.
A man with papulopustular acne
Combined oral contraceptives are not applicable to male patients, whose moderate disease is treated with a topical retinoid, an oral antibiotic, and benzoyl peroxide.
Hyperandrogenism unresponsive to topicals

Correct. Oral contraceptives are considered for patients with hyperandrogenism and when acne is unresponsive to both topical retinoids and topical or oral antibiotics. Oestrogen decreases sebum production and reduces ovarian androgen production.
Any adolescent, as first-line therapy
Combined oral contraceptives sit well down the systemic treatment list and are considered for specific indications rather than used as universal first-line therapy.
C.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 28

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
C.q: A 38-year-old man has a moveable, round, firm nodule on the back with a visible central pore. It occasionally discharges foul-smelling material. It is not currently red or tender. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Abscess
An abscess is warm, tender, and erythematous with purulent contents developing acutely, not a chronic mass with intermittent discharge.
Epidermoid cyst

Correct. An epidermoid cyst is a cystic enclosure of epithelium within the dermis filled with keratin, presenting as a single moveable round protruding mass with a central pore or punctum communicating with the surface.
Dermatofibroma
Dermatofibroma is a firm dermal nodule with a brown halo and positive dimple sign, most commonly on the legs.
Lipoma
A lipoma is a soft, mobile subcutaneous overgrowth of fat without a central punctum and does not discharge material.
C.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 54

C.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
C.q: A 44-year-old woman presents with a change in one fingernail and arrives wearing dark polish on every nail. What examination step is specified when evaluating a nail for a possible neoplasm?
opts: Defer examination until pigment has been present for a year
Delayed recognition contributes to worse outcomes, so waiting a year is the opposite of what is advised.
Remove polish and inspect every nail

Correct. History and examination should document onset, evolution, trauma, bleeding, pain or cold sensitivity, prior treatments, medications, immune status, human papillomavirus risk, and personal or family melanoma history, and polish must be removed so that every nail can be inspected.
Perform a potassium hydroxide preparation before any inspection
Confirming fungus matters when onychomycosis is suspected, but it does not replace inspection of the nail unit for a neoplasm.
Inspect only the symptomatic nail to avoid unnecessary examination
Comparing every nail is what identifies a single-digit change, which is the pattern that raises melanoma.
C.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 93

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
C.q: A 52-year-old woman has a soft, mobile, non-tender subcutaneous mass on the upper back that has enlarged very slowly over years. There is no overlying punctum, redness, or warmth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Abscess
An abscess is warm, tender, and erythematous with purulent contents rather than a painless mass present for years.
Dermatofibroma
Dermatofibroma is a firm 0.5 to 1 cm dermal nodule with a brown halo and a dimple sign, not a soft subcutaneous mass.
Liposarcoma
Rapid growth, fixation, or pain would raise a sarcoma; a slowly enlarging soft mobile mass is characteristic of the benign lesion.
Lipoma
Correct. A lipoma is a benign localised overgrowth of fat cells in subcutaneous tissue and the most common soft tissue tumour, typically soft, mobile, and asymptomatic unless compressing a structure.
C.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 105

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
C.q: A 16-year-old girl starting treatment for acne of the face and back asks how quickly it will work. What education is accurate?
opts: No improvement for at least six months
This understates the response and may prompt unnecessary escalation to systemic therapy while a working regimen is dismissed as ineffective.
4 to 6 weeks, with all sites responding equally
The timeline is right for the face but the claim of uniform response is wrong, and it is the part that causes patients to abandon treatment for truncal acne before it has had time to work.
4 to 6 weeks; back and chest take 3 to 4 months

Correct. Improvement in lesions can take 4 to 6 weeks, clinical improvement is measured by the number of new lesions after 6 to 8 weeks of therapy, and areas on the back and chest are slowest to respond, taking 3 to 4 months.
Response cannot be measured objectively
Response is measured objectively by the number of new lesions after 6 to 8 weeks, which is what allows a regimen to be judged and changed.
C.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 36

C.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
C.q: A 67-year-old woman presents on day four of a dermatomal vesicular eruption with new lesions still appearing. Within what window should antiviral therapy ideally be started, and when should it still be given beyond that window?
opts: Within 72 hours only, never after

This is the closest wrong answer because the 72-hour target is correct. But refusing treatment beyond it would deny antivirals to patients with active new lesion formation or ophthalmic disease, who still benefit.
Only after polymerase chain reaction confirms it

Typical unilateral dermatomal vesicles are diagnosed clinically, and polymerase chain reaction is reserved for atypical, disseminated, vaccine-modified, or immunocompromised presentations. Waiting for it forfeits the treatment window.
Only once postherpetic neuralgia develops
Postherpetic neuralgia is the chronic complication defined as pain persisting at least 90 days after rash onset. Antivirals are an acute-phase treatment.
Within 72 hours, and later if lesions still form

Correct. Antivirals should be started as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours of rash onset, and treatment is still given after 72 hours when new lesions are forming or there is ophthalmic involvement.
C.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 106

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 52-year-old man taking allopurinol for four weeks has fever, stinging eyes, and painful swallowing, followed by painful erythema progressing to flaccid bullae and sheet-like skin loss over about 40 percent of his body surface. Lateral pressure on normal skin causes the epidermis to slide. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Toxic epidermal necrolysis

Correct. Toxic epidermal necrolysis is drug-induced in over 80 percent of cases, with allopurinol the most common trigger worldwide. It produces confluent epidermal detachment over 30 percent of the body surface with a positive Nikolsky sign.
Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Stevens-Johnson syndrome sits at the other end of the same spectrum, with less than 10 percent detachment. The 40 percent extent here places it beyond that boundary.
Pemphigus vulgaris
Pemphigus produces flaccid bullae with a positive Nikolsky sign but evolves over months from oral erosions rather than over days after a new drug.
Erythema multiforme major
Erythema multiforme major produces target lesions, is usually associated with herpes simplex virus, and involves far less mucosa and body surface.
C.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 88

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 33-year-old woman presents with widespread itchy wheals that have been appearing and disappearing for three days. Individual lesions last a few hours, blanch fully, and leave no mark. There is no fever, no joint pain, and no bruising at resolved sites. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
opts: Intramuscular epinephrine
Epinephrine is given immediately for anaphylaxis. There is no airway, respiratory, or circulatory compromise described here, so this treats a far more severe condition than the patient has.
Skin biopsy before treatment

Biopsy is indicated when urticarial vasculitis is suspected — lesions persisting beyond 24 hours and leaving bruising. This patient's lesions last hours and leave no mark, so those features are specifically absent.
A second-generation antihistamine

Correct. Second-generation antihistamines are first-line for urticaria. Urticaria results from mast cell degranulation releasing histamine, prostaglandins, and leukotrienes, causing transient dermal oedema.
A first-generation antihistamine
First-generation antihistamines are sedating, and the second-generation agents are the ones named as first line. Scheduled diphenhydramine imposes sedation without added benefit.
C.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 39

C.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 57-year-old man has a suspicious pigmented growth on the back that the clinician wishes to sample in a way that removes the entire lesion with deep and wide margins. What biopsy technique is appropriate?
opts: Curettage of the lesion surface
Curettage scrapes tissue away and fragments the specimen, which prevents assessment of depth and margins. It does not provide the intact specimen an excision gives.
Punch biopsy

A punch biopsy cuts deep into the fat layers and is good for rashes or deeper bumps, often needing one or two stitches. It samples the lesion in depth but does not remove the whole of it with wide margins.
Fine needle aspiration of the lesion
Fine needle aspiration retrieves cells rather than architecture and is used for deeper masses and nodes. It cannot assess whether a cutaneous lesion has been removed with adequate margins.
Excisional biopsy
Correct. An excisional biopsy removes the whole lesion taking all deep and wide margins, and always needs stitches to close the wound.
C.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 26

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
C.q: A 35-year-old man returns from a hotel stay with several itchy welts on exposed skin. Examination shows wheals and papules with a haemorrhagic punctum arranged in rows of three. He did not feel the bites occur. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Scabies
Scabies produces intense nocturnal itching over weeks with burrows in the finger webs and flexures, not painless welts on exposed skin after a single stay.
Bedbugs

Correct. Bedbugs are nocturnal feeders hiding in cracks and crevices of headboards and furniture. Bites are painless, multiple, and grouped in a linear fashion, with a row of three known as breakfast, lunch, and dinner, and reactions may be wheals and papules with a haemorrhagic punctum.
Flea bites
Flea bites cluster on the lower legs and ankles rather than forming rows of three on exposed skin after hotel exposure.
Cercarial dermatitis
Cercarial dermatitis follows freshwater exposure with prickling within 30 minutes and severe itching 10 to 12 hours later.
C.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 33

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 46-year-old man is found to have hundreds of small papules over the trunk and extremities consistent with generalised granuloma annulare. What screening is most appropriate?
opts: Fasting glucose and haemoglobin A1c
Correct. Fasting glucose and haemoglobin A1c are used to screen for diabetes in generalised granuloma annulare, alongside a lipid panel and thyroid studies for associated systemic disease.
Chest radiograph
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy belongs to the erythema nodosum workup, where it raises Löfgren syndrome. It is not the screening priority for generalised granuloma annulare.
No screening is indicated

The localised variant is largely a clinical diagnosis needing little workup, but the generalised form carries specific screening recommendations. Applying the localised approach to disseminated disease would miss them.
Immunoglobulin A tissue transglutaminase
Celiac screening is the high-priority association for dermatitis herpetiformis, where all patients should be screened. Granuloma annulare has a different set of associations.
C.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 51

C.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
C.q: A 45-year-old woman with numerous naevi asks how she should check her own moles between clinic visits. What do the letters of the ABCDE recognition rule stand for?
opts: Asymmetry, border, colour, diameter, evolution

Correct. Asymmetry means one half does not match the other; border refers to irregular, notched, or poorly defined edges; colour describes variegation with brown, red, white, black, or blue within one lesion; diameter and evolution complete the rule.
Age, burn history, complexion, dysplasia, exposure
These resemble risk factors rather than lesion features, and the rule describes the lesion itself.
Asymmetry, border, colour, dermoscopy, excision
Dermoscopy and excision are steps in evaluation and management rather than features of the lesion.
Asymmetry, bleeding, crusting, depth, erosion
Bleeding and ulceration are red flags in their own right, but they are not the letters of this rule, and a misremembered mnemonic produces systematic blind spots in screening.
C.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 46

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
C.q: A 40-year-old man has a painful fluctuant nodule 4 mm across on the back of the neck. He is afebrile and it is a single lesion. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Immediate incision and drainage
Incision and drainage is for large furuncles, with the material cultured to evaluate for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. A 4 mm lesion does not require it as a first step.
Warm compresses plus oral cephalexin

Oral antibiotics are indicated if a lesion under 5 mm fails to resolve with drainage, if the lesion is over 5 mm, if cellulitis is expanding, or if the patient is immunocompromised. None of those applies yet, which makes this the most tempting overtreatment.
Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole

Coverage for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is used when it is cultured or suspected. Presuming it in an afebrile patient with a single small lesion that needs no antibiotic at all is two steps too far.
Warm compresses without antibiotics
Correct. Warm compresses are usually sufficient for small furuncles, and no antibiotics are given if the patient is afebrile with a single lesion under 5 mm.
C.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 65

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
C.q: A 3-year-old has several tense, clear-to-cloudy blisters on the trunk arising on intact skin. Some have ruptured, leaving shallow moist erosions ringed by a collarette of scale. There is no lymphadenopathy. What organism and mechanism are responsible?
opts: Staphylococcus or Streptococcus, via a skin break
That description belongs to non-bullous impetigo, which is the more common form and follows a break in the skin. Bullous disease is exclusively staphylococcal and arises on intact skin.
Autoantibody against the basement membrane
Antibodies against the basement membrane produce bullous pemphigoid, a disease of adults over 60 with tense 1 to 3 cm bullae. This is a toxin-mediated infection in a young child.
Staphylococcus aureus alone, via epidermolytic toxin

Correct. Bullous impetigo is caused exclusively by Staphylococcus aureus, which releases epidermolytic toxins producing epidermal splitting. Bullae occur on intact skin, rupture to leave collarettes, and lymphadenopathy is uncommon — in contrast to non-bullous disease, where it is common.
Streptococcus pyogenes, by dermal invasion
Streptococcus pyogenes contributes to non-bullous impetigo and is the main organism in erysipelas, but bullous impetigo is exclusively staphylococcal.
C.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 89

C.io: b — Identify medical strategies for common benign skin lesions in infants, adolescents, adults and the elderly
C.q: A 5-month-old girl has a large hemangioma of the face lying close to the eye and the corner of the mouth. What complications should be considered?
opts: No complications occur
Involution does occur, but the proliferative phase can produce functional compromise before it, which is why specific indications for treatment exist.
Systemic hypertension from shunting
This is not among the listed complications; the concerns are local mass effect and extracutaneous involvement.
Malignant transformation to angiosarcoma
Hemangiomas of infancy are benign and most are medically insignificant. Malignant transformation is not among the described complications.
Compression of vital structures
Correct. Hemangiomas may compress vital structures, block vision, interfere with feeding or respiration, obstruct the external auditory canal, and occur at extracutaneous sites.
C.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 71

C.io: 4 — Discuss clinical principles and decision-making
C.q: A student is seeing a 46-year-old woman with an undifferentiated complaint and is unsure how to begin working through it. What are the first three steps of the clinical reasoning process?
opts: Generate hypotheses, gather, then test
Generating hypotheses before gathering and organising information inverts the sequence and invites premature anchoring on a diagnosis.
Apply a guideline, then confirm it fits
Guidelines are common practice and often follow an if-then rule, but they should be applied appropriately to the individual rather than substituted for the reasoning process.
Treat symptoms, observe, then diagnose
Treating signs and symptoms before a definitive diagnosis describes the naturalistic or event-driven approach, used mostly in emergency medicine for unstable patients and atypical presentations.
Gather, interpret, then represent the problem

Correct. The process begins with gathering initial patient information, then organising and interpreting it, then synthesising the information into a problem representation, before hypotheses are generated and tested.
C.cite: 1. svClinical Reasoning and Problem Solving.pptx, Slide 11

C.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
C.q: A 50-year-old labourer has a thickened, dry, scaly right palm that he has attributed to hard physical work. He also has scaling on both soles. What is the likely diagnosis, and how does it typically present?
opts: Tinea manuum

Correct. Tinea manuum is associated with tinea pedis, and both palms and soles can be infected at the same time. Patients are often unaware of the infection, believing the changes are due to dry skin or hard physical labour, and the involved palm is thickened, dry, and scaly.
Irritant contact dermatitis

Occupational irritant dermatitis is a genuine consideration in a labourer, which is what makes his own explanation plausible. But the coexisting plantar scaling points to a dermatophyte infection spreading between sites.
Dyshidrotic eczema
Dyshidrotic eczema produces crops of intensely pruritic deep-seated vesicles on the palms and lateral fingers that desquamate. There are no vesicles described here.
Chronic paronychia
Chronic paronychia is inflammation of the proximal nail folds from prolonged wet work, producing swollen tender folds and thickened discoloured nail plates rather than a diffusely scaly palm.
C.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 56

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 24-year-old man presents six hours after a day at the beach with painful erythema, warmth, and tenderness across the shoulders and back. There is no blistering. What is the most appropriate acute management?
opts: Immediate systemic corticosteroids
Systemic corticosteroids are not part of the described management of uncomplicated sunburn. First-degree injury confined to the epidermis resolves with supportive care.
Cool compresses, early anti-inflammatories, hydration

Correct. Acute management is cool compresses and cool rather than cold water immersion, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs started early to reduce prostaglandin-mediated inflammation and pain, oral hydration, and topical moisturisers. First-degree sunburn resolves in 3 to 5 days with desquamation.
Cold immersion and delayed anti-inflammatories

Both halves are wrong in instructive ways: cool rather than cold water is specified, and the benefit of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs depends on starting them early, before the prostaglandin cascade is established.
Prophylactic oral antibiotics
Risk of secondary infection is associated with second-degree burns where blistering has occurred, and this patient has none. Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended.
C.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 96

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
C.q: A 39-year-old man presents with an engorged tick attached to his flank after a hike in an endemic area. What single action is emphasised first in the management of a tick-borne illness such as Lyme disease?
opts: Await the appearance of erythema migrans before acting
Erythema migrans identifies stage 1 infection and prompts clinical diagnosis and treatment, but waiting for it before removing an attached tick prolongs exposure.
Administer prophylactic intravenous antibiotics to all patients
Oral doxycycline is first line, and intravenous therapy is reserved for particular manifestations rather than given universally.
Send the tick for species identification before any treatment
Identification may be of interest but does not precede removal, and waiting delays both removal and treatment.
Remove the tick immediately
Correct. The management sequence begins with removing the tick immediately, followed by antibiotics, which are indicated in all stages.
C.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 79

C.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 34-year-old woman has been applying a topical corticosteroid to the same area of eyelid skin for several months. What adverse effects should be anticipated?
opts: Hyperpigmentation, hypertrichosis, and thickening of the dermis
This reverses the pigment and thickness changes. Prolonged corticosteroid exposure thins rather than thickens the skin and produces hypopigmentation rather than hyperpigmentation.
Permanent loss of hair follicles at the treated site

Follicular destruction with permanent hair loss characterises scarring alopecias. Topical corticosteroid atrophy affects epidermal and dermal thickness rather than destroying the follicular stem cell compartment.
Photosensitivity, dryness, and irritation
Irritation, dryness, and photosensitivity are the important clinical considerations for topical retinoids such as adapalene, tretinoin, and tazarotene. They belong to a different topical class.
Atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, and hypopigmentation

Correct. Prolonged use of topical corticosteroids may cause atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, and hypopigmentation. This is why potency is selected according to site and severity and why the usual course is twice daily for two weeks.
C.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 41

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
C.q: A 35-year-old woman has a firm 8 mm nodule on her lower leg with a brown halo and a slightly raised centre. When the skin on either side is squeezed together, the lesion dimples downward. What is this sign, and what does dermoscopy typically show?
opts: Nikolsky sign
Nikolsky sign is the slipping away of the top layers of skin when rubbed, positive in pemphigus. It has nothing to do with a firm dermal nodule.
The dimple sign, seen in lipoma

The sign is correctly named but attached to the wrong lesion. A lipoma is a soft, benign overgrowth of subcutaneous fat and is on the differential for other nodules rather than being the dimple-sign lesion.
Darier sign
Darier sign is urtication of a lesion after stroking and points to mastocytosis rather than to a fibrous dermal nodule.
The dimple sign

Correct. The dimple sign is characteristic of dermatofibroma, which is a firm 0.5 to 1 cm nodule formed by dense clusters of dermal fibroblasts, most commonly on the legs. Dermoscopy often shows a peripheral pigment network with a central white area.
C.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 46

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pigmented skin lesions
C.q: A 4-year-old boy has a circumscribed light brown patch on the trunk resembling a café au lait spot, within which several darker pigmented macules and papules are visible. What is this lesion?
opts: A dysplastic naevus
A dysplastic naevus is at least 5 mm with irregular indistinct borders and is diagnosed by biopsy. Its appearance does not include discrete darker spots on a café au lait background.
A blue nevus
Blue naevi are blue, blue-grey, or blue-black lesions of the dorsal hands and feet, scalp, buttocks, or sacral region.
Nevus spilus

Correct. Nevus spilus, the spotted nevus, is a variant of congenital naevus present at birth or in the first years of life, most commonly on the trunk and extremities. Darkly pigmented macules or papules sit within a background that is circumscribed and similar in appearance to a café au lait spot, and it rarely progresses to melanoma. Management is observation, periodic evaluation, and sun protection.
A cafe au lait macule
Café au lait macules are uniform light tan to brown macules without darker macules within them, and their size thresholds define significance in neurofibromatosis.
C.cite: CMS I Pigmented Skin Lesions - Shahsv-2.pptx, Slide 34

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
C.q: A 28-year-old man is stung by a wasp and within minutes develops widespread urticaria, wheezing, and hypotension. What is the immediate treatment?
opts: Cleaning, ice, and local anaesthetic
That is the management of a mild local cutaneous reaction. Applying it to anaphylaxis would leave a patient with airway and circulatory compromise untreated.
An oral antihistamine at home
Oral antihistamines address urticaria but do nothing for the airway and circulatory collapse of anaphylaxis.
Local wound debridement
Debridement has no role. Extensive oedema at the sting site with induration describes a severe local reaction rather than a wound requiring surgery.
Intramuscular or subcutaneous epinephrine
Correct. For an anaphylactic reaction to a hymenoptera sting the treatment is subcutaneous or intramuscular epinephrine with emergency department transfer and supportive measures.
C.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 44

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
C.q: A 55-year-old man with diabetes has an asymptomatic brownish patch in a skin fold noted on routine examination. Where is erythrasma most commonly found, and what is the typical symptom profile?
opts: Scalp, thighs, and trunk, with follicular pustules
Those are the common sites of folliculitis, whose lesions are pustules pierced by a central hair.
Face and lower leg, with sudden high fever
The face and lower extremity with sudden high fever describes erysipelas, an acute streptococcal infection rather than a chronic asymptomatic intertriginous one.
Axilla, groin, and perineum, recurrent and painful
That distribution and symptom profile belong to hidradenitis suppurativa, which affects apocrine-bearing skin with recurrence more than twice in six months.
Inner thighs, groin, and fourth toe web; often silent

Correct. The most common sites are the inner thighs, crural region, scrotum, and between the fourth and fifth toes, with the axilla, under the breasts, and intergluteal folds less common. It is usually asymptomatic and may be pruritic.
C.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 81

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
C.q: A 23-year-old man presents with a painful swelling in the natal cleft, and the clinician reviews what predisposed him to it. Which set of risk factors is associated with pilonidal disease?
opts: Prematurity and low birth weight

Those are the birth history factors associated with infantile hemangiomas, which are congenital vascular lesions of infancy. Pilonidal disease arises in young adults from hair and debris drawn into a natal cleft pit, so a neonatal history has no bearing on it.
Venous insufficiency and lymphoedema
Those relate to stasis dermatitis and erysipelas rather than to a follicular disease of the natal cleft.
Female sex, pregnancy, oestrogen excess
Oestrogen excess states are associated with nevus araneus, the spider angioma, which resolves after delivery or cessation of hormonal contraception.
Obesity, sedentary life, dense cleft hair
Correct. Those are the listed risk factors, and the male to female ratio is 3 to 1.
C.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 39

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
D.q: A 31-year-old camper develops a prickling sensation lasting about 30 minutes after wading in a freshwater lake, followed 10 to 12 hours later by severe itching and then erythematous papules. What is this condition, and what completes its life cycle?
opts: Cercarial dermatitis; snails complete the cycle

Correct. Cercarial dermatitis, also called swimmer's itch or clam digger's itch, results from penetration of the skin by cercarial forms of parasitic flatworms. Host animals such as waterfowl and muskrats pass eggs in feces into water, the eggs hatch and infect snails within 12 hours, and cercariae are released about 5 weeks later.
Cutaneous larva migrans; from contaminated soil
Cutaneous larva migrans is acquired from soil rather than water and produces an advancing serpentine track rather than an immediate prickling sensation and later papules.
Bedbug bites from campsite bedding
Bedbug bites are painless linear groups of wheals on exposed skin without the immediate prickling and delayed pruritus after water exposure.
Scabies; a burrowing mite
Scabies produces intense nocturnal pruritus over weeks with burrows in the finger webs and flexures rather than an immediate reaction after a single water exposure.
D.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 89

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
D.q: A 54-year-old woman is found on routine examination to have several smooth, firm, deep red papules under 5 mm on the trunk that blanch with pressure. She has never noticed them. What education should be given?
opts: Benign, but can progress to malignancy

The first half is correct, which is what makes this the most tempting distractor. But cherry angiomas remain benign; they do not transform, and framing them as premalignant would prompt needless procedures.
They indicate liver disease
It is nevus araneus, the spider angioma, whose history includes asking about alcohol use and medications hazardous to the liver, along with pregnancy and hormone use.
Benign capillary proliferation

Correct. Cherry angiomas are acquired vascular lesions formed by capillary or venule proliferation, very common and increasing with age. Treatment is unnecessary unless they bother the patient, and patients should be aware that new lesions will likely develop and there is no way to prevent them.
Biopsy is needed to diagnose them
The clinical features are characteristic enough for diagnosis by inspection, and treatment is not needed unless the patient is bothered.
D.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 87

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 30-year-old woman has widespread intensely itchy raised weals that have come and gone for four days. Individual lesions last a few hours, blanch fully, and leave no mark. She has no fever, joint pain, or bruising at resolved sites. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Urticaria
Correct. Urticaria results from mast cell degranulation producing transient pruritic weals. Individual lesions last less than 24 hours, blanch fully, and resolve without residual change.
Urticarial vasculitis
Urticarial vasculitis is distinguished by lesions persisting beyond 24 hours that leave bruising, often with arthralgia and low complement — all specifically absent here.
Contact dermatitis
Contact dermatitis produces a sharply demarcated eczematous eruption at the site of exposure rather than migratory blanching weals.
Erythema multiforme
Erythema multiforme produces fixed target lesions that remain in place for days, rather than migratory weals lasting hours.
D.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 37

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
D.q: A 57-year-old man with diabetes has an asymptomatic brownish patch in the crural region and scaling between the fourth and fifth toes. Under a Wood's lamp the affected skin fluoresces coral-red. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Contact dermatitis
Contact dermatitis requires an exposure and produces a sharply demarcated pruritic eruption rather than an asymptomatic fluorescing patch.
Tinea cruris
Tinea cruris occupies the same sites and is the main mimic, but dermatophytes do not fluoresce coral-red, and tinea cruris typically spares the scrotum.
Cutaneous candidiasis
Candidal intertrigo produces beefy erythema with satellite papules and pustules rather than an asymptomatic brown patch with coral-red fluorescence.
Erythrasma

Correct. Erythrasma is a chronic superficial infection of intertriginous skin by Corynebacterium minutissimum, favouring the inner thighs, crural region, scrotum, and fourth toe web, and coral-red fluorescence under a Wood's lamp is diagnostic.
D.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 81

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
D.q: A 41-year-old man has a moveable nodule on the back with a central punctum, which he refers to as a sebaceous cyst. Why is that term a misnomer for an epidermoid cyst?
opts: It has no lining, being a pseudo-cyst
A pseudo-cyst without a cellular lining describes the digital mucous cyst, which represents extrusion of mucinous contents from a joint space.
It arises from apocrine glands
The cyst arises from enclosed epithelium rather than from any gland, and its content is keratin. Apocrine involvement describes hidradenitis suppurativa.
It contains lipid-laden macrophages
Collections of lipid-laden macrophages form xanthelasma, the soft yellow cholesterol plaques of the medial eyelids.
Enclosed epithelium filled with keratin
Correct. An epidermoid cyst is formed by cystic enclosure of epithelium within the dermis and becomes filled with keratin. It is often called a sebaceous cyst because it appears to contain sebum.
D.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 53

D.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
D.q: A 30-year-old woman with tinea corporis asks whether the infection can spread to her mouth, and a student asks why dermatophytes never involve mucous membranes. What is the correct explanation?
opts: They survive only on dead keratin
Correct. Dermatophytes infect and survive only on dead keratin, involving the superficial portion of the skin at the stratum corneum, plus hair and nails. They cannot survive on mucous membranes.
Salivary enzymes kill them
The limitation is the absence of dead keratin rather than an antimicrobial property of saliva. Candida, which is not a dermatophyte, colonises mucosa freely.
They can involve mucosa if immunocompromised
The constraint is structural rather than immunological. Immunosuppression extends the severity and extent of dermatophytosis but does not create keratin where there is none.
They require sebum
Sebum matters in tinea capitis, where post-pubertal changes in sebum fatty acid content are believed to inhibit dermatophyte growth. But the organisms depend on keratin rather than requiring sebum.
D.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 6

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 29-year-old man of Northern European ancestry has an intensely itchy, burning eruption of grouped small vesicles and papules symmetrically over both elbows, knees, and buttocks. Most lesions are excoriated. He has autoimmune thyroid disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Scabies
Scabies is on the differential because it also itches intensely, but it shows burrows in the web spaces and a positive skin scraping, and it favours flexural rather than extensor sites.
Dermatitis herpetiformis

Correct. Dermatitis herpetiformis produces intensely pruritic grouped vesicles and papules symmetrically on extensor surfaces, driven by immunoglobulin A antibodies against epidermal transglutaminase in gluten-sensitive individuals.
Atopic dermatitis
Atopic dermatitis in adults is flexural with elevated immunoglobulin E and lichenified plaques rather than grouped extensor vesicles.
Contact dermatitis
Contact dermatitis follows an exposure and traces the shape of the contactant rather than appearing symmetrically on elbows, knees, and buttocks.
D.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 17

D.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
D.q: A 76-year-old man has a biopsy-proven invasive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma on the dorsal forearm. What is the preferred management?
opts: Cryotherapy
Cryotherapy is a lesion-directed therapy for actinic keratosis. It is not the treatment for invasive carcinoma, and follow-up is required in any case.
Topical imiquimod or fluorouracil
Imiquimod, topical fluorouracil, or curettage and electrodesiccation are options for carcinoma in situ without high-risk features. Applying them to invasive disease under-treats it.
Surgical excision or Mohs surgery

Correct. Surgical excision or Mohs micrographic surgery is preferred for invasive squamous cell carcinoma, with at least annual skin and lymph node examination and closer intervals for high-risk or immunosuppressed patients. All suspected invasive lesions are referred to dermatology or an experienced surgeon.
Radiotherapy
Surgery is the preferred modality. Radiotherapy has a role in selected patients rather than as universal first line.
D.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 26

D.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 29-year-old hairdresser reports recurrent episodes of intensely itchy blisters on her hands. Examination shows multiple grouped 1 to 2 mm vesicles on the lateral aspects of the fingers and the adjacent interdigital surfaces, some coalescing, on a poorly defined pink base with surrounding dryness. She reports previous episodes that persisted for several weeks, dried up, and then peeled. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atopic dermatitis of the hands

Adult atopic dermatitis does affect the hands, but it produces dry, lichenified plaques at flexures, hands, and neck rather than recurrent crops of vesicles on the lateral fingers that resolve by desquamation.
Allergic contact dermatitis

Allergic contact dermatitis is plausible in a hairdresser exposed to dyes, but it produces a well-demarcated eruption at the site of allergen contact rather than grouped tapioca vesicles confined to the lateral fingers and interdigital surfaces with a relapsing weeks-long cycle.
Nummular eczema

Nummular eczema produces well-demarcated coin-shaped plaques 1 to 10 cm across, most often on the extremities, with prominent scale and crusting. Its lesions are plaques rather than grouped millimetre vesicles on the finger margins.
Dyshidrotic eczema

Correct. Dyshidrotic eczema is a chronic, relapsing eruption of intensely pruritic vesicles on the hands and feet, classically described as tapioca vesicles. They may coalesce into bullae, persist for several weeks, then desiccate and resolve with desquamation — the exact course she describes.
D.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 65

D.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
D.q: A 70-year-old woman has a basal cell carcinoma on the nasal ala that has recurred after a previous excision. When should Mohs micrographic surgery be considered for basal cell carcinoma?
opts: Only after topical therapy fails twice

Topical imiquimod or fluorouracil is used for selected superficial basal cell carcinoma, with clinical clearance confirmed afterwards. Mohs selection depends on site and risk rather than on prior topical failure.
High-risk sites, recurrence, or tissue sparing

Correct. Mohs surgery is indicated for high-risk anatomic sites, recurrent tumours, aggressive histology, or where tissue-sparing is needed. The overall goal is complete eradication with minimal cosmetic and functional deformity.
Every basal cell carcinoma
Mohs is resource-intensive and reserved for the situations listed. Using it universally would be neither practical nor necessary for low-risk truncal tumours.
Never; surgery is not required
Basal cell carcinoma is capable of significant local destruction when delayed or histologically aggressive, and surgical management is central.
D.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 38

D.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
D.q: A 58-year-old woman presents with right-sided facial weakness, painful vesicles in the right ear canal, and vertigo. What treatment is added beyond antivirals?
opts: No additional treatment
The diagnosis is right but the regimen is incomplete, and the corticosteroid is the part specifically added in this syndrome rather than in uncomplicated zoster.
A corticosteroid instead of an antiviral
Idiopathic facial palsy does not produce painful vesicles in the ear canal. The vesicles identify a zoster reactivation and mandate antiviral therapy.
A systemic corticosteroid

Correct. Ramsay Hunt syndrome, or herpes zoster oticus, is peripheral facial palsy with painful vesicles of the ear canal, auricle, or oropharynx, sometimes with hearing loss, tinnitus, or vertigo. Antiviral therapy plus a systemic corticosteroid is started early when not contraindicated.
Urgent ophthalmology referral
Herpes zoster ophthalmicus involves the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, with Hutchinson sign on the nose raising ocular risk. The ear canal and facial nerve are a different territory.
D.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 104

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
D.q: A 19-year-old woman whose sister developed a large keloid after ear piercing asks how to avoid the same problem. What is described as the most important element in the management of keloids?
opts: Compression for one week after injury
Compression therapy is used with pressure maintained over an extended period rather than for a single week, and it is a treatment rather than the overarching principle.
Intralesional steroid alone
Intralesional steroids eventually flatten lesions and reduce collagen production, and they may cause tissue atrophy. They are one modality among several rather than the most important element.
Early excision of every lesion
Excision carries a 50 to 100 percent recurrence rate with lesions often larger than the original, so early surgery is not the cornerstone.
Prevention, including avoiding ear piercing

Correct. Prevention is described as the most important treatment. High-risk patients should be advised to avoid cosmetic procedures such as ear piercing, and post-surgical education includes avoiding stretching of an immature scar and avoiding hot baths.
D.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 15

D.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 72-year-old man is referred with a red, warm, tender left lower leg. He has bilateral chronic ankle swelling and brown discoloration of both gaiter regions, but the left leg has become acutely more swollen and painful over two days. He is afebrile. What consideration should most urgently shape the evaluation?
opts: Acute unilateral swelling suggests thrombosis

Correct. The differential for stasis dermatitis explicitly flags that acute unilateral swelling or pain should raise concern for deep venous thrombosis. Chronic bilateral changes with a new unilateral acute change is precisely that pattern.
Bilateral change makes cellulitis likely

This inverts the reasoning. Bilateral chronic change argues against cellulitis, which is characteristically unilateral; distinguishing stasis dermatitis from cellulitis is one of the two primary clinical priorities in this condition.
Start compression immediately

Starting compression before excluding deep venous thrombosis and confirming arterial adequacy is exactly the sequence the lecture warns against. Compression is the cornerstone of management only after those questions are settled.
No fever excludes a vascular event
Fever is neither required for nor exclusive to venous thrombosis, and this patient is indeed afebrile. Using a normal temperature to rule out a thrombotic event would be a serious error.
D.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 115

D.io: b — Identify medical strategies for common benign skin lesions in infants, adolescents, adults and the elderly
D.q: An 83-year-old nursing home resident with limited mobility and incontinence is at risk of pressure injury. What is the single best measure?
opts: Restricting fluids

Incontinence is managed with skin care and barrier creams, and nutrition assessment is part of prevention. Restricting fluids risks dehydration and malnutrition, both of which worsen tissue tolerance.
Prophylactic hydrocolloid dressings
Silicone and hydrocolloid dressings appear in the management of an established injury. They do not substitute for relieving the pressure that causes the damage.
Repositioning every eight hours
Repositioning every two hours is specified. Tying it to eight-hour shifts leaves long periods of unrelieved pressure, which is the mechanism of injury.
Prevention, with two-hourly repositioning

Correct. The best measure is prevention: frequent skin assessments, nutrition assessment, moisture control and skin care with the skin kept clean and dry, incontinence managed and barrier creams applied, and repositioning every two hours.
D.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 35

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 63-year-old woman with toxic epidermal necrolysis is admitted to the burn unit. What scoring system should be calculated within 24 hours and repeated on day three?
opts: The Fitzpatrick scale
The Fitzpatrick scale classifies baseline ultraviolet sensitivity by skin type and guides photoprotection counselling. It has no role in grading a drug reaction.
The minimal erythema dose
The minimal erythema dose is determined during phototesting for drug-induced photosensitivity and polymorphous light eruption. It is a photobiology measurement rather than a severity score.
SCORTEN

Correct. SCORTEN should be calculated within 24 hours of admission and repeated on day 3. Each variable scores one point, including age over 40 years, presence of malignancy, heart rate over 120 beats per minute, and the initial extent of epidermal detachment.
The Parkland formula
The Parkland formula estimates fluid resuscitation volumes and may be adapted for the fluid losses of toxic epidermal necrolysis. It guides therapy rather than scoring severity or prognosis.
D.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 89

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pigmented skin lesions
D.q: A 33-year-old woman has a sharply circumscribed, darkly pigmented papule under 7 mm on the thigh. What is this lesion also called, and what is its typical demographic?
opts: Blue nevus, adolescence, dorsal hands
Common blue naevi are deeply pigmented lesions under 1 cm arising in adolescence at characteristic sites.
Reed nevus, lower extremities in the thirties

Correct. Pigmented spindle cell nevus, also called Reed nevus, occurs commonly in the thirties with females affected more than males, found on the extremities and mainly the lower extremities, especially the thigh. It is a sharply circumscribed darkly pigmented papule usually less than 7 mm.
Spitz nevus, children, face and neck
Spitz naevus is a separate lesion — solitary, pink or red, hairless, firm, and dome-shaped, usually on the face, neck, or extremities, sometimes resembling melanoma.
Dysplastic naevus, irregular borders
A dysplastic naevus is at least 5 mm with irregular, indistinct borders, whereas the Reed nevus is sharply circumscribed.
D.cite: CMS I Pigmented Skin Lesions - Shahsv-2.pptx, Slide 41

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
D.q: A 6-week-old girl born prematurely has a bright red papule on the scalp. It began as a faint blanched area with fine telangiectasias at birth and has grown noticeably over the past fortnight. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pyogenic granuloma
Pyogenic granuloma is an acquired lesion that grows rapidly after trauma and bleeds easily, uncommon at this age.
Infantile hemangioma

Correct. Infantile hemangiomas are the most common tumours of infancy, more frequent in preterm and female infants with a head and neck predilection. The earliest sign is blanching followed by fine telangiectasias, then a red macule, then rapid proliferation.
Nevus flammeus
Nevus flammeus is present at birth as a flat pink-purple patch, grows only in proportion to the child, and never involutes.
Nevus simplex
Nevus simplex is a superficial variant on the nape, glabella, or eyelids that becomes more noticeable when the infant cries and does not proliferate.
D.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 67

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
D.q: A 22-year-old woman has a firm, bulbous nodule at the site of an ear piercing performed two years ago. The lesion extends well beyond the original piercing site and has continued to enlarge. What distinguishes this from a hypertrophic scar?
opts: It stays within the wound margins
Staying within the wound margins is the hypertrophic scar pattern. Extension beyond them is the defining keloid feature.
It is always painless
Keloids are often asymptomatic but may be pruritic or produce burning pain, and hypertrophic scars are also typically asymptomatic. Symptoms do not separate them.
It developed within four weeks
Rapid development within four weeks characterises a hypertrophic scar. The keloid develops slowly and keeps enlarging over months to years.
It extends beyond the wound margins

Correct. A keloid extends beyond the wound site margins, develops slowly, continues to enlarge for months to years, and shows no regression with a tendency to recur. A hypertrophic scar develops rapidly within four weeks, remains within the wound margins, and flattens with time.
D.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 13

D.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 4-year-old girl has a typical history and examination for atopic dermatitis. Her parents ask whether blood tests are needed to confirm the diagnosis. What is the most accurate response?
opts: Biopsy every child before treatment
Biopsy is reserved for atypical or refractory disease. Performing one routinely subjects a child to an invasive procedure for a diagnosis that is made clinically.
Check an immunoglobulin E level in every child

Elevated immunoglobulin E does support the diagnosis, which is what makes this tempting, but it is explicitly not routinely tested. Making it a required confirmation adds cost and delay without changing management.
Culture every child at diagnosis
Culture is appropriate when secondary infection is suspected. Routine culture of uninfected atopic skin produces colonisation results that invite unnecessary antibiotic treatment.
It is clinical; no routine laboratory testing

Correct. The diagnosis is usually clinical, supported by family history, personal history of atopy, and a recurrent history of rash. Immunoglobulin E may be elevated but is not routinely tested, and routine laboratory testing is not required.
D.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 56

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pigmented skin lesions
D.q: A newborn boy is born with a large pigmented plaque over the posterior scalp and upper back. What additional evaluation should be considered?
opts: Observation alone with no imaging

The size relationship is right but management depends on melanoma risk together with cosmetic and functional considerations. The goal is to remove as much as possible while preserving function, decided per patient rather than mandated.
Genetic testing of the parents
Congenital naevi arise from somatic mutations rather than inherited ones, so parental genetic testing would not inform the child's risk.
Complete excision in every case
Size is the principal determinant of risk, and imaging has a defined role in specific anatomical distributions.
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and spine

Correct. Congenital melanocytic naevi arise from somatic mutations and are evident at birth or shortly after. The larger the lesion, the higher the risk for melanoma. With naevi on the head or axial locations, neurocutaneous melanosis must be considered, and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with or without the total spine is obtained concordant with the anatomic location.
D.cite: CMS I Pigmented Skin Lesions - Shahsv-2.pptx, Slide 30

D.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
D.q: A 34-year-old man with untreated human immunodeficiency virus infection has multiple red-purple macules and plaques on the trunk. What is the first management priority?
opts: Start or optimise antiretroviral therapy

Correct. Oral examination is essential when Kaposi sarcoma is suspected, since hard palate lesions are common and may be the presenting site. For acquired immunodeficiency syndrome-associated disease the first priority is to begin or optimise antiretroviral therapy, because immune restoration is the cornerstone of treatment.
Start systemic chemotherapy first

The examination is right but the sequence is wrong. Immune restoration through antiretroviral therapy is the cornerstone for epidemic disease, with systemic therapy reserved for extensive or visceral involvement.
Observation alone
Observation leaves an immunodeficiency untreated, and the specifically emphasised examination is of the oral cavity.
Intralesional vincristine
Intralesional vincristine or vinblastine is palliative local therapy used in classic disease of older adults rather than the priority in epidemic disease, and the essential examination is oral.
D.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 66

D.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 21-year-old woman presents with a rash on her trunk. Ten days before the current eruption she noticed a single oval, sharply demarcated salmon-coloured plaque about 4 cm across on her upper back that became scaly and began to clear in the centre. Now numerous smaller similar lesions have appeared over the trunk, with their long axes aligned along the lines of the ribs. She feels well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Tinea corporis

A single annular scaly plaque with central clearing genuinely resembles the herald patch, which is why this is the classic trap. But tinea corporis does not then produce a widespread secondary eruption aligned along the rib lines a week or two later.
Pityriasis rosea

Correct. A herald patch occurs in 50 to 90 percent of cases, preceding the exanthem: a single 2 to 5 cm round or oval, sharply demarcated pink or salmon-coloured plaque on the chest, neck, or back that clears centrally, leaving a collarette of scale. The eruption of smaller similar lesions follows 1 to 2 weeks later.
Guttate psoriasis

Guttate psoriasis produces raindrop-shaped papules and plaques 2 to 3 weeks after a streptococcal or upper respiratory infection. It is not preceded by a single herald patch and does not follow the oblique rib lines.
Secondary syphilis

Secondary syphilis can mimic pityriasis rosea closely and classically involves the palms and soles, which are not described here. It also lacks the preceding solitary herald patch that defines this presentation.
D.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 169

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
D.q: Computed tomography of a 48-year-old man with suspected necrotizing fasciitis shows gas in the soft tissue fascial planes. What does this indicate about the likely organism?
opts: Gas is present in every case
Absence of gas does not exclude necrotizing fasciitis, and group A streptococcal disease specifically does not produce it. Requiring gas for the diagnosis would miss the common streptococcal form.
Gas means the infection is superficial
Gas in the fascial planes indicates deep involvement. Necrotizing fasciitis involves the tissue surrounding muscles, nerves, fat, and blood vessels.
Gas means a fungal cause
Necrotizing fasciitis is a bacterial infection that may be polymicrobial with aerobic, anaerobic, or mixed flora. Gas points to a gas-forming bacterium rather than a fungus.
Gas suggests Clostridium, not group A streptococcus
Correct. Gas may be present with Clostridium perfringens infection but is not present with group A streptococcal infection. Ultrasound is also useful for demonstrating air bubbles in soft tissue.
D.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 129

D.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
D.q: A 58-year-old woman with obesity has candidal intertrigo of both inframammary folds. Beyond antifungal therapy, what environmental measure is central to treatment?
opts: Apply an occlusive ointment to the folds

Occlusion traps the moisture and heat that produce intertrigo in the first place. Occlusive barriers are the approach to diaper dermatitis, where the exposure is urine and stool rather than trapped moisture.
Dry the folds and reduce friction and occlusion

Correct. Correcting the environment is central: gently dry the folds, reduce friction and occlusion, use moisture-wicking fabric or absorbent material, and address incontinence or hyperhidrosis. Intertrigo itself is caused by friction, moisture, and heat trapped in body folds.
Apply a high-potency corticosteroid
Potent steroids in occluded flexural skin cause atrophy and striae rapidly and can allow candidal overgrowth to extend.
Increase the frequency of hot showers
Hot water and prolonged wetting worsen maceration in the folds. Gentle drying is what is required.
D.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 72

D.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
D.q: A 13-year-old boy has several elevated round papules under 1 cm with a rough greyish surface on the fingers. Paring one reveals tiny red-black dots. Skin lines are interrupted where the lesions sit. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Verruca vulgaris

Correct. Common warts are elevated round papules under 1 cm with a rough greyish surface, most often on the hands and fingers, and tiny red or black dots representing thrombosed dilated capillaries become more prominent when the surface is trimmed.
Molluscum contagiosum
Molluscum lesions are smooth pearly dome-shaped papules with central umbilication rather than a rough surface with thrombosed capillaries.
Clavus
A corn has a central cone of hard keratin, hurts on direct downward pressure, and the skin lines run THROUGH it rather than being interrupted.
Seborrheic keratosis
Seborrheic keratoses have a stuck-on appearance with comedone-like openings and occur in older adults.
D.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 142

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
D.q: An 8-year-old girl has an itchy scalp, low-grade fever, occipital lymphadenopathy, and irritability. Wet combing recovers several moving 2 mm insects, and small oval structures are cemented to hair shafts near the scalp. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pediculosis capitis

Correct. Head lice are blood-sucking wingless insects about 2 mm long, common in children aged 3 to 12, producing pruritus, low-grade fever, regional lymphadenopathy, and irritability. Live lice found on combing indicate active infestation.
Scabies
Scabies spares the head and neck in older children and adults and produces burrows in the finger webs and flexures.
Tinea capitis
Tinea capitis produces scaly patches with hair loss and broken hairs rather than mobile insects and nits attached to shafts.
Seborrheic dermatitis
Seborrheic dermatitis produces greasy yellow scale that is not cemented to the hair shaft, and it does not cause lymphadenopathy or fever.
D.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 25

D.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 43-year-old factory worker splashes a concentrated alkali solution on the forearm, while a colleague of the same age has had weeks of soreness from repeated soap exposure. How does the timing of an irritant reaction to a strong alkali differ from that of a reaction to a mild irritant such as soap?
opts: Alkalis act in minutes; soaps over weeks

Correct. Symptoms present differently depending on the exposure: mild irritants such as soaps may present with subacute symptoms that progress over weeks, while alkalis and acids may present minutes after exposure or delayed up to 24 hours or more. Concentrated agents can lead to chemical burns and necrosis.
Both act only after weeks
This would delay recognition of a chemical burn. Strong alkalis can produce symptoms within minutes and can cause necrosis, so treating the exposure as a slow cumulative process is dangerous.
Alkalis over weeks; soaps in minutes
The two are reversed. Assigning the slow course to the corrosive agent is the error most likely to lead to an untreated chemical injury.
Neither acts before 48 to 72 hours
A delayed hypersensitivity time course belongs to allergic contact dermatitis, which is a type IV reaction. Irritant dermatitis is direct barrier damage rather than immunological sensitisation.
D.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 81

D.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 36-year-old man has greasy yellow scale over the scalp, eyebrows, and nasolabial folds. What organism is responsible for seborrheic dermatitis, and where is the condition typically found?
opts: An acquired dermatophyte infection
Dermatophytes cause tinea infections and are diagnosed by potassium hydroxide preparation. Malassezia is a resident organism whose overgrowth, not acquisition, produces the condition.
Staphylococcus aureus colonisation
Staphylococcus aureus causes bacterial infections such as impetigo, folliculitis, and furuncles. Greasy yellow scale at sebum-rich sites is not a staphylococcal presentation.
Malassezia overgrowth at sebum-rich sites

Correct. Seborrheic dermatitis is caused by overgrowth of Malassezia, which is normal skin flora. It is typically found on the scalp as dandruff, and on the eyebrows, under facial hair, in the nasolabial creases, forehead, nose, behind the ears, and in the external auditory canal.
Malassezia overgrowth at flexural sites

The organism is correct but the distribution is wrong. Seborrheic dermatitis follows sebaceous gland density rather than flexures, which is why the scalp, eyebrows, and nasolabial creases are affected.
D.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 93

D.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 45-year-old man with plaque psoriasis of the elbows and knees is prescribed calcipotriene. What is the most important clinical consideration for this agent?
opts: Irritation and photosensitivity
Irritation, dryness, and photosensitivity are the considerations for topical retinoids such as adapalene, tretinoin, and tazarotene. Calcipotriene is a vitamin D analogue rather than a retinoid.
Reserve it for the face and eyelids
Tacrolimus and pimecrolimus are the calcineurin inhibitors used at sensitive sites such as the face and eyelids. Calcipotriene has a different mechanism and a different role.
Caution over nephrotoxicity
Correct. Calcipotriene is a vitamin D analogue described as having the quickest action among the first-line options, with caution regarding nephrotoxicity.
Risk of cutaneous atrophy

Atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, and hypopigmentation are the risks of prolonged topical corticosteroid use, not of the vitamin D analogue. The drug class is right but the adverse effect belongs to its first-line companion.
D.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 163

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
D.q: A 62-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of fever to 39.1 degrees Celsius, chills, and myalgias, followed within a day by a painful red area on her left shin. Examination shows a brightly erythematous plaque raised above the surrounding skin with a sharply defined border, and red streaks extending proximally. She has tinea pedis. What is the most likely organism and the drug of choice?
opts: Streptococcus pyogenes, treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
The organism is right but the drug is aimed at methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and has poor streptococcal activity. Penicillin V is the named agent.
Corynebacterium minutissimum, treated with topical erythromycin
Corynebacterium minutissimum causes erythrasma, which is chronic, asymptomatic, and non-febrile. Sudden high fever with a rapidly spreading plaque excludes it.
Streptococcus pyogenes, treated with penicillin V

Correct. Group A streptococcus is the most common organism in erysipelas, which involves the upper dermis and superficial cutaneous lymphatics. Penicillin V is the pharmacotherapy, with clindamycin if the patient is penicillin allergic. Tinea pedis is a listed risk factor.
Staphylococcus aureus, treated with cephalexin

Staphylococcus aureus is a cause of cellulitis, which is the deeper process with indistinct borders. The raised plaque with a clear line of demarcation and the lymphatic streaking identify erysipelas instead.
D.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 104

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pigmented skin lesions
D.q: A 42-year-old Black woman has multiple small, smooth, firm dark brown papules 1 to 3 mm on the face and neck. What is the diagnosis, and how does it relate to seborrheic keratosis?
opts: Melanocytic naevi
Common acquired naevi are usually under 6 mm with homogeneous surface and colour and peak in the thirties. Dermatosis papulosa nigrans lesions are keratinocytic rather than melanocytic.
Dermatosis papulosa nigrans, a premalignant variant

The lesion is identified correctly but it is not premalignant. Framing a benign genetic condition as premalignant would prompt unnecessary destructive treatment on facial skin prone to dyspigmentation.
Syringomas
Syringomas are skin-coloured 1 to 2 mm papules of the lower eyelids appearing at puberty rather than dark brown papules of the face and neck.
Dermatosis papulosa nigrans, a benign variant

Correct. Dermatosis papulosa nigrans consists of multiple small, smooth, firm black or dark brown papules 1 to 5 mm on the face and neck, identical to small seborrheic keratoses. It is thought to be genetic and is believed to be a developmental defect of the hair follicle.
D.cite: CMS I Pigmented Skin Lesions - Shahsv-2.pptx, Slide 19

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 34-year-old woman with tender pretibial nodules undergoes a deep incisional biopsy. What finding confirms the diagnosis?
opts: Septal panniculitis without vasculitis, with Miescher's granulomas
Correct. Biopsy shows septal panniculitis without vasculitis and Miescher's granulomas. A deep incisional biopsy is needed because the pathology lies in the subcutaneous fat.
Lobular panniculitis with vasculitis
The pattern is inverted on both counts. Erythema nodosum is specifically a septal panniculitis and specifically without vasculitis, which is how it is distinguished from other panniculitides.
Palisading granulomas with central necrobiosis and mucin
Palisading granulomas around degenerating collagen with mucin deposition is the granuloma annulare finding. That condition produces annular surface plaques rather than deep tender nodules.
Full-thickness epidermal necrosis
Full-thickness epidermal necrosis is the biopsy finding of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. It is an epidermal process rather than a disease of the subcutaneous fat.
D.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 44

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
D.q: An 84-year-old nursing home resident has thick flaking scale over the hands and trunk but reports no itching at all. What is this presentation?
opts: Crusted scabies

Correct. Hyperkeratotic or crusted scabies presents as thick flaking scale containing millions of mites. These patients are highly infectious, and pruritus is usually absent — which is exactly why the diagnosis is missed and outbreaks occur.
Psoriasis
