Psoriasis is on the scabies differential and produces well-demarcated plaques with silvery scale. Applying a corticosteroid to crusted scabies would suppress inflammation while the mite burden increases.
Ordinary scabies
Ordinary scabies is defined by severe itching, and this patient has none. The absence of pruritus alongside thick scale is what marks the crusted form.
Xerosis of aging

Dry scaly skin in an older adult is common, which is what makes this the natural assumption. But treating crusted scabies as simple xerosis leaves a highly infectious patient untreated in a congregate setting.
D.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 12

D.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 26-year-old woman has grouped papules and papulopustules around the mouth, and the clinician is distinguishing perioral dermatitis from its principal differential diagnoses. What finding would most specifically point to acne vulgaris instead?
opts: Open or closed comedones
Correct. Acne vulgaris is more likely when open or closed comedones are present. Perioral dermatitis produces grouped monomorphic papules, papulovesicles, or papulopustules without comedones.
Scale on scalp and nasolabial folds
Prominent scale at those sites describes seborrheic dermatitis, the third differential listed, rather than acne.
Papulopustules on the face
Papulopustules occur in perioral dermatitis, rosacea, and acne alike. A finding common to all three differentials cannot select among them.
Central erythema with telangiectasia
Central facial erythema, flushing, telangiectasia, papulopustules, or ocular symptoms describe rosacea, which is a different item on the differential.
D.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 100

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
D.q: A 34-year-old man with suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever has blood drawn before treatment is started. What laboratory abnormalities are characteristic, and what is the gold standard diagnostic test?
opts: Hypernatraemia and hyperglycaemia
The sodium abnormality is a mild hyponatraemia, and glucose is not a described feature.
Thrombocytopenia with a normal white count

Correct. Those are the characteristic laboratory findings, and the indirect immunofluorescence assay is the gold standard. Cerebrospinal fluid may show leukocytosis, moderately elevated protein, and normal glucose.
Eosinophilia with raised immunoglobulin E
Eosinophilia with raised immunoglobulin E suggests parasitic or atopic disease rather than a rickettsial infection.
Leukocytosis with thrombocytosis
The white cell count is characteristically normal with an increase in bands, and the platelet count falls rather than rises. Expecting a raised white count would argue against the diagnosis wrongly.
D.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 85

D.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 31-year-old woman has recurrent crops of intensely itchy 1 to 2 mm vesicles on the lateral aspects of her fingers and palms. They persist for several weeks, dry up, and then peel. Between episodes her hands are dry but clear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Irritant contact dermatitis
Irritant dermatitis produces a glazed, well-demarcated eruption with erythema and scaling at the site of exposure. It does not produce recurrent crops of deep-seated vesicles that peel.
Scabies
Scabies favours the finger webs and volar wrists with burrows and intense nocturnal itch, and it does not run in self-limited crops that peel and clear.
Dyshidrotic eczema

Correct. Dyshidrotic eczema produces intensely pruritic deep-seated vesicles on the palms, lateral fingers, and soles, classically described as tapioca vesicles. They persist for weeks, desiccate, and resolve with desquamation.
Bullous pemphigoid
Bullous pemphigoid produces tense 1 to 3 cm bullae on the trunk and flexures of patients over 60, not millimetre vesicles on the finger margins of a young adult.
D.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 65

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
D.q: A 42-year-old woman has central facial papules and pustules, and the clinician looks for the one lesion type that would settle whether this is acne. What is the hallmark lesion of acne vulgaris, and why does it matter diagnostically?
opts: The nodule, whose presence defines the diagnosis
Nodules occur in severe acne and drive the decision to use isotretinoin, but they are a severity marker rather than the hallmark that identifies the disease.
The comedone, whose absence argues against acne and toward rosacea

Correct. Comedones are the hallmark of acne vulgaris, and the differential specifically distinguishes rosacea by papules and pustules in the middle third of the face with telangiectasias, flushing, and an absence of comedones.
The pustule, whose absence argues against acne
Pustules are among the inflammatory lesions of acne but are shared with rosacea, folliculitis, and perioral dermatitis. They cannot serve as the distinguishing lesion.
The papule, which is unique to acne among facial eruptions
Papules occur across acne, rosacea, perioral dermatitis, and folliculitis. Acne is described as polymorphic, with several lesion types present at once.
D.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 13

D.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 61-year-old man has several intensely itchy, well-demarcated coin-shaped plaques 2 to 4 cm on both lower legs, with prominent scale and crusting. Each plaque is uniform throughout, with no clearing in the middle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Nummular eczema
Correct. Nummular eczema produces intensely pruritic round coin-shaped plaques 1 to 10 cm, most often on the extremities, and the plaques are uniform in appearance without central clearing.
Psoriasis
Plaque psoriasis produces well-demarcated salmon-pink plaques with adherent silvery scale on extensor elbows and knees, sacrum, and scalp rather than scattered coin-shaped lesions of the lower legs.
Pityriasis rosea
Pityriasis rosea follows a herald patch with a truncal eruption along the rib lines, and its lesions clear centrally leaving a collarette of scale.
Tinea corporis
Tinea corporis is the main differential and looks very similar, but it has an annular appearance with central clearing. Uniformity throughout is what separates them.
D.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 72

D.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
D.q: A 20-year-old man has hypopigmented scaly macules over the upper back and shoulders confirmed as pityriasis versicolor. What is first-line treatment, and when is systemic therapy appropriate?
opts: Topical first line; oral if refractory

Correct. Topical therapy is first line, including ketoconazole shampoo or cream, selenium sulfide, zinc pyrithione, ciclopirox, or topical terbinafine. Systemic therapy with oral fluconazole or itraconazole is reserved for extensive, recurrent, or topical-refractory disease.
A high-potency topical corticosteroid
Corticosteroid exposure is listed among the factors that make the condition more common, alongside heat, humidity, oily skin, sweating, and immunosuppression.
Oral terbinafine first line
Oral terbinafine is specifically not effective for this organism, even though topical terbinafine is among the topical options. Malassezia is a yeast rather than a dermatophyte.
Oral fluconazole for everyone
Systemic therapy is reserved rather than routine, and it requires review of hepatic risk, pregnancy status, and drug interactions that most patients do not need to undergo.
D.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 82

D.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
D.q: A 49-year-old woman is being counselled after a melanoma diagnosis and asks what most determines her outlook. What is the dominant prognostic variable?
opts: Fitzpatrick skin type
Skin type predicts baseline ultraviolet sensitivity and contributes to risk, but it does not determine prognosis once a melanoma is diagnosed.
Lesion diameter
Diameter is the D of the ABCDE rule and a screening feature, but it is not the prognostic variable that drives survival.
Anatomic subtype
Subtype describes the growth pattern and typical site. Thickness remains the dominant prognostic variable across subtypes.
Breslow thickness

Correct. Survival drops sharply with increasing Breslow thickness and with nodal or distant spread. Breslow thickness is the dominant prognostic variable and must be accurately measured at the time of initial biopsy — which is why a shave biopsy that transects the base can compromise staging.
D.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 55

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 2-week-old neonate develops blisters at sites of handling and diapering, and genetic testing is planned. Which subtype carries the greatest long-term risk of squamous cell carcinoma and requires the most intensive multidisciplinary surveillance?
opts: Acquired epidermolysis bullosa
Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita is an autoimmune rather than inherited disease and falls outside the four inherited types classified by cleavage level.
Epidermolysis bullosa simplex

Simplex disease results from keratin 5 and 14 mutations with intraepidermal cleavage, is localised to the palms and soles, and heals without scarring. Absence of scarring is why it does not carry the same malignancy burden.
Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa

Correct. Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa causes severe scarring, and the multidisciplinary team includes haematology and oncology specifically for squamous cell carcinoma surveillance. Scarring subtypes carry the malignancy risk.
Junctional epidermolysis bullosa

Junctional disease is generalised with poor wound healing, nail dystrophy, and enamel defects, and it is severe. But the scarring that drives squamous cell carcinoma surveillance characterises the dystrophic form.
D.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 30

D.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
D.q: A 60-year-old man with diabetes has three thickened, discoloured, crumbling toenails with distal onycholysis. He asks for oral terbinafine. What must be done first?
opts: Start terbinafine empirically

Dermatophytes, especially Trichophyton rubrum, do cause most cases, which makes empiric treatment tempting. But confirming first avoids months of hepatically monitored therapy for a nail that was never fungal.
Obtain a Wood's lamp examination
A Wood lamp evaluates pigment change in selected fungal and bacterial infections and may support Microsporum scalp infection. It is not the confirmatory test for nail disease.
Confirm the fungus first

Correct. Fungus must be confirmed before oral therapy, since many dystrophic nails are not fungal. Testing options include potassium hydroxide microscopy, periodic acid-Schiff stain of nail clippings, fungal culture, or polymerase chain reaction, sampling the most proximal accessible diseased nail bed.
Remove the nails surgically first
Nail avulsion is not the described first step. Confirming the diagnosis governs whether systemic therapy is justified.
D.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 51

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 42-year-old man develops an exaggerated sunburn-like reaction on sun-exposed skin within hours of starting a new medication. The reaction is dose-dependent and occurred on the very first exposure. What mechanism is responsible?
opts: Phytophotodermatitis from plant contact
Phytophotodermatitis follows contact with furanocoumarins in plants such as limes, celery, and parsley. It requires a chemical contactant rather than a systemic drug.
Photoallergy, immunologic and needing sensitisation

The two mechanisms are swapped. A reaction on first exposure that is dose-dependent cannot be an immunologic photoallergy, which requires prior sensitisation, and photopatch testing is aimed at photoallergy rather than phototoxicity.
Phototoxicity, non-immunologic and dose-dependent

Correct. Phototoxicity is non-immunologic and dose-dependent — the drug absorbs ultraviolet energy, generating reactive oxygen species and direct cellular damage that resembles an exaggerated sunburn. Photopatch testing is the gold standard for photoallergy, the other mechanism.
Polymorphous light eruption

Polymorphous light eruption is idiopathic rather than drug-induced, and antinuclear antibody testing is performed to exclude lupus rather than to confirm the eruption. The temporal link to a new medication points to a drug reaction.
D.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 98

D.io: 3 — Define posttest probability
D.q: A clinician estimates the likelihood of a condition in a 60-year-old woman before ordering a test, then revises that estimate once the result returns. How do pretest and posttest probability differ?
opts: Posttest ignores the clinical picture
Posttest probability depends on where the patient started, which is why pretest probability from history, risk factors, and prevalence matters.
They are the same quantity
They are distinct quantities, and the difference between them is precisely what a test contributes.
Pretest applies only to screening
Pretest probability applies to any clinical question, including diagnostic testing that complements history and physical examination.
Pretest is before the result, posttest after

Correct. Pretest probability is the likelihood of a condition before the test result is known, informed by signs and symptoms, history and risk factors, and how common the condition is in the population. Posttest probability is the likelihood after the result is known.
D.cite: 1. svClinical Reasoning and Problem Solving.pptx, Slide 9

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pigmented skin lesions
D.q: A 36-year-old man with a family history of melanoma has more than a hundred naevi. Several are at least 6 mm with irregular, indistinct borders and variation in colour within a single lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Dysplastic naevus

Correct. Dysplastic melanocytic naevi are at least 5 mm with irregular indistinct borders, common in Caucasians, with family history as a risk factor. Dysplastic nevus syndrome may produce over 100 naevi by adolescence.
Malignant melanoma
Melanoma cannot be excluded on inspection, which is why changing or developing lesions are biopsied, but the described set of many similar atypical naevi defines the dysplastic phenotype.
Congenital melanocytic naevus
Congenital naevi are evident at birth or shortly after rather than appearing in numbers through adolescence.
Common acquired melanocytic naevus
Common acquired naevi are usually under 6 mm with homogeneous surface and colour and sharp demarcation.
D.cite: CMS I Pigmented Skin Lesions - Shahsv-2.pptx, Slide 43

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
D.q: A 16-year-old girl has multiple 1 to 2 mm firm skin-coloured papules symmetrically distributed on the lower eyelids that appeared around puberty. What is the origin of these lesions?
opts: Hyperplasia of sebaceous glands around a central pore
Sebaceous hyperplasia produces whitish-yellow or skin-coloured papules with a central dell, typically in older adults rather than at puberty.
Benign neoplasms of eccrine ducts
Correct. Syringomas are benign neoplasms of eccrine sweat ducts. They appear at puberty and are more common in females, presenting as multiple 1 to 2 mm papules and usually asymptomatic.
Collections of lipid-laden macrophages

Lipid-laden macrophages form xanthelasma, which appears as soft yellow cholesterol plaques and is on the syringoma differential — but xanthelasma is yellow and plaque-like rather than small firm papules.
Benign neoplasms of apocrine glands
Apocrine gland inflammation characterises hidradenitis suppurativa. Syringomas arise from the eccrine duct.
D.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 58

D.io: b — Discuss unique considerations of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus skin infections, including risk factors, presentation, and treatment
D.q: A furuncle on the neck of a 37-year-old man is incised and drained, and the culture grows methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Which oral regimens are appropriate?
opts: Dicloxacillin or cephalexin
Dicloxacillin and cephalexin are the empiric oral agents for ordinary staphylococcal furuncles and carbuncles, and they are beta-lactams — precisely the class methicillin resistance defeats.
Penicillin V or amoxicillin
Penicillin V is the drug for erysipelas, where group A streptococcus is the organism. Neither agent covers methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, doxycycline, or clindamycin
Correct. When methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is cultured or suspected, the oral options given are trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, doxycycline, and clindamycin.
Topical mupirocin alone
Mupirocin ointment applied to the nares is used to address the Staphylococcus aureus carrier state in recurrent folliculitis. It is not adequate treatment for a drained methicillin-resistant abscess.
D.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 66

D.io: c — Identify medical care strategies for cutaneous viral and fungal infections for infant, child, adolescent, adult and elderly populations
D.q: A 6-year-old girl with varicella is febrile and uncomfortable, and her father asks what he may give her. What analgesic caution applies?
opts: Give systemic corticosteroids
Systemic corticosteroids are not part of varicella management, and immunosuppression during an active viral infection carries clear risk.
Give antivirals instead of analgesia
Early oral antivirals are considered for higher-risk patients rather than all children, and they do not substitute for symptom relief.
Avoid aspirin; caution with ibuprofen

Correct. Management is supportive, avoiding aspirin in children and using caution with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Early oral antivirals are considered for higher-risk patients and intravenous acyclovir for severe disease.
Avoid all analgesics
Supportive care is the mainstay and symptom relief is appropriate; it is aspirin specifically that is avoided, with caution around non-steroidal agents.
D.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 87

D.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
D.q: A 24-year-old man has painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on the buttock that have broken down into shallow ulcers. He asks whether the location tells him which virus type he has. What is the correct response?
opts: Either type causes either site

Correct. Either herpes simplex virus type can cause oral or genital infection, and lesion location does not reliably determine type. Infections can occur anywhere on the skin, and typing requires a type-specific test.
The vesicle appearance identifies the type
Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base breaking down to shallow painful ulcers is the appearance of both types. Morphology does not distinguish them.
Genital lesions are always type 2

This is the common assumption the lecture corrects. Type 1 causes a substantial share of genital infection, and acting on location alone gives false reassurance about transmission and recurrence patterns.
The prodrome identifies the type
Tenderness, pain, mild paraesthesia, or burning before the lesions appear is characteristic of herpes simplex virus generally rather than of one type.
D.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 112

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
D.q: A 55-year-old man with diabetes presents with an extremely painful lesion on the back of the neck. Examination shows a deep, indurated plaque with several separate openings draining pus. He has malaise, chills, and a fever of 38.4 degrees Celsius. What is the lesion?
opts: A cutaneous abscess
The lesion is identified correctly but antibiotics alone leave the collection undrained. Incision and drainage is the mainstay, with antibiotics as an adjunct.
A carbuncle

Correct. A carbuncle is two or more confluent furuncles with separate heads, arising in several hair follicles, and systemic symptoms are more common with a carbuncle than a furuncle. Incision and drainage is the mainstay, supported by oral antibiotics.
Folliculitis
Folliculitis is superficial inflammation of the follicle producing small pustules pierced by a central hair, not a deep indurated plaque with several draining openings and systemic symptoms.
A furuncle

A furuncle is a deep-seated abscess of a single hair follicle and adjacent subcutaneous tissue, presenting as a firm tender nodule with a single opening. The multiple separate heads here define a carbuncle.
D.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 67

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
D.q: A 52-year-old man living in a shelter has linear excoriations of the back and waist, while a 6-year-old girl in the same clinic has an itchy scalp. How does the presentation of pediculosis corporis differ from that of pediculosis capitis?
opts: Spread by head-to-head contact

Direct head-to-head contact is the primary route for head lice. Body lice are carried in the seams of clothing and bedding, which is why that infestation is associated with crowding and infrequent laundering rather than with close head contact.
It is always asymptomatic
Pubic lice are often asymptomatic or produce mild symptoms; body lice cause pruritus with excoriation.
Linear excoriations of the back and waist

Correct. Body lice produce pruritus with linear excoriations primarily on the back, neck, shoulders, and waist, and post-inflammatory pigmentation in chronic cases. Head lice affect the scalp with pruritus, low-grade fever, regional lymphadenopathy, and irritability.
Burrows in the finger webs

Burrows in the finger webs are the pathognomonic lesion of scabies, produced by a mite tunnelling through the stratum corneum. Body lice live in clothing and feed on the skin without burrowing, so they leave linear excoriations rather than tunnels.
D.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 26

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 31-year-old man of Northern European ancestry presents with an intensely pruritic, burning eruption of grouped small vesicles and papules symmetrically distributed over the elbows, knees, and buttocks. Most lesions are excoriated. He has autoimmune thyroid disease. What direct immunofluorescence finding is expected on perilesional skin?
opts: No deposits; mites on scraping
That describes scabies, which is on the differential because it also itches intensely. Scabies shows burrows in the web spaces and a positive skin scraping with no immunoglobulin A deposits.
Granular immunoglobulin A in dermal papillae

Correct. Dermatitis herpetiformis is caused by immunoglobulin A antibodies against epidermal transglutaminase in genetically susceptible individuals consuming gluten. The immune complexes deposit in the dermal papillae, and perilesional direct immunofluorescence showing granular immunoglobulin A is the gold standard test.
Net-like intercellular immunoglobulin G

A net-like intercellular pattern is the pemphigus finding, reflecting antibodies against keratinocyte adhesion molecules. Pemphigus presents with flaccid bullae and mucosal erosions rather than a pruritic extensor eruption.
Linear immunoglobulin G at the basement membrane

Linear immunoglobulin G and complement C3 at the basement membrane zone is the bullous pemphigoid pattern, and the differential states explicitly that direct immunofluorescence distinguishes the two. Bullous pemphigoid also produces tense blisters in the elderly rather than grouped excoriated vesicles on extensor surfaces.
D.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 125

D.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
D.q: A 54-year-old man has a pigmented lesion on the upper back that his wife says has changed. Examination shows an 11 mm lesion whose halves do not match, with a notched border and brown, black, and blue-grey areas within it. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Dysplastic naevus
A dysplastic naevus has irregular indistinct borders but does not typically show blue-grey areas within it or a documented change, and biopsy is what separates them.
Seborrheic keratosis
Seborrheic keratoses have a uniform stuck-on velvety surface with comedone-like openings on dermoscopy rather than asymmetry and colour variegation.
Malignant melanoma

Correct. The lesion meets the ABCDE criteria: asymmetry, an irregular notched border, colour variegation with brown, black, and blue within one lesion, a diameter over 6 mm, and evolution reported by a family member.
Solar lentigo
Solar lentigines are uniformly pigmented flat macules; a lesion that has diverged from its uniform neighbours is what raises melanoma.
D.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 46

D.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 24-year-old man is diagnosed with pityriasis rosea. The eruption began four days ago and is mildly itchy. He is otherwise well and not pregnant-exposed or immunocompromised. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Reassurance, with an antihistamine for itch

Correct. Pityriasis rosea is self-limited and the mainstay is reassurance. Oral antihistamines or topical steroids can be used cautiously for pruritus, and phototherapy or natural sunlight may help if begun in the first week of the eruption.
Reassurance alone, no treatment for itch

Reassurance is the correct foundation but this stops one step short. The itch is treatable, and declining to address a symptom the patient has reported leaves him uncomfortable for the several weeks the eruption lasts.
Oral terbinafine
Terbinafine treats dermatophyte infection. Tinea corporis is the classic mimic of the herald patch, but the diagnosis here is already established and pityriasis rosea is not a fungal disease.
Oral acyclovir for all patients
Acyclovir is reserved for severe cases, consistent with the suspected viral aetiology. Routine antiviral therapy for a mild self-limited eruption is not indicated.
D.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 171

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 31-year-old woman with biopsy-confirmed erythema nodosum has bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest radiograph together with fever and arthralgia. What is the most appropriate referral?
opts: Infectious disease, for probable endemic mycosis
Infectious disease referral is for endemic mycoses or tuberculosis, both of which can cause erythema nodosum. The specific triad here names a different syndrome.
Gastroenterology, for probable inflammatory bowel disease

Gastroenterology referral is appropriate when inflammatory bowel disease is suspected, and inflammatory bowel disease is a genuine systemic association. But it would not explain bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.
Dermatology, for repeat biopsy
Dermatology referral is for atypical or biopsy-confirmed cases, and a biopsy has already been done. Repeating it would not address the systemic findings.
Pulmonology or rheumatology, for probable Löfgren syndrome

Correct. Löfgren syndrome is the association referred to pulmonology or rheumatology. The combination of erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, fever, and arthralgia is its recognised presentation.
D.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 45

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
D.q: A 66-year-old man with cellulitis of the leg has an area that is tense, cyanotic, and bronzed with blanching. What is the significance of this finding?
opts: The expected look of resolving cellulitis
Resolving cellulitis fades from erythema without becoming tense, cyanotic, or bronzed. Mistaking necrosis for improvement is the error that delays the surgery this patient needs.
Devitalised tissue; antibiotics cannot reach it
Correct. Devitalised tissue that is tense, cyanotic, necrotic, bronzed, and blanched will not be perfused, so antibiotics will not get to the site. Surgical debridement is required.
Deep vein thrombosis; anticoagulate
Deep vein thrombosis produces swelling and pain but not bronzed necrotic skin, and anticoagulation would not address non-perfused devitalised tissue.
Increase the dose and observe
Increasing the dose does not solve the problem, which is that no blood is reaching the tissue to carry any dose of any antibiotic there.
D.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 111

D.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
D.q: A 68-year-old woman describes three days of burning pain in a band across her left flank, followed by an eruption. Examination shows grouped vesicles on an erythematous base confined to a single band that stops abruptly at the midline. What are the three clinical phases of this condition?
opts: Prodromal fever, generalised eruption, desquamation
Generalised eruption and desquamation describe other conditions. Herpes zoster is characteristically dermatomal, and its hallmark is that it does not cross the midline.
Pre-eruptive, acute eruptive, postherpetic neuralgia

Correct. The pre-eruptive phase is characterised by dysesthesia or pain within the affected dermatome with lesion onset by 48 to 72 hours; the acute eruptive phase produces grouped herpetiform vesicles on an erythematous base with new lesions forming over 3 to 5 days; and postherpetic neuralgia is the chronic phase.
Pre-eruptive, eruptive, and scarring
Vesicles may eventually scar if inflammation is intense, but scarring is a possible outcome rather than a named clinical phase. The recognised third phase is postherpetic neuralgia.
Incubation, contagious, and latency
Latency is part of the pathophysiology — the virus remains latent in cranial nerve or dorsal root ganglia — but it is not one of the three clinical phases of the disease episode.
D.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 97

D.io: b — Identify medical care strategies for pigmented skin lesions in adult and elderly populations
D.q: A 70-year-old woman has several beige to dark brown papules and plaques 5 to 15 mm on the trunk that feel velvety and appear stuck onto the skin surface. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Seborrheic keratoses

Correct. Seborrheic keratoses are benign papules and plaques, beige to brown to black, 2 to 20 mm in diameter, feeling velvety or warty and appearing stuck or pasted onto the skin. They are common in older adults and are easily mistaken for neoplasms.
Malignant melanoma

The stuck-on appearance and velvety texture are characteristic of a benign keratosis, though the resemblance to neoplasm is exactly why the lesion is taught. Genuine asymmetry, border irregularity, or colour variation would change the assessment.
Solar lentigines
Solar lentigines are macules — flat, without elevation. These lesions are raised papules and plaques with a palpable velvety surface.
Dermatosis papulosa nigrans
Dermatosis papulosa nigrans lesions are identical to small seborrheic keratoses but are 1 to 5 mm and occur on the face and neck rather than the trunk.
D.cite: CMS I Pigmented Skin Lesions - Shahsv-2.pptx, Slide 17

D.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
D.q: A 36-year-old man with untreated human immunodeficiency virus infection has multiple red-purple macules and plaques on the trunk. Oral examination reveals similar lesions on the hard palate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Kaposi sarcoma

Correct. Kaposi sarcoma develops in the cells lining blood and lymph vessels and is associated with human herpesvirus 8, producing red or purple macules, plaques, or nodules on skin or mucous membranes. Hard palate lesions are common and may be the presenting site.
Purpura
Purpura is a non-blanching deposit of blood rather than a proliferative vascular tumour, and it does not form palpable plaques on the palate.
Bacillary angiomatosis
Bacillary angiomatosis is on the differential in advanced immunodeficiency but produces friable vascular papules and responds to antibiotics.
Cherry angiomas
Cherry angiomas are small smooth deep red papules of the trunk that increase with age and do not involve mucosa.
D.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 64

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
D.q: A 5-year-old boy has several lesions around the nose and mouth. Examination shows golden-yellow adherent crusts over shallow erosions, with palpable regional lymphadenopathy. He is afebrile and there are only four lesions. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Oral cephalexin

Cephalexin is the oral drug of choice for children, but oral therapy is reserved for more extensive disease. Four lesions is a limited number, so topical treatment is preferred and carries fewer side effects.
Topical mupirocin over the intact crusts
The agent and route are right but the technique is wrong, and it matters: crusts must be removed first or the ointment cannot reach the infected erosion beneath.
Topical mupirocin, removing crusts first

Correct. Topical therapy is used for a single or limited number of non-bullous lesions, and mupirocin ointment is adequate for most cases of impetigo and as effective as oral therapy with fewer side effects. Crusts should be removed before applying it.
Oral penicillin V

Treatment should cover both staphylococci and streptococci, and penicillin V does not cover Staphylococcus aureus. Penicillin V is the drug for erysipelas, where group A streptococcus is the organism.
D.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 94

D.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
D.q: A 63-year-old man has had erythematous scaly patches and plaques on the trunk for four years, several larger than 5 cm. They have been treated as psoriasis and eczema without lasting response, and pruritus is prominent. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Tinea corporis
Tinea corporis produces annular plaques with an advancing scaly border and central clearing, and a potassium hydroxide preparation would be positive.
Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma

Correct. Mycosis fungoides begins in the skin and may remain confined there for years, producing localised or generalised erythematous patches or scaly plaques frequently over 5 cm on the trunk. Chronicity, treatment resistance, and large or oddly distributed lesions are the discriminators.
Secondary syphilis
Secondary syphilis produces a widespread eruption often involving palms and soles over weeks rather than fixed plaques persisting for years.
Eczematous dermatitis
Eczematous dermatitis is also on the differential and is likewise separated by chronicity and treatment resistance.
D.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 70

D.io: 4 — Discuss clinical principles and decision-making
D.q: A clinician searches for published evidence to answer a specific question about a 65-year-old smoker with chest pain and haemoptysis, and finds none that applies. What are the limitations of applying evidence-based medicine at the bedside?
opts: It is time consuming and evidence is often unavailable
Correct. The limitations given are that the process is time consuming and that many clinical questions do not have relevant evidence to answer them.
It applies only to surgical decisions
The framework applies across clinical questions, with the worked example being whether a chest radiograph or computed tomography better evaluates a smoker with chest pain and haemoptysis.
It always answers definitively but is expensive
The difficulty is that many questions lack relevant evidence, so a definitive answer is often exactly what is not available.
It cannot be combined with guidelines
Clinical guidelines are common practice and sit alongside evidence appraisal rather than being incompatible with it.
D.cite: 1. svClinical Reasoning and Problem Solving.pptx, Slide 22

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
D.q: A 40-year-old man in Connecticut develops an expanding erythematous oval lesion 8 cm across with central clearing and a darker punctate centre at the site of a recent tick bite. What stage is this?
opts: Stage 3, late persistent infection
Stage 2 occurs days to weeks later and involves the skin, central nervous system, cardiac, musculoskeletal, and ocular systems. A solitary erythema migrans lesion is stage 1.
Stage 1, early localised infection

Correct. Stage 1 early localised infection is characterised by erythema migrans, a lesion greater than 5 cm that expands with central clearing and often a darker punctate centre, also called a bull's-eye. A patient with this lesion should be diagnosed and treated on that basis, and testing is most helpful in patients from non-endemic regions with non-diagnostic symptoms.
Stage 2, early disseminated infection
The staging is right but withholding treatment is wrong and consequential. Serology may be negative early, and delay permits progression to disseminated disease.
Cellulitis at the bite site
Stage 3 occurs months to years later, with monoarticular or oligoarticular arthritis of the knee or weight bearing joints as the classic manifestation.
D.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 72

D.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 42-year-old man has mild plaque psoriasis affecting the elbows and knees. He has not used any treatment. What is the most appropriate first-line approach?
opts: Methotrexate immediately

Methotrexate belongs to moderate-to-severe disease or to disease that has failed topical therapy. Starting an antimetabolite for untreated mild plaques on the elbows and knees treats far above the severity present.
Emollients, topical steroids, calcipotriene

Correct. First-line treatment of mild plaque psoriasis is emollients, topical steroids, and calcipotriene, a vitamin D analogue with the quickest action, with phototherapy using ultraviolet B best for smaller stubborn areas. Salicylic acid and coal tar are second line.
Salicylic acid and coal tar
Salicylic acid and coal tar are listed as second-line agents for mild disease. Starting with them skips the more effective first-line options.
A tapering course of oral prednisone
Systemic steroids carry a specific hazard in psoriasis, since pustular psoriasis may follow systemic steroid withdrawal, and that form is abrupt and life-threatening.
D.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 163

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 71-year-old man with a lifetime of outdoor work has multiple rough, scaly erythematous papules on the scalp and dorsal hands, each 2 to 8 mm, that feel like sandpaper when palpated. What molecular event is the critical step in their development?
opts: Ultraviolet-induced TP53 mutation

Correct. Actinic keratoses are intraepidermal keratinocytic dysplasias induced by cumulative ultraviolet B exposure, and ultraviolet-induced mutations in TP53 are the critical molecular event. They represent a field cancerisation process.
Hyperinsulinaemia driving keratinocyte growth
That mechanism produces insulin-resistant acanthosis nigricans through insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor cross-activation. It is unrelated to ultraviolet damage.
Immunoglobulin A complex deposition
Immunoglobulin A deposition in the dermal papillae is the mechanism of dermatitis herpetiformis, a gluten-driven blistering disease.
Ultraviolet-induced melanocyte proliferation

Localised melanocyte proliferation within the epidermis produces solar lentigines, which are benign pigmented macules rather than keratinocytic dysplasias. Both follow chronic ultraviolet exposure, which is why this is the closest wrong answer.
D.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 112

E.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
E.q: A 27-year-old man in equatorial Africa presents with rapidly progressive violaceous nodules on both legs. He is not known to have human immunodeficiency virus infection and is not taking immunosuppressive therapy. Which clinical form of Kaposi sarcoma is described as often aggressive and potentially rapidly fatal in young Black men in equatorial Africa?
opts: The iatrogenic form
The iatrogenic form occurs in the setting of immunosuppressive therapy, notably after transplantation, and is addressed in part by discussing immunosuppression reduction with the transplant team.
The classic form
The classic form affects older men with a chronic course and is rarely fatal, associated with human herpesvirus 8 in the setting of age-related immune senescence.
The endemic form

Correct. The endemic form is often aggressive disease in young Black men in equatorial Africa and can be rapidly fatal, in contrast to the classic form in older men, which follows a chronic course and is rarely fatal.
The epidemic form
The epidemic form is associated with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, and its cornerstone of treatment is immune restoration with antiretroviral therapy.
E.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 63

E.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
E.q: A 27-year-old woman has folliculitis of the thighs that has failed to respond to antibacterial treatment, and a hair is plucked from an affected follicle. What test should be performed on it?
opts: Direct immunofluorescence
Direct immunofluorescence detects immune deposits in autoimmune blistering disease. Folliculitis is an infectious or irritant process.
A potassium hydroxide wet mount

Correct. In resistant cases a potassium hydroxide wet mount using a plucked hair is used to rule out fungal, specifically dermatophyte, folliculitis. Culture and Gram stain from an unroofed pustule are also performed.
A Wood's lamp examination
Coral-red fluorescence identifies erythrasma caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum. It is not performed on a plucked hair and does not detect dermatophytes.
A Tzanck smear
A Tzanck smear evaluates vesicular lesions for herpesvirus changes and is used to rule out herpetic whitlow in paronychia. It is not the plucked-hair test.
E.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 44

E.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
E.q: A 28-year-old woman is prescribed topical permethrin for scabies. What counselling should be given about the response to treatment?
opts: Overnight to all skin; persistent itch means failure

The application is right but the interpretation is wrong, and it leads to unnecessary repeat treatment. Persistent post-scabietic pruritus is expected and is managed with mid to high potency corticosteroids or intralesional triamcinolone.
Overnight to all skin; itch may persist for weeks

Correct. Topical permethrin is applied overnight to the entire skin surface with special attention to creases. Most patients experience relief in about 3 days, but rash and pruritus may persist afterwards, which patients must be warned about or they will assume treatment failure.
To visible areas only; resolves in 24 hours
Both halves fail. Treatment must cover the entire skin surface because burrows are not all visible, and promising resolution in a day guarantees the patient concludes the drug did not work.
Twenty minutes then rinse; no other measures
Overnight application is required, and bedding and clothing should be washed or set aside for 14 days in a plastic bag in a warm area, with high heat of 60 degrees Celsius needed to kill mites.
E.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 19

E.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
E.q: A 55-year-old man has confirmed dermatophyte onychomycosis of two fingernails and four toenails. What is the usual duration of first-line oral terbinafine for each?
opts: Six weeks fingernails, twelve weeks toenails

Correct. Oral terbinafine is first-line for most dermatophyte nail disease, usually 6 weeks for fingernails and 12 weeks for toenails, with hepatic disease and interactions reviewed and baseline liver tests obtained per labelling and patient risk.
Twelve weeks fingernails, six weeks toenails
The two durations are swapped. Toenails grow more slowly and require the longer course, so reversing them under-treats the site that needs more time.
Two weeks for both
A two-week course is far too short for nail disease, and omitting the hepatic review discards the principal safety consideration for terbinafine.
Lifelong therapy
Defined courses are given, and itraconazole is available as an alternative. Indefinite systemic antifungal therapy is not the approach.
E.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 52

E.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
E.q: A 58-year-old woman has a melanoma on the calf with a Breslow thickness of 1.4 mm and is being planned for definitive local treatment. What are the recommended re-excision margins for melanoma by thickness?
opts: Margins set by lesion diameter
Breslow thickness is the dominant prognostic variable and what governs margins, not surface diameter.
No re-excision after the biopsy
Re-excision is the definitive local treatment; the initial biopsy establishes the diagnosis and thickness.
1 cm in situ, 2 cm under 1 mm, 3 cm over 1 mm
Each margin is inflated by roughly a centimetre, which would cause unnecessary tissue loss and reconstruction without oncological benefit.
0.5 to 1 cm in situ, 1 cm under 1 mm, 1 to 2 cm over

Correct. Definitive local treatment uses a 0.5 to 1 cm margin for in situ disease, 1 cm for tumours under 1 mm, and 1 to 2 cm for tumours over 1 mm. Expert-centre referral applies to melanoma deeper than 1 mm or with lymph node involvement.
E.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 52

E.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
E.q: A 30-year-old man is about to be started on carbamazepine for newly diagnosed epilepsy. Which human leukocyte antigen association should prompt caution before prescribing it?
opts: Human leukocyte antigen Cw6
Human leukocyte antigen Cw6 is seen in 90 percent of early-onset psoriasis and 50 percent of late-onset cases. It is a psoriasis susceptibility marker.
Human leukocyte antigen B27
Human leukocyte antigen B27 is frequently associated with psoriatic arthritis and the spondyloarthropathies. It has no role in predicting severe cutaneous drug reactions.
Human leukocyte antigen B*15:02

Correct. Human leukocyte antigen B*15:02 is the risk allele associated with carbamazepine, while human leukocyte antigen B*58:01 is associated with allopurinol. Both are listed risk factors for Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
Human leukocyte antigen B*58:01
That allele is the allopurinol association. The two are frequently confused because both appear together as risk factors, but pairing them with the wrong drug would misdirect the screening entirely.
E.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 80

E.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pigmented skin lesions
E.q: A 25-year-old woman has symmetrical, well-defined, completely white non-scaly macules and patches on the dorsal hands and around the mouth. They fluoresce under a Wood's lamp. Her mother has autoimmune thyroid disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Vitiligo

Correct. Vitiligo is an autoimmune disease causing depigmentation through T cell mediated destruction of melanocytes, producing asymptomatic white non-scaly macules and patches with distinct margins that fluoresce under a Wood's lamp, usually symmetrical.
Pityriasis versicolor
Pityriasis versicolor produces hypopigmented rather than completely depigmented macules WITH fine scale on scraping, on the upper trunk and shoulders.
Leprosy
Leprosy produces hypopigmented anaesthetic patches with nerve involvement and is far less likely in this setting.
Postinflammatory hypopigmentation
Postinflammatory change requires prior inflammation at the site and produces partial, indistinctly bordered pigment loss.
E.cite: CMS I Pigmented Skin Lesions - Shahsv-2.pptx, Slide 22

E.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
E.q: A 74-year-old man with a lifetime of outdoor work has multiple 0.3 to 0.5 cm pink papules on the scalp and dorsal hands. Several are more apparent to touch than to sight. One lesion is thick, indurated, and has begun to bleed. What does that single lesion most require?
opts: Biopsy

Correct. The most important distinction for actinic keratosis is early squamous cell carcinoma or carcinoma in situ, especially when a lesion is thick, indurated, ulcerated, enlarging, painful, bleeding, persistent, or recurrent. Those features change the lesion from one to treat destructively to one to sample.
Field-directed therapy

Field-directed therapy is indicated when multiple lesions occupy a field of sun-damaged skin, and it is appropriate for his burden generally. But it does not address the single lesion whose features suggest carcinoma.
Observation for one year
Annual review is a reasonable surveillance interval for stable disease. A bleeding indurated lesion has already declared itself and should not wait.
Reassurance
Actinic keratosis is premalignant and lies on a biologic continuum with keratinocyte carcinoma, so it is not benign, and this lesion in particular carries red-flag features.
E.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 13

E.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
E.q: A 38-year-old man with recurrent tinea pedis is being counselled on preventing further episodes. What patient education point is described as essential?
opts: Sharing antifungal foot powder with household members
Antifungal foot powder is used in the patient's own shoes. Sharing personal items is discouraged in dermatophyte infections generally.
Walking barefoot in community showers to allow air drying
Sandals should be used in community showers, since the infection spreads by contact with infected desquamated skin.
Drying between the toes after bathing

Correct. Drying between the toes after bathing is marked as essential, alongside antifungal foot powder for shoes, wearing open-toed sandals when possible, using sandals in community showers, and changing socks frequently.
Soaking the feet daily in warm water
Prolonged moisture is the predisposing condition rather than a treatment. Moisture control is a core part of management.
E.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 45

E.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
E.q: A 30-year-old woman has an asymptomatic ring of flesh-coloured to pink papules on the dorsum of her hand that has slowly enlarged over months. There is no scale, and a potassium hydroxide preparation is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Tinea corporis
Tinea corporis produces an annular plaque with an advancing SCALY border, and the negative potassium hydroxide preparation together with the absence of scale argues against it.
Granuloma annulare

Correct. Localised granuloma annulare produces flesh-coloured to erythematous papules in an annular ring on the dorsal hands, feet, and ankles, and it is characteristically asymptomatic and without scale.
Erythema multiforme
Erythema multiforme produces fixed targetoid lesions with three concentric zones, usually acute and often after herpes simplex virus infection.
Sarcoidosis
Cutaneous sarcoidosis can be annular but is far less common, and granuloma annulare is the expected diagnosis for an asymptomatic non-scaly ring on the dorsal hand.
E.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 50

E.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
E.q: A 34-year-old man presents with recurrent painful red nodules and draining lesions in both axillae and the groin. He has had four such episodes in the past six months and two lesions previously drained. He is obese and smokes. Examination shows inflamed nodules and several sinus tracts. What three elements establish the diagnosis?
opts: Typical lesions, distribution, and biopsy
Biopsy would show follicular occlusion by keratinous material, but it is explicitly not usually required. Requiring it would make a clinical diagnosis unnecessarily invasive.
Typical lesions, axilla and groin, recurrence

Correct. Hidradenitis suppurativa is primarily a clinical diagnosis requiring three key elements: typical lesions, characteristic distribution in the axilla and groin, and recurrence more than twice in six months. Biopsy is not usually required.
One abscess with a family history
One episode cannot satisfy the recurrence criterion, which is what separates this condition from an isolated furuncle or abscess.
Typical lesions, distribution, positive culture

The first two elements are right, which makes this the closest wrong answer, but the third is recurrence rather than culture. Hidradenitis suppurativa is an inflammatory process of the apocrine glands rather than a primary infection, and culture is not part of the diagnostic triad.
E.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 74

E.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
E.q: A 52-year-old woman has fine red lines on both cheeks that disappear when pressed with a glass slide. How is a telangiectasia defined, and what is its behaviour on pressure?
opts: A capillary proliferation forming a papule
Capillary proliferation producing a deep red papule describes a cherry angioma, which is a raised lesion rather than a dilated vessel.
A dilated capillary under 1 mm that does not blanch
The size and nature are right but the blanching is the key physical property, and getting it wrong would lead a clinician to mistake a dilated vessel for extravasated blood.
A congenital malformation
Telangiectasias are acquired vascular lesions and may be primary or secondary to numerous diseases.
A dilated capillary under 1 mm that blanches

Correct. Telangiectasias are acquired vascular lesions consisting of permanently dilated capillaries under 1 mm. They blanch, may be single or grouped with a central punctum, may be primary or secondary, and are associated with numerous diseases.
E.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 88

E.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
E.q: A 63-year-old woman has widespread tense bullae and a pruritic prodrome. The clinician plans a biopsy. What specimen and technique will best establish the diagnosis?
opts: Patch testing for an allergen
Patch testing diagnoses allergic contact dermatitis. Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune disease of the basement membrane rather than a delayed hypersensitivity to an external allergen.
Potassium hydroxide of blister fluid
A potassium hydroxide preparation detects fungal elements and has no role in an autoimmune blistering disease. Blister fluid is not the specimen that answers this question.
Bulla centre for immunofluorescence alone

Direct immunofluorescence requires perilesional tissue, because the immune deposits are demonstrated in skin adjacent to the blister rather than within the blister roof or base. Sampling the lesion centre alone risks a falsely negative study.
Lesion histology, perilesional immunofluorescence

Correct. Bullous pemphigoid is diagnosed by biopsying the lesion for histopathology and perilesional tissue for direct immunofluorescence examination. Serum indirect immunofluorescence or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay can identify anti-basement membrane zone antibodies.
E.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 124

E.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
E.q: A 49-year-old man has a warm, tender, erythematous area on the right lower leg with indistinct borders and surrounding oedema. What feature most reliably distinguishes cellulitis from erysipelas?
opts: Cellulitis has indistinct, unraised borders

Correct. Erysipelas involves the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics, producing a plaque raised above the surrounding skin with a clear line of demarcation. Cellulitis involves the deeper dermis and subcutaneous tissue and therefore has borders that are indistinct and not raised.
Only cellulitis produces fever
Fever occurs in both, and erysipelas characteristically produces high fever of 38 to 40 degrees Celsius with sudden onset within 48 hours of the skin changes.
Only erysipelas is streptococcal

Streptococcus pyogenes is the most common erysipelas organism, but group A beta-haemolytic streptococci also cause cellulitis alongside Staphylococcus aureus. The organism does not separate them reliably.
Cellulitis is bilateral, erysipelas unilateral
Cellulitis most commonly affects the lower leg and is almost never bilateral. Bilateral leg redness should prompt consideration of stasis dermatitis rather than either infection.
E.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 107

E.io: 7 — Recall counseling strategies to help patients adhere to treatment plans
E.q: A 61-year-old woman has not been taking a medication prescribed for her three months ago and is reluctant to say why. Which barriers to treatment and medication adherence should be considered?
opts: Cost, health literacy, and culture

Correct. Barriers to treatment and medication adherence include the cost and affordability of medications or services, low health literacy or lack of understanding, and cultural or religious considerations.
Barriers cannot be anticipated
The named barriers are precisely those a clinician can anticipate and address during counselling.
Cost of medications only
Cost is one barrier among several, and addressing it alone leaves understanding and cultural factors unaddressed.
Patient motivation only
Framing non-adherence as a motivational failing overlooks the structural and educational barriers explicitly listed.
E.cite: 1. svClinical Reasoning and Problem Solving.pptx, Slide 29

E.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
E.q: A 3-month-old infant with blistering at sites of minor friction is being investigated to establish where in the skin the split is occurring. What diagnostic test is considered the gold standard for establishing the level of cleavage in epidermolysis bullosa?
opts: Skin biopsy with transmission electron microscopy

Correct. Skin biopsy with transmission electron microscopy is the gold standard for determining the cleavage plane. Immunofluorescence antigen mapping localises missing or reduced proteins, and genetic testing is confirmatory and guides prognosis and family counselling.
Genetic testing alone
Genetic testing is confirmatory and guides prognosis and family counselling, but it is not the test that establishes where in the skin the split occurs.
Direct immunofluorescence for immunoglobulin A deposits

Granular immunoglobulin A in the dermal papillae is the finding of dermatitis herpetiformis. Epidermolysis bullosa is an inherited structural protein disorder rather than an immune deposition disease.
Immunofluorescence antigen mapping

Immunofluorescence antigen mapping is genuinely part of the workup and localises missing or reduced proteins, which makes it the closest wrong answer. But the gold standard for the cleavage plane itself is electron microscopy.
E.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 31

E.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
E.q: A 28-year-old woman has a single asymptomatic annular ring of flesh-coloured papules on the dorsum of the foot. What course should be expected?
opts: Lifelong immunosuppression is required
The course is right but the proportion is reversed — localised disease is the common form at about 75 percent, and the generalised or disseminated variant is the minority.
Progression to malignancy
The proportion is right, which makes this the closest wrong answer, but granuloma annulare is benign and self-limiting. An oncology referral is considered only if lymphoma is separately suspected.
Benign and self-limiting

Correct. The localised variant accounts for about 75 percent of cases, presenting as flesh-coloured to erythematous papules in an annular ring on the dorsal hands, feet, and ankles, and is asymptomatic. Granuloma annulare is a benign, self-limiting granulomatous dermatosis.
Invariable recurrence after clearing

Systemic therapy and phototherapy are reserved for generalised or treatment-resistant disease through a dermatology referral. Committing localised asymptomatic disease to systemic immunosuppression is far beyond what it needs.
E.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 50

E.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
E.q: An 18-year-old boy is prescribed a topical antibiotic for acne, and benzoyl peroxide is added to the regimen. Why is benzoyl peroxide recommended alongside topical or oral antibiotic therapy for acne?
opts: It is comedolytic and normalises keratinisation
Comedolysis and normalisation of hyperkeratinisation describe topical retinoids. Topical antimicrobials are explicitly described as not comedolytic.
It suppresses Cutibacterium and limits resistance

Correct. Benzoyl peroxide is keratolytic and anti-inflammatory and suppresses Cutibacterium acnes. It is recommended alongside antimicrobials specifically to reduce the risk of bacterial resistance, and combination products exist for that purpose.
It inhibits tyrosinase and lightens pigment
Tyrosinase inhibition with improvement of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is a property of azelaic acid.
It decreases sebum excretion
Decreased sebum excretion is the mechanism of isotretinoin, and oestrogen in combined oral contraceptives also decreases sebum production.
E.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 22

E.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
E.q: A 56-year-old man is found on routine examination to have several smooth, firm, deep red papules under 5 mm on the trunk that blanch with pressure. He has never noticed them and they are asymptomatic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Cherry angioma

Correct. Cherry angiomas are acquired vascular lesions formed by capillary proliferation, very common and increasing with age, appearing as smooth firm deep red papules under 5 mm on the trunk that blanch with pressure.
Nevus araneus
A spider angioma has a central arteriole with radiating capillaries and is associated with oestrogen excess or liver disease.
Pyogenic granuloma
Pyogenic granuloma grows rapidly after trauma, is friable, and bleeds spontaneously, most often on the head, neck, and fingers.
Petechiae
Petechiae are non-blanching deposits of blood 1 to 2 mm, whereas these lesions blanch.
E.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 86

E.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
E.q: A 55-year-old man presents with a single intensely itchy patch on the posterior neck that has been present for over a year. He describes rubbing it frequently, particularly when stressed or trying to fall asleep. Examination shows a well-demarcated thickened plaque with exaggerated skin markings, excoriation, scale, and altered pigmentation. What is the central principle of management?
opts: Reassurance alone

Recurrence is expected unless the initiating itch is controlled, and telling a patient simply to stop scratching without addressing sleep, anxiety, neuropathic symptoms, and the primary dermatosis rarely succeeds.
Break the itch-scratch cycle

Correct. Lichen simplex chronicus results from repeated rubbing and scratching, so management centres on breaking the itch-scratch cycle with education, treatment of the trigger, emollients, behavioural substitution, nail care, and safe physical occlusion, alongside a limited course of an appropriate potent topical corticosteroid.
Indefinite potent topical corticosteroid

A potent topical corticosteroid is used, but for a limited course. Continuing it indefinitely invites atrophy, striae, and telangiectasia, and it leaves the scratching behaviour that drives the plaque entirely unaddressed.
An oral antifungal
The thickening here is lichenification from chronic rubbing, not a fungal infection. Treating it as tinea leaves the true driver untouched and delays effective management.
E.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 183

E.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
E.q: A 28-year-old woman has multiple smooth, slightly elevated, flat-topped, light-brown papules across her forehead and dorsal hands. She reports they seemed to multiply along the line where she shaves her legs. What form is this?
opts: Molluscum contagiosum
Molluscum lesions are dome-shaped pearly papules with central umbilication rather than flat-topped papules, and they are caused by a poxvirus rather than human papillomavirus.
Seborrheic keratoses
Seborrheic keratoses have a stuck-on appearance with comedone-like openings and are not spread by shaving.
Flat warts

Correct. Flat warts are multiple smooth, slightly elevated, flat-topped, skin-coloured to light-brown papules common on the face, forehead, dorsal hands, and shins, and shaving can spread lesions through autoinoculation. Observation is reasonable because spontaneous resolution is likely.
Verruca vulgaris
Common warts are elevated round papules with a rough greyish surface, typically on the fingers and palms, rather than smooth flat-topped papules on the face and shins.
E.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 143

E.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
E.q: A 58-year-old woman has a translucent skin-coloured papule over the distal interphalangeal joint of her index finger, with a longitudinal groove in the adjacent nail. What is the nature of this lesion?
opts: An overgrowth of dense fibrous tissue
Overgrowth of dense fibrous tissue extending beyond wound margins describes a keloid.
An eccrine duct neoplasm
Eccrine duct neoplasms are syringomas, which appear at puberty as multiple small papules on the eyelids.
A pseudo-cyst of mucin extruded from the joint

Correct. Digital mucous cysts are pseudo-cysts without a cellular lining or true capsule. They represent extrusion of mucinous contents from a local joint space into the surrounding dermis, typically over the distal interphalangeal joint, and may distort the nail.
A true cyst lined by epithelium
Epithelial enclosure filled with keratin describes the epidermoid cyst. The absence of a true lining is what makes this lesion a pseudo-cyst.
E.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 107

E.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
E.q: A 50-year-old man has an intensely pruritic eruption of violaceous flat-topped papules on both wrists, and a biopsy is taken from one lesion. What histopathological finding is most characteristic?
opts: Granulomas around degenerated collagen
Palisaded granulomas around altered collagen describe granuloma annulare. That is a different reaction pattern entirely and does not produce pruritic violaceous flat-topped papules.
Subepithelial blistering with neutrophils

That description belongs to bullous pemphigoid, where light microscopy shows neutrophils aligned in a straight narrow row at the dermal-epidermal junction. Lichen planus produces a lymphocytic band rather than a neutrophilic line with blistering.
A band-like lymphocytic infiltrate

Correct. Biopsy in lichen planus shows band-like infiltration of lymphocytes in the dermis. Additional characteristic findings include hyperkeratosis without parakeratosis, vacuolisation of the basal layer, Civatte bodies in the lower epidermis, and saw-tooth shaped rete ridges.
Parakeratosis with neutrophilic microabscesses

Parakeratosis with neutrophilic collections is the psoriasis pattern. Lichen planus is specifically described as showing hyperkeratosis without parakeratosis, which makes this a precise inversion of the correct finding.
E.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 177

E.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
E.q: A 6-year-old unvaccinated boy has a generalised itchy eruption concentrated on the trunk, scalp, and face. Macules, papules, vesicles, and crusts are all visible at the same time. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Hand, foot and mouth disease
Hand, foot and mouth disease produces oral ulcers with vesicles on the palms and soles rather than a truncal eruption in mixed stages.
Scabies
Scabies produces intensely pruritic papules and burrows in the finger webs, wrists, and axillae over weeks, sparing the head and neck in adults.
Varicella

Correct. Primary varicella-zoster virus infection causes a generalised pruritic eruption in multiple stages of healing, with macules, papules, vesicles, and crusts appearing simultaneously and lesions concentrated on the trunk, scalp, and face.
Herpes zoster
Herpes zoster is reactivation confined to one or two adjacent dermatomes that stops abruptly at the midline, not a generalised eruption.
E.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 84

E.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
E.q: A 27-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has an abrupt eruption of small pustules on the thighs and buttocks after wearing occlusive workout clothing. Each pustule sits on an erythematous base and is pierced by a central hair. He is afebrile. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Furunculosis
A furuncle is a deep-seated abscess of the follicle and adjacent subcutaneous tissue, presenting as a painful fluctuant nodule rather than superficial pustules.
Acne vulgaris
Acne affects hormonally responsive sebaceous areas and its hallmark lesion is the comedone, which is not described.
Miliaria
Miliaria results from occluded eccrine ducts and produces tiny non-follicular vesicles or papules rather than pustules pierced by a hair.
Folliculitis

Correct. Folliculitis is inflammation within the wall and ostia of the hair follicle, producing small papules and pustules on an erythematous base pierced by a central hair, most often from Staphylococcus aureus. Diabetes and occlusive clothing are listed risk factors.
E.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 41
